domains.name: Drug classes: actions, adverse effects & contraindications
Insulin in type 2: start, titrate, intensify
Special situations: pregnancy, cancer, steroids, pancreatic, PTDM, MODY, Ramadan

banks.title: Insulin therapy in type 1 and type 2 diabetes

mcq.subtopic: ASCVD: cardioprotective agent irrespective of A1C
mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 4 years attends clinic 6 weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and ramipril 5 mg. He has stopped smoking and walks 30 minutes daily. He has had no hypoglycemia.

BP 124/76 mmHg, pulse 62/min, BMI 27.8 kg/m². Echocardiography: LVEF 55%, no heart failure symptoms.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best change to his glucose-lowering therapy?
hints: His A1C is already below 7%. Ask what else, besides glucose, the medication plan must now achieve.
ADA ties certain drug classes to established ASCVD 'irrespective of A1C' and regardless of metformin use.

explanation.summary: Established ASCVD calls for an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA with proven cardiovascular benefit, whatever the A1C and whether or not metformin is used; empagliflozin is the only such option offered.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Add empagliflozin. ADA Recommendation 9.7 (grade A) states that in adults with type 2 diabetes and established or high risk of ASCVD, the plan should include a medication with demonstrated benefit to reduce cardiovascular events (a GLP-1 RA and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor) for glycemic management and comprehensive cardiovascular risk reduction, irrespective of A1C. Figure 9.4 places this on the left-hand, 'cardiovascular and kidney risk reduction' side of the algorithm, and the text adds that it applies 'with or without metformin use'. Section 10 (Rec 10.40a–c) says the same. Table 9.2 lists canagliflozin and empagliflozin as the SGLT2 inhibitors with MACE benefit (EMPA-REG OUTCOME: 3-point MACE HR 0.86 in people with established CVD). A GLP-1 RA with proven benefit (dulaglutide, liraglutide or semaglutide) would have been an equally acceptable choice, but none is offered here. An A1C of 6.8% (51 mmol/mol) is not a reason to withhold the drug: the indication is cardiovascular, and because SGLT2 inhibitors do not cause hypoglycemia, adding one to metformin is safe at this A1C. Metformin can continue; the cardioprotective agent is added to it, not substituted for it.

distractors.B: Glimepiride is CV-safe but has no MACE benefit (Table 9.2: neutral) and adds hypoglycemia and weight gain in a man already at goal.
distractors.C: DPP-4 inhibitors are neutral for MACE (Table 9.2) and would not reduce his cardiovascular risk.
distractors.D: Being at the A1C goal does not remove the indication: Rec 9.7 applies irrespective of A1C, so leaving therapy unchanged is therapeutic inertia.
distractors.E: Pioglitazone has only 'potential benefit' for MACE in Table 9.2, causes fluid retention and weight gain, and there is no reason to stop metformin.

pearls: ASCVD, HF or CKD → SGLT2i and/or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit, irrespective of A1C and of metformin (Rec 9.7, Fig 9.4).
SGLT2i with MACE benefit in Table 9.2: canagliflozin and empagliflozin only.
Add the cardioprotective drug to metformin; do not wait for the A1C to rise.
explanation.objective: Select an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit for a person with type 2 diabetes and established ASCVD whose A1C is already at goal.

mcq.subtopic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 11 years and ischemic cardiomyopathy is referred by her cardiologist. Her LVEF is 30% and she has NYHA class II dyspnea. She takes sacubitril–valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 20 mg and metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. She has had no hypoglycemia, genital infections or recent hospital admissions.

BP 112/70 mmHg, pulse 66/min, BMI 29.5 kg/m². Mild ankle edema, clear lungs.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her glucose-lowering therapy?
hints: One comorbidity dominates the drug choice here, and it is not the A1C.
ADA names one class for HF with either reduced or preserved EF, for both glycemia and prevention of HF hospitalization.

explanation.summary: In type 2 diabetes with HFrEF, an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF benefit is recommended for glycemia and to prevent HF hospitalization, irrespective of A1C.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Dapagliflozin. ADA Recommendation 9.8 (grade A) states that adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure, with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, should receive an SGLT2 inhibitor for both glycemic management and prevention of HF hospitalization, irrespective of A1C. Section 10 (Rec 10.41a) adds that this reduces worsening HF and cardiovascular death. Table 9.2 lists HF benefit for canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and ertugliflozin, and dapagliflozin in DAPA-HF reduced worsening HF or cardiovascular death (HR 0.74) in people with EF ≤40%, with or without diabetes. Her eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² is well above the level at which an SGLT2 inhibitor can be started (≥20 per Rec 11.7a and Figure 9.4). Its glucose-lowering effect will be intermediate, which is acceptable because the main purpose is cardiac. Because she is on furosemide, check volume status and kidney function after starting (Table 9.2), and consider reducing the diuretic if she becomes volume-depleted. Metformin may continue in stable HF while eGFR stays above 30 (Rec 10.45).

distractors.A: Alogliptin gives no HF benefit; EXAMINE showed no significant rise in HF hospitalization, but the FDA advises considering stopping it if HF develops, so it is a poor choice in established HFrEF.
distractors.C: Glipizide is HF-neutral but adds hypoglycemia and weight and gives no cardiac benefit.
distractors.D: Basal insulin is not needed at A1C 7.6% without catabolic features, is HF-neutral at best and causes weight gain and hypoglycemia.
distractors.E: Pioglitazone increases the risk of HF and fluid retention; Table 9.2 says not to use it in the setting of HF.

pearls: HF (HFrEF or HFpEF) → SGLT2i irrespective of A1C (Rec 9.8, Rec 10.41a).
Avoid pioglitazone in HF; Table 9.2 lists a potential HF risk with saxagliptin.
Metformin may continue in stable HF if eGFR >30, but avoid it in unstable or hospitalized HF (Rec 10.45).
explanation.objective: Choose an SGLT2 inhibitor for a person with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old woman from Dammam with type 2 diabetes for 9 years has symptomatic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (LVEF 60%, elevated NT-proBNP, enlarged left atrium). Despite furosemide 40 mg daily she has NYHA class II–III dyspnea and was admitted twice last year with decompensated HF. She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily (for 14 months), losartan 100 mg and spironolactone 25 mg.

BP 128/78 mmHg, BMI 37.2 kg/m², waist 112 cm. Bilateral ankle edema.
mcq.question: Which change to her glucose-lowering plan is most likely to improve her heart failure symptoms and reduce further heart failure events?
hints: She already takes the class that every HF patient with diabetes should have. What second comorbidity drives the next choice?
For obesity plus symptomatic HFpEF, ADA gives a grade-A recommendation to an incretin-based drug with outcome data in exactly this population.

explanation.summary: Obesity with symptomatic HFpEF calls for a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide, grade A) or a GLP-1 RA with proven benefit (grade A for symptoms, B for events), irrespective of A1C; tirzepatide is the only such option.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Add tirzepatide. Rec 9.8 (SGLT2 inhibitor for HF) is already met. For obesity plus symptomatic HFpEF, ADA 2026 adds Rec 9.9a: the glucose-lowering plan should include a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit for HF-related symptoms and reduction in HF events, irrespective of A1C (grade A). Rec 9.9b gives the GLP-1 RA alternative (semaglutide; grade A for symptoms, B for events). Section 10 repeats both (Recs 10.44d–e). The evidence is SUMMIT: in people with HFpEF (EF ≥50%) and obesity, tirzepatide reduced the composite of CV death or worsening HF (HR 0.62), mostly through fewer worsening-HF events, and improved KCCQ symptom scores. The semaglutide trials (STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM) showed symptom and exercise-capacity gains. Tirzepatide also brings very high weight loss and very high glucose-lowering efficacy (Table 9.2) without hypoglycemia. Keep empagliflozin and metformin: the classes are complementary. When she is on a full tirzepatide dose, reassess the diuretic dose, because weight loss and lower filling pressures can lead to over-diuresis.

distractors.A: Basal insulin would lower glucose but causes weight gain, gives no HF benefit and is not needed at A1C 7.4%.
distractors.B: Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and increases HF risk; Table 9.2 says not to use it in HF.
distractors.C: Saxagliptin carries a 'potential risk' for HF in Table 9.2 (SAVOR-TIMI 53 HF-hospitalization signal).
distractors.E: 10 mg is the HF dose of empagliflozin; increasing to 25 mg adds a little glucose lowering but no further HF benefit, and does nothing for her obesity.

pearls: Obesity + symptomatic HFpEF → tirzepatide (Rec 9.9a, grade A) or a GLP-1 RA (Rec 9.9b), on top of the SGLT2i.
SUMMIT (tirzepatide) is an HF-events trial; STEP-HFpEF (semaglutide) is mainly a symptoms and function trial.
Review diuretic doses as weight falls on incretin therapy.
explanation.objective: Add a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist for a person with type 2 diabetes, obesity and symptomatic HFpEF who is already taking an SGLT2 inhibitor.

mcq.subtopic: CKD with albuminuria: SGLT2 inhibitor irrespective of A1C
mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 14 years and hypertension attends his annual review. Last year his metformin was reduced to 500 mg twice daily because his eGFR had fallen. He also takes losartan 100 mg (maximum dose), amlodipine 10 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg. He has no history of ASCVD, heart failure or hypoglycemia.

BP 132/78 mmHg, BMI 29.1 kg/m². Fundoscopy shows mild nonproliferative retinopathy.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step in his diabetes medication plan?

options.text: Increase metformin to 1,000 mg twice daily

hints: Interpret the kidney panel first: what CKD stage and albuminuria category does he have?
ADA recommends a kidney-protective class in CKD 'irrespective of A1C', and its eGFR floor for starting is well below his value.

explanation.summary: Confirmed CKD (eGFR 38, UACR >300 mg/g) on a maximal ARB calls for an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney benefit, irrespective of A1C.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Add dapagliflozin. He has CKD G3b with severely increased albuminuria (A3), confirmed on two samples. ADA Recommendation 9.10 (grade A) states that adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD (eGFR 20–60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or albuminuria) should use an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit, for glycemia and to slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular events, irrespective of A1C. Section 11 (Rec 11.7a) says SGLT2 inhibitors should be started at eGFR ≥20 and can continue until kidney failure. Dapagliflozin (DAPA-CKD), canagliflozin (CREDENCE) and empagliflozin (EMPA-KIDNEY) have dedicated kidney-outcome trials; Table 9.2 lists all three as beneficial for CKD progression. ADA notes that the glucose-lowering effect is reduced below eGFR 45, but the kidney and heart benefit remains, so his A1C of 7.0% is irrelevant to the decision. Expect a small early creatinine rise; do not stop the drug for a rise <30% without volume depletion (Section 11). He is also a candidate for finerenone (Rec 11.8: eGFR ≥25, albuminuria, on maximal RAS blockade), which can be started together with the SGLT2 inhibitor (Rec 11.9).

distractors.B: Glipizide gives no kidney or heart protection and increases hypoglycemia risk, which is higher in CKD.
distractors.C: Linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment but is neutral for CKD progression (Table 9.2), so it does not meet the cardiorenal indication.
distractors.D: Being at the A1C goal does not remove the indication: Rec 9.10 applies irrespective of A1C. Leaving therapy unchanged leaves his albuminuric CKD untreated.
distractors.E: ADA says to reduce the metformin dose once eGFR is <45 (and stop it below 30); doubling it at eGFR 38 contradicts ADA and exceeds KDIGO's half-maximum dose.

pearls: CKD (eGFR 20–60 and/or albuminuria) → SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit, irrespective of A1C (Rec 9.10).
Start SGLT2i at eGFR ≥20; glucose lowering fades below 45, but organ protection persists.
Albuminuria on maximal RAS blockade: consider finerenone too (Rec 11.8, 11.9).
explanation.objective: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor for kidney protection in type 2 diabetes with albuminuric CKD and an A1C at goal.

mcq.stem: A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has CKD followed by nephrology. Her eGFR has been stable at 17–19 mL/min/1.73 m² for a year and she is not on dialysis. She has never taken an SGLT2 inhibitor. She takes glipizide 5 mg daily, ramipril 10 mg, furosemide 40 mg, atorvastatin and calcitriol. Metformin was stopped 3 years ago. She reports two episodes of shakiness and sweating relieved by juice in the past month. BMI 30.4 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition for her glycemic management?
hints: Her eGFR is below two important starting thresholds. Which classes does that rule out?
ADA prefers one class at eGFR <30 because it lowers glucose regardless of kidney function, without hypoglycemia, and reduces cardiovascular events.

explanation.summary: At eGFR <30 a GLP-1 RA is preferred for glycemic management (low hypoglycemia risk, cardiovascular benefit); SGLT2 inhibitors are not started below eGFR 20 and metformin is contraindicated below 30.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Add semaglutide subcutaneously once weekly. ADA Recommendation 9.11 (grade B) states that in advanced CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) a GLP-1 RA is preferred for glycemic management because of its lower risk of hypoglycemia and its cardiovascular event reduction. GLP-1 RAs lower glucose regardless of kidney function, and Table 9.2 notes that dulaglutide, liraglutide and semaglutide need no dose adjustment for kidney function. Semaglutide also has a dedicated kidney-outcome trial (FLOW; primary kidney composite HR 0.76), although FLOW enrolled eGFR ≥25. Her other options are limited by her eGFR of 18. SGLT2 inhibitors are started only at eGFR ≥20 (Rec 11.7a, Figure 9.4), although they may be continued below that level if already established. Metformin is contraindicated below 30. When the GLP-1 RA is started, reassess glipizide (Rec 9.17): she already has hypoglycemia, and sulfonylureas accumulate in advanced CKD, so reducing or stopping glipizide is appropriate. Monitor kidney function if severe GI adverse effects cause volume depletion (Table 9.2).

distractors.A: SGLT2 inhibitors are not initiated below eGFR 20 (Rec 11.7a); at 18 she is below the starting threshold, and the glucose-lowering effect would be minimal anyway.
distractors.B: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is <30 (Table 9.2).
distractors.C: Pioglitazone is generally not recommended in kidney impairment because of fluid retention (Table 9.2), and she already needs a loop diuretic.
distractors.E: She is already having hypoglycemia; increasing a sulfonylurea in advanced CKD increases the risk further.

pearls: eGFR <30 → GLP-1 RA preferred for glucose lowering (Rec 9.11).
Start an SGLT2i at eGFR ≥20; once started it may continue until dialysis.
No renal dose adjustment for dulaglutide, liraglutide or semaglutide; avoid exenatide and lixisenatide at eGFR or CrCl ≤30.
explanation.objective: Select a GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic management in type 2 diabetes with advanced CKD (eGFR <30).

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has been on in-center hemodialysis three times weekly for 2 years. He had coronary artery bypass surgery 4 years ago. The transplant team has advised weight reduction before he can be listed for a kidney transplant. He takes linagliptin 5 mg daily and insulin glargine 14 units at bedtime, plus sevelamer, a statin, aspirin and carvedilol. His glucose meter shows readings of 110–260 mg/dL (6.1–14.4 mmol/L) with no hypoglycemia.

BMI 35.4 kg/m². Residual urine output is about 200 mL/day.

labs.name: A1C
labs.ref: <5.7% (<39 mmol/mol); interpret with caution on dialysis

mcq.question: Which change to his glucose-lowering therapy is most appropriate?
hints: Which of these drugs are cleared by the kidney, and which are contraindicated on dialysis?
ADA says people on dialysis can safely start GLP-1-based therapy, provided the agent is not dependent on kidney clearance.

explanation.summary: On dialysis, a GLP-1 RA that is not kidney-cleared (such as semaglutide) can be started for cardiovascular risk reduction, weight loss and glucose lowering; it replaces the DPP-4 inhibitor.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Replace linagliptin with semaglutide. Rec 9.11 states that a GLP-1 RA is preferred for glycemic management in advanced CKD, and that 'individuals on dialysis can be safely initiated or continued on GLP-1–based therapy (that is not dependent on kidney clearance) to reduce cardiovascular risk and mortality' (grade C). Semaglutide needs no dose adjustment for kidney function (Table 9.2). It suits this man: he has established coronary disease, needs weight loss to be listed for transplant, and lowers glucose without hypoglycemia. The DPP-4 inhibitor must stop when the GLP-1 RA starts, because ADA Rec 9.18 says the combination adds no glucose lowering. GI adverse effects can cause volume depletion, so start low and titrate slowly, in coordination with the dialysis team, who will watch interdialytic weight and blood pressure. A1C is less reliable on dialysis because of anemia and erythropoietin therapy, so glucose monitoring (ideally CGM) should guide titration of glargine, which may need reducing as semaglutide takes effect (Rec 9.22).

distractors.A: SGLT2 inhibitors are not initiated in people on dialysis; they may only be continued until dialysis or transplantation (Table 9.2).
distractors.B: Exenatide is cleared by the kidney and should be avoided when creatinine clearance is ≤30 mL/min (ADA Section 9).
distractors.C: Glyburide is generally not recommended in CKD because active metabolites accumulate and cause prolonged hypoglycemia.
distractors.D: Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30, and therefore on dialysis (Table 9.2).

pearls: Dialysis: GLP-1-based therapy that is not kidney-cleared can be started (Rec 9.11, grade C).
Avoid exenatide and lixisenatide at eGFR or CrCl ≤30.
Stop the DPP-4 inhibitor when starting a GLP-1 RA (Rec 9.18).
explanation.objective: Choose a non-renally cleared GLP-1 receptor agonist for a person with type 2 diabetes on hemodialysis.

mcq.subtopic: Continuing an SGLT2 inhibitor as eGFR falls
mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric CKD has taken empagliflozin 10 mg daily for 3 years, together with losartan 100 mg, semaglutide 1 mg weekly and insulin glargine 18 units. His eGFR trend is shown below. His UACR has fallen from 1,100 to 840 mg/g (124 to 95 mg/mmol). He is not on dialysis and the nephrologist expects kidney replacement therapy in 1–2 years. A1C is 7.2% (55 mmol/mol). He has had no genital infections, ketoacidosis or volume depletion.

He has read that empagliflozin 'does not work below eGFR 20' and asks whether he should stop it.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best management of his empagliflozin?

options.text: Stop empagliflozin because eGFR is now below 20

hints: Separate two thresholds: the eGFR for starting a drug and the eGFR for continuing it.
Table 9.2 and Section 11 say how long an established SGLT2 inhibitor may be continued.

explanation.summary: An SGLT2 inhibitor that is already established is continued as eGFR falls below 20, until dialysis or transplantation; the threshold of 20 applies only to starting it.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Keep empagliflozin at 10 mg daily. The series shows slow, steady progression of CKD (about 5 mL/min/1.73 m² per year), not an acute fall. ADA uses eGFR 20 only as a starting threshold: SGLT2 inhibitors 'should be initiated in individuals with eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m² but can safely continue until kidney failure' (Rec 11.7a). Table 9.2 says they 'may continue until dialysis or transplantation'. KDIGO 2022 (practice point 1.3.6) agrees. His glucose-lowering effect from empagliflozin is now minimal, as Table 9.2 notes for eGFR <45, but the drug is there for kidney and cardiovascular protection, and that benefit persists: his UACR has fallen on treatment. Glycemia is managed by semaglutide and glargine, which is why his A1C is at goal. Keep the sick-day rules: hold empagliflozin during acute illness, poor intake or before surgery, because of the ketoacidosis and volume-depletion risks. Stop it when dialysis starts.

distractors.A: Higher doses add little glucose lowering at this eGFR and no extra kidney benefit; the kidney-protective dose is 10 mg.
distractors.C: Swapping one SGLT2 inhibitor for another adds nothing, and starting a 'new' agent at eGFR 18 would fall below the starting threshold.
distractors.D: This confuses the starting threshold with a stopping rule. Rec 11.7a and Table 9.2 allow continuation until kidney failure.
distractors.E: Pioglitazone has no kidney benefit and causes fluid retention, a particular problem in advanced CKD (Table 9.2).

pearls: SGLT2i: start at eGFR ≥20; continue below 20 until dialysis or transplantation.
Below eGFR 45 the glucose-lowering effect fades, but kidney and heart protection do not.
Gradual eGFR decline on an SGLT2i is disease progression, not drug toxicity.
explanation.objective: Continue an established SGLT2 inhibitor in a person with type 2 diabetes whose eGFR declines below 20 mL/min/1.73 m² before kidney failure.
references: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD, practice point 1.3.6

mcq.subtopic: CKD when an SGLT2 inhibitor is unsuitable
mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years is seen in clinic. Last year, while taking dapagliflozin, he was admitted with Fournier gangrene requiring surgical debridement; dapagliflozin was stopped. He had three earlier episodes of balanitis. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, ramipril 10 mg (maximum tolerated), atorvastatin 40 mg and amlodipine 5 mg. He has no heart failure and no history of pancreatitis or medullary thyroid cancer.

BP 134/80 mmHg, BMI 31.0 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
hints: His kidney disease still needs an organ-protective drug, but one class is now off the table. Why?
ADA Rec 9.10 gives two kidney-protective classes. Which agent in the other class has a dedicated kidney-outcome trial?

explanation.summary: Albuminuric CKD still needs a kidney-protective agent; after Fournier gangrene on an SGLT2 inhibitor, the alternative in Rec 9.10 is a GLP-1 RA with demonstrated kidney benefit (semaglutide).
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Semaglutide. He has CKD G3a with severely increased albuminuria (A3) on a maximally tolerated ACE inhibitor. ADA Rec 9.10 (grade A) offers two choices for slowing CKD progression and reducing cardiovascular events: an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit in this population. Rec 11.7b says the same for GLP-1 RAs. Necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier gangrene) is a listed SGLT2 inhibitor adverse effect (Table 9.2), and his recurrent genital infections put him at high risk; Table 9.2 advises avoiding SGLT2 inhibitors in high-risk individuals. ADA notes that semaglutide has shown benefit for CVD, mortality and kidney outcomes in CKD and 'can be used as another first-line agent for people with CKD'. In FLOW (eGFR 50–75 with UACR >300 mg/g, or eGFR 25–<50 with UACR >100 mg/g), semaglutide 1 mg weekly reduced the primary kidney composite by 24% (HR 0.76) and also reduced MACE and all-cause death. He fits that population. Semaglutide also helps weight and glucose. Continue metformin at his eGFR; consider finerenone for residual albuminuria (Rec 11.8).

distractors.A: Canagliflozin is another SGLT2 inhibitor; the Fournier gangrene risk is a class effect, so re-exposure after a life-threatening episode is inappropriate.
distractors.B: Glimepiride lowers glucose but has no kidney or cardiovascular benefit and adds hypoglycemia and weight gain.
distractors.C: Pioglitazone is neutral for CKD progression and causes fluid retention; Table 9.2 says it is generally not recommended in kidney impairment.
distractors.E: Sitagliptin is neutral for kidney outcomes (Table 9.2) and would not slow his CKD.

pearls: CKD in T2D: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit; semaglutide (FLOW) is the GLP-1 RA with a dedicated kidney trial.
Fournier gangrene and recurrent genital infection → avoid the SGLT2i class.
FLOW entry: eGFR 50–75 with UACR >300 mg/g, or eGFR 25–<50 with UACR >100 mg/g.
explanation.objective: Choose a GLP-1 receptor agonist with kidney-outcome evidence for albuminuric CKD when SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years has MASH cirrhosis with ascites requiring monthly paracentesis, a variceal bleed 6 months ago and two admissions for hepatic encephalopathy (Child–Pugh class C). She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, spironolactone, furosemide, propranolol, lactulose and rifaximin. Her appetite is poor and she has lost 6 kg of muscle mass over a year. Her daughter's glucose-meter log shows fasting values of 190–240 mg/dL (10.6–13.3 mmol/L) and afternoon values up to 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L).

BMI 24.1 kg/m² (dry weight estimate).
mcq.question: Which glucose-lowering approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Metformin increased to the maximum dose

hints: Do her A1C and her meter readings agree? Why might the A1C be misleading?
Figure 9.4 has a one-line instruction for the decompensated end of the liver-disease spectrum.

explanation.summary: Figure 9.4 says to use insulin in decompensated cirrhosis; metformin should be stopped because of lactic acidosis risk, and incretin, thiazolidinedione and sulfonylurea options are unsuitable.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Insulin glargine, with metformin stopped. Her A1C of 6.4% is falsely reassuring: anemia, variceal blood loss and hypersplenism shorten red-cell survival, while her meter readings show sustained hyperglycemia. For MASLD and MASH, Figure 9.4 favors GLP-1 RAs, tirzepatide and pioglitazone, but it gives one explicit instruction for the decompensated end of the spectrum: 'Use insulin in the setting of decompensated cirrhosis.' The evidence for incretins and pioglitazone in MASH comes from people with compensated disease (for example, ESSENCE enrolled F2–F3 fibrosis). In decompensated cirrhosis these drugs bring problems: GLP-1-based therapy worsens anorexia and sarcopenia, and pioglitazone causes fluid retention. Insulin can be titrated, works regardless of hepatic function, and does not worsen weight loss. Metformin should be stopped: its lactic acidosis risk rises with hepatic decompensation (impaired lactate clearance), recurrent bleeding and hypoperfusion. Start a modest basal dose, because hepatic insulin clearance and gluconeogenesis are impaired and hypoglycemia is a real risk. Use glucose monitoring, ideally CGM, rather than A1C to guide titration.

distractors.A: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, and the risk is higher with impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis and poor intake; they also leave metformin in place.
distractors.C: Increasing metformin in decompensated cirrhosis raises the lactic acidosis risk; it should be stopped, not increased.
distractors.D: Pioglitazone helps MASH in compensated disease but causes fluid retention, a serious problem with refractory ascites.
distractors.E: Semaglutide is preferred in compensated MASH, but in decompensated cirrhosis with poor appetite and muscle loss its anorexia and weight loss are harmful; Figure 9.4 specifies insulin.

pearls: Decompensated cirrhosis → insulin (Figure 9.4).
A1C is unreliable with anemia, bleeding or hypersplenism; use glucose monitoring or CGM.
The benefits of GLP-1 RA, tirzepatide and pioglitazone in MASH apply to noncirrhotic or compensated disease.
explanation.objective: Choose insulin for glycemic management in a person with type 2 diabetes and decompensated MASH cirrhosis.

mcq.subtopic: Obesity without cardiorenal disease: weight-centric choice
mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old Saudi software engineer in Riyadh has had type 2 diabetes for 2 years. He takes metformin extended-release 2,000 mg daily. Despite a structured lifestyle program he has gained 4 kg in a year. He says his main goal is to lose weight, and he is willing to inject a medication. He has no ASCVD, heart failure or CKD and no personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or pancreatitis.

BP 128/82 mmHg, BMI 36.4 kg/m², waist 118 cm.
mcq.question: Which addition best serves both his glycemic and his weight goals?
hints: With no cardiorenal disease, the right-hand side of Figure 9.4 applies: weight and glycemic goals.
Look for the agent rated 'very high' for both glucose lowering and weight loss.

explanation.summary: Without ASCVD, HF or CKD, weight is a primary treatment goal; tirzepatide (or semaglutide) has very high efficacy for both glucose and weight.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Tirzepatide. In people without ASCVD, HF or CKD, ADA says the choice should be informed by weight management, MASLD risk and achieving glycemic goals (right side of Figure 9.4). Rec 9.16 asks that intensification consider individualized weight goals, and Section 8 (Rec 8.16, 8.18) says to prioritize drugs with a beneficial effect on weight, preferring semaglutide or tirzepatide. Figure 9.4 rates semaglutide and tirzepatide 'very high' for weight loss, and Table 9.2 rates tirzepatide 'very high' for glucose lowering and weight loss, with no intrinsic hypoglycemia. In SURPASS-2, tirzepatide lowered A1C and weight more than semaglutide 1 mg when added to metformin. His A1C is 1.4 percentage points above a goal of <7%, and an agent of this potency could bring him to goal while treating his obesity. Metformin should continue. Counsel him about GI effects with dose escalation and peri-procedural aspiration risk, and that the medication is intended long term (Rec 8.19).

distractors.A: Acarbose has intermediate efficacy and is weight-neutral; frequent GI effects limit its use, and it does not address his weight goal.
distractors.B: Dapagliflozin is a reasonable oral agent with modest (intermediate) weight loss, but it falls well short of tirzepatide for both A1C and weight in a man whose priority is weight.
distractors.C: Glimepiride causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, the opposite of his goals.
distractors.D: Pioglitazone causes weight gain and fluid retention; Table 9.2 lists 'gain' for weight.

pearls: No ASCVD, HF or CKD → right side of Figure 9.4: choose by weight and glycemic goals.
Very high efficacy for both glucose and weight: semaglutide and tirzepatide.
Weight-promoting classes are insulin, sulfonylureas and TZDs: use them judiciously in obesity.
explanation.objective: Select a high-efficacy weight-reducing agent for a person with type 2 diabetes and obesity without cardiorenal disease.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old woman, a teacher in Jeddah, is found to have type 2 diabetes at a workplace screening. She has no polyuria, polydipsia or weight loss. She has no cardiovascular, kidney or liver disease and no family history of medullary thyroid cancer. You agree an A1C goal of <7% (<53 mmol/mol). She has no strong preference about tablets or injections.

BP 126/80 mmHg, BMI 32.0 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which initial treatment plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Basal insulin plus metformin, started together
Lifestyle change alone, with A1C rechecked in 3 months
Metformin alone, with a second drug added at 3 months if needed
Sulfonylurea alone, with metformin added at 3 months if needed

hints: How far above her goal is she, and does she have any feature that makes insulin necessary?
ADA suggests initial combination therapy when A1C is 1.5–2.0% above the goal, to shorten the time to reach it.

explanation.summary: With A1C 2% above goal and no catabolic features, ADA supports initial combination therapy; metformin plus a GLP-1 RA also addresses her obesity without hypoglycemia.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Metformin plus semaglutide, started together. ADA Rec 9.6 (grade A) states: 'Consider combination therapy in adults with type 2 diabetes for initial treatment to shorten time to attainment of individualized glycemic goals.' The text adds that initial combination should be considered when A1C is 1.5–2.0% above the individualized goal, and that when A1C is ≥1.5% above goal many people will need dual therapy or a more potent agent. Her A1C of 9.0% (75 mmol/mol) is 2.0 percentage points above <7%. Pharmacotherapy should start at diagnosis without delay. Pairing metformin with semaglutide uses a 'very high' weight-loss agent (Figure 9.4; dulaglutide and liraglutide are rated 'high') that lowers A1C by roughly 1% to ≥2% when added to metformin, without hypoglycemia, which fits her obesity (Figure 9.4, Table 9.2). Insulin is not required: she has no symptoms of hyperglycemia, no ketosis or weight loss, her A1C is ≤10% and her glucose is <300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) (Rec 9.20). The Saudi Diabetes CPG 2021 likewise uses 'more than 1.5% above target' as the trigger for dual therapy in newly diagnosed people.

distractors.A: Insulin at diagnosis is for symptomatic or catabolic presentations or A1C >10% / glucose ≥300 mg/dL (Rec 9.20); she has none of these, so insulin adds hypoglycemia and weight without need.
distractors.B: ADA says pharmacotherapy should start at diagnosis without delay; lifestyle alone at A1C 9.0% is unlikely to reach goal.
distractors.D: Stepwise therapy is acceptable but slower; at 2% above goal, ADA supports starting a combination to shorten the time to goal.
distractors.E: A sulfonylurea first causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, and delaying metformin has no advantage.

pearls: A1C 1.5–2.0% above goal → consider initial combination therapy (Rec 9.6).
Insulin at diagnosis: symptoms or catabolism, A1C >10% (>86 mmol/mol) or glucose ≥300 mg/dL (≥16.7 mmol/L).
Adding a GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide to metformin usually lowers A1C by 1% to ≥2%.
explanation.objective: Recommend initial combination therapy for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with an A1C about 2% above goal and no catabolic features.

mcq.subtopic: No DPP-4 inhibitor with GLP-1-based therapy
mcq.stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years takes a fixed-dose combination of sitagliptin–metformin 50/1,000 mg twice daily. His A1C is 8.3% (67 mmol/mol) and his BMI is 33.5 kg/m². He has no cardiovascular or kidney disease, and his eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m². After shared decision-making you prescribe subcutaneous semaglutide, starting at 0.25 mg weekly and titrating upward.
mcq.question: Which accompanying change to his oral therapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace sitagliptin–metformin with linagliptin plus metformin
Replace sitagliptin–metformin with metformin alone, 1,000 mg twice daily

hints: Think about mechanism: what does a DPP-4 inhibitor do to endogenous GLP-1, and what does a pharmacologic GLP-1 RA add?
ADA has a specific recommendation against one combination here.

explanation.summary: A DPP-4 inhibitor adds no glucose lowering on top of a GLP-1 RA, so the sitagliptin component stops and metformin continues at the same dose.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Replace sitagliptin–metformin with metformin alone, 1,000 mg twice daily. ADA Rec 9.18 (grade B): 'Concurrent use of DPP-4 inhibitors with a GLP-1 RA or a dual GIP and GLP-1 RA is not recommended due to lack of additional glucose lowering beyond that of a GLP-1–based therapy.' A DPP-4 inhibitor works by slowing breakdown of endogenous GLP-1. A GLP-1 RA gives pharmacologic receptor activation many times higher, so the DPP-4 inhibitor adds cost and pill burden without benefit. Fixed-dose combinations are a common trap: the sitagliptin is easy to miss inside a 'metformin' tablet. Prescribing metformin alone at the same total dose (2,000 mg/day) keeps his metformin exposure unchanged. Stopping the DPP-4 inhibitor also reduces cost and pill burden, consistent with ADA's call to reevaluate the medication plan regularly and adjust it as needed (Rec 9.14). NICE NG28 (2026, 1.24.6) and KDIGO 2022 (practice point 4.2.3) make the same recommendation.

distractors.A: Continuing sitagliptin alongside semaglutide is the combination Rec 9.18 advises against: no added glucose lowering, extra cost.
distractors.B: Halving the combination reduces the metformin dose unnecessarily and still leaves a DPP-4 inhibitor alongside the GLP-1 RA.
distractors.C: Linagliptin is still a DPP-4 inhibitor; changing to it does not remove the redundancy.
distractors.E: Saxagliptin is also a DPP-4 inhibitor, and it carries an HF signal; the swap keeps the redundancy.

pearls: No DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide (Rec 9.18).
Check fixed-dose combinations for a hidden DPP-4 inhibitor when starting incretin therapy.
Continue metformin when adding a GLP-1 RA unless contraindicated.
explanation.objective: Discontinue a DPP-4 inhibitor when starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist, including when it is hidden in a fixed-dose combination.

mcq.subtopic: Reassess hypoglycemia-causing drugs when adding a new agent
mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years had coronary artery bypass surgery 3 years ago. He lives alone in Taif and drives daily. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and glimepiride 4 mg each morning. Twice in the past month he felt sweaty and shaky before lunch; his meter showed 62 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L) on both occasions and he treated himself with dates. You agree an A1C goal of <7.5% (<58 mmol/mol) and decide to add subcutaneous semaglutide for cardiovascular risk reduction.

BMI 28.4 kg/m².
mcq.question: In addition to starting semaglutide, which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue glimepiride and add a mid-morning snack

hints: He is near goal and already having hypoglycemia, and the new drug will lower A1C further. Which current drug causes the lows?
ADA asks you to reassess the need for, or dose of, certain drug classes every time a new glucose-lowering drug is started.

explanation.summary: When a new glucose-lowering drug is started, ADA asks you to reassess sulfonylureas, meglitinides and insulin; with existing hypoglycemia and an A1C near goal, stopping glimepiride is best.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Discontinue glimepiride. ADA Rec 9.17 (grade A): 'When initiating a new glucose-lowering medication, reassess the need for and/or dose of medications with higher hypoglycemia risk (i.e., sulfonylureas, meglitinides, and insulin) to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia and treatment burden.' He already has level 1 hypoglycemia (54–69 mg/dL [3.0–3.8 mmol/L]), an A1C of 7.3% that is within his individualized goal, and he lives alone and drives, so hypoglycemia is especially dangerous. Semaglutide will lower A1C by about 1% or more and does not cause hypoglycemia itself, but it increases sulfonylurea-related lows. Section 13 (Rec 13.14a) and Section 6 (Rec 6.6) also call for deintensifying hypoglycemia-causing drugs, or switching to a lower-risk class, in older adults at high hypoglycemia risk. Glimepiride brings no cardiovascular, kidney or weight benefit (Table 9.2), so it is the drug to remove. Metformin and the new GLP-1 RA stay. Recheck glucose patterns in 2–4 weeks, and A1C in 3 months.

distractors.A: Adding a DPP-4 inhibitor to a GLP-1 RA adds no glucose lowering (Rec 9.18) and does nothing about the hypoglycemia.
distractors.B: Feeding the sulfonylurea treats the symptom, not the cause, and encourages weight gain; hypoglycemia risk remains.
distractors.D: Increasing the sulfonylurea in a man already having lows, while adding another glucose-lowering drug, is dangerous.
distractors.E: Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia, is affordable and is well tolerated at his eGFR; stopping it removes useful therapy without addressing the cause.

pearls: Starting a new drug → reassess sulfonylurea, meglitinide and insulin doses (Rec 9.17).
Older adults who live alone and drive need hypoglycemia-sparing regimens (Rec 13.13, 13.14a).
GLP-1 RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors cause hypoglycemia mainly when combined with sulfonylureas or insulin.
explanation.objective: Deintensify a sulfonylurea when adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist in an older adult with hypoglycemia.

mcq.subtopic: Indicators of high CVD risk (primary prevention)
mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 3 years attends clinic. She has hypertension treated with perindopril, dyslipidemia treated with rosuvastatin, and smokes 10 cigarettes a day despite counseling. She has never had chest pain, stroke, claudication or heart failure, and a recent exercise test was normal. She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. She prefers a once-weekly medication if an addition is needed.

BP 134/82 mmHg, BMI 31.2 kg/m².

labs.name: LDL cholesterol
labs.ref: goal <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L) at high risk

mcq.question: Which addition to her glucose-lowering therapy is most appropriate?
hints: She has no established ASCVD. Does Figure 9.4 still put her on the 'cardiovascular risk reduction' side?
Count her risk factors against ADA's working definition of 'high risk': an age threshold plus a number of additional risk factors.

explanation.summary: Age ≥55 with two or more additional risk factors marks high CVD risk in Figure 9.4, so a GLP-1 RA (or SGLT2 inhibitor) with proven CV benefit is recommended; dulaglutide's outcome trial included many people without established CVD.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Dulaglutide. Rec 9.7 applies to 'established or high risk' of ASCVD. Figure 9.4 defines indicators of high risk as 'most comprise ≥55 years of age with two or more additional risk factors (including obesity, hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia, or albuminuria)'. She is 57 and has four: obesity, hypertension, smoking and dyslipidemia. So the plan should include a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit, irrespective of A1C. The figure notes that the recommendation is weaker for high-risk indicators than for established CVD, and that absolute benefit rises with baseline risk. That trade-off belongs in shared decision-making, but it does not favor an agent without CV benefit. Dulaglutide (once weekly, as she prefers) has MACE benefit in Table 9.2. Its trial, REWIND, included many people with risk factors but no established CVD (MACE HR 0.88), the population closest to hers. It also gives high glucose lowering and weight loss. Smoking cessation and LDL lowering remain essential alongside it.

distractors.A: Acarbose has intermediate glucose-lowering efficacy and no proven cardiovascular benefit, and GI effects limit adherence.
distractors.C: Glimepiride is CV-safe (CAROLINA) but neutral for MACE, and adds weight and hypoglycemia.
distractors.D: Linagliptin is CV-neutral (CARMELINA, CAROLINA) and would not reduce her cardiovascular risk.
distractors.E: Pioglitazone has only 'potential benefit' for MACE and causes weight gain, edema and fractures; it is not a first choice for primary cardiovascular risk reduction.

pearls: High CVD risk in Figure 9.4: age ≥55 plus ≥2 of obesity, hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia or albuminuria.
Rec 9.7 covers 'established or high risk' ASCVD: GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2i with proven benefit.
REWIND (dulaglutide) included many primary-prevention participants with risk factors only.
explanation.objective: Recognize ADA's indicators of high cardiovascular risk and select a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit for primary prevention.

mcq.subtopic: GLP-1 RAs with proven MACE benefit
mcq.stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, prior ischemic stroke and peripheral artery disease takes metformin and empagliflozin. His A1C is 7.9% (63 mmol/mol). He agrees to add an injectable incretin-based drug and asks for one with proven reduction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
mcq.question: According to ADA 2026 Table 9.2, which of the following has demonstrated MACE benefit?
hints: Not every incretin-based drug has a positive cardiovascular outcome trial; some were only noninferior.
Table 9.2 lists three GLP-1 RAs with MACE benefit and calls one dual agonist's MACE effect 'under investigation'.

explanation.summary: Table 9.2 lists dulaglutide, liraglutide and semaglutide (SC and oral) with MACE benefit; exenatide once weekly and lixisenatide are neutral, and tirzepatide is 'under investigation'.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Liraglutide. ADA 2026 Table 9.2 lists the GLP-1 RAs with demonstrated MACE benefit as dulaglutide, liraglutide and semaglutide (SC and oral). Exenatide once weekly and lixisenatide are listed as neutral, and the MACE effect of the dual GIP/GLP-1 RA tirzepatide is 'under investigation'. Liraglutide's benefit comes from LEADER (3-point MACE HR 0.87). EXSCEL (exenatide extended-release) and ELIXA (lixisenatide) showed noninferiority but not superiority. Figure 9.5 advises that 'If CVD is present, consider GLP-1 RA with proven CVD benefit; oral or injectable GLP-1 RAs are appropriate.' He already takes empagliflozin, and Figure 9.4 supports combining the two classes for additive risk reduction (Section 10, Rec 10.40d). GLP-1 RA outcome trials also show fewer strokes, which is relevant after his ischemic stroke. A tirzepatide cardiovascular outcomes trial has since been reported, but ADA 2026 still lists its MACE effect as under investigation, so key on the ADA table for this exam.

distractors.A: Exenatide extended-release was noninferior in EXSCEL but did not significantly reduce MACE; Table 9.2 lists it as neutral.
distractors.C: Lixisenatide was neutral in ELIXA (post-acute coronary syndrome), and secondary sources report that the standalone product has left the US market (it remains in iGlarLixi).
distractors.D: Sitagliptin is an oral DPP-4 inhibitor, not an injectable, and is MACE-neutral (TECOS).
distractors.E: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 lists tirzepatide's MACE effect as 'under investigation'.

pearls: MACE benefit (Table 9.2): dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide SC and oral.
Neutral: exenatide once weekly, lixisenatide; tirzepatide is 'under investigation' in ADA 2026.
SGLT2i plus GLP-1 RA may be combined in ASCVD for additive benefit (Rec 10.40d).
explanation.objective: Identify which GLP-1 receptor agonists have demonstrated MACE reduction according to ADA 2026.

mcq.subtopic: On a GLP-1 RA with ASCVD: add an SGLT2 inhibitor
mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man had an ST-elevation myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and has taken semaglutide 2 mg weekly for 12 months with good tolerance. He lost 7 kg on semaglutide. His diet and activity are good. He has no heart failure, no hypoglycemia and no history of genital infections.

BP 122/74 mmHg, BMI 29.0 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reach his glycemic goal of <7%?
hints: He is on a maximal GLP-1 RA dose and still above goal. Figure 9.4 says what to consider next for someone with ASCVD already on a GLP-1 RA.
Pick the option that lowers glucose and also adds cardiovascular protection, without hypoglycemia.

explanation.summary: For ASCVD with A1C above goal on a GLP-1 RA, Figure 9.4 says to add an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven CVD benefit, which adds glucose lowering and cardiovascular protection.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Add empagliflozin. The ASCVD pathway of Figure 9.4 reads: 'If glycemia is above goal … For individuals on a GLP-1 RA, consider adding SGLT2i with proven CVD benefit or vice versa.' Section 10 (Rec 10.40d, grade B) supports combining an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 RA, each with proven CV benefit, for additive reduction of cardiovascular and kidney events. Empagliflozin has MACE and HF benefit (Table 9.2). With eGFR 71 it will also lower A1C usefully (intermediate to high efficacy; each oral class added generally lowers A1C by about 0.7–1.0%), enough to bring 7.8% close to goal, without hypoglycemia and with modest further weight loss. GLP-1 RAs, dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are the first choices for intensification because they reduce the need for drugs that cause hypoglycemia or weight gain. Before starting, counsel him on genital hygiene, hydration and sick-day rules (hold during acute illness or prolonged fasting, and 3–4 days before scheduled surgery).

distractors.B: Glimepiride lowers A1C but is MACE-neutral, causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, and adds nothing for his ASCVD.
distractors.C: Basal insulin is not yet needed at A1C 7.8%. It brings hypoglycemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit, while a cardioprotective oral option remains unused.
distractors.D: A DPP-4 inhibitor adds no glucose lowering on top of a GLP-1 RA (Rec 9.18).
distractors.E: Semaglutide 2 mg is at least as potent as liraglutide and both have MACE benefit; switching within the class will not lower A1C further.

pearls: ASCVD on a GLP-1 RA and above goal → add an SGLT2i with proven CVD benefit, or vice versa (Fig 9.4).
SGLT2i + GLP-1 RA combination: additive CV and kidney protection (Rec 10.40d).
Use cardioprotective, hypoglycemia-sparing classes before insulin or sulfonylureas when possible.
explanation.objective: Intensify therapy in a person with ASCVD on a maximal GLP-1 RA by adding an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit.

mcq.subtopic: At glycemic goal but new albuminuric CKD: switch to a preferred agent
mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends her annual review. She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, glimepiride 2 mg daily, lisinopril 40 mg (maximum dose) and atorvastatin 20 mg. She has had no hypoglycemia. She has no heart failure or ASCVD. Her results over the last 6 months are shown.

BP 128/78 mmHg, BMI 27.6 kg/m².

exhibit.title: Kidney function over 6 months
exhibit.note: First-morning urine samples; no infection, fever or heavy exercise before sampling.

mcq.question: Which change to her glucose-lowering regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue the current regimen because A1C is at goal

hints: Has CKD been confirmed? Look at the number of abnormal samples and the time span.
ADA says people with cardiorenal comorbidity who already meet their glycemic goal 'may benefit from switching' to which medications?

explanation.summary: Persistent albuminuria for more than 3 months confirms CKD; ADA recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor (or GLP-1 RA) irrespective of A1C, and at goal it is sensible to swap the sulfonylurea for it.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Replace glimepiride with empagliflozin. Three samples over 6 months show UACR of 290–335 mg/g with a stable eGFR in the mid-50s, so she has confirmed CKD, G3a/A2–A3. The sediment is bland, which makes diabetic kidney disease likely. Rec 9.10 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit irrespective of A1C. The ADA text adds that individuals with these comorbidities 'already achieving their individualized glycemic goals with other medications may benefit from switching to these preferred medications'. Glimepiride is the logical drug to swap out. It gives no kidney or heart protection (Table 9.2), its hypoglycemia risk rises as eGFR falls, and stacking an SGLT2 inhibitor on top of it at an A1C of 6.6% would add hypoglycemia risk for little glycemic gain. Empagliflozin has dedicated kidney-outcome evidence (EMPA-KIDNEY) and will keep A1C near goal. Metformin continues at eGFR 56. Recheck UACR, eGFR and potassium; with persisting albuminuria on maximal RAS blockade she may also qualify for finerenone (Rec 11.8).

distractors.A: Sitagliptin adds glucose lowering she does not need and is neutral for CKD progression; it does not meet the cardiorenal indication.
distractors.B: Being at the A1C goal does not remove the indication: Rec 9.10 applies irrespective of A1C. Leaving the regimen unchanged ignores confirmed albuminuric CKD.
distractors.D: Pioglitazone is neutral for CKD, causes fluid retention and is generally not recommended in kidney impairment (Table 9.2).
distractors.E: Linagliptin is kidney-neutral, and there is no reason to stop metformin at eGFR 56.

pearls: Confirm albuminuria with 2 of 3 samples over 3–6 months before labeling CKD.
At goal with new CKD, HF or ASCVD → switch a non-protective drug (often the sulfonylurea) to an SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA.
Rec 9.10 applies irrespective of A1C.
explanation.objective: Interpret serial UACR results to confirm CKD and replace a sulfonylurea with an SGLT2 inhibitor in a person at glycemic goal.

mcq.subtopic: Oral options with proven MACE benefit
mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman had an ischemic stroke 8 months ago with good recovery. She has type 2 diabetes for 10 years and takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, clopidogrel, atorvastatin 80 mg and amlodipine. Since a bad experience with insulin injections during her stroke admission, she firmly declines any injectable medicine. She has no heart failure and no history of genital infections, pancreatitis or thyroid cancer.

BP 126/76 mmHg, BMI 30.2 kg/m².
mcq.question: According to ADA 2026, which oral agent is best supported for reducing her risk of further major adverse cardiovascular events?
hints: Not every SGLT2 inhibitor has MACE benefit in Table 9.2. Check the MACE column, not the HF or CKD columns.
Rec 9.7 asks for 'demonstrated' cardiovascular benefit. For each offered agent, check whether the MACE column of Table 9.2 says 'benefit', 'neutral' or only 'potential benefit'.

explanation.summary: Table 9.2 lists MACE benefit for semaglutide SC and oral; among SGLT2 inhibitors only canagliflozin and empagliflozin have MACE benefit, while dapagliflozin and ertugliflozin are MACE-neutral.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Semaglutide (oral). She has established ASCVD (ischemic stroke), so Rec 9.7 calls for a GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor 'with demonstrated benefits to reduce cardiovascular events'. Because she declines injections, the choice must be oral. Table 9.2 gives MACE benefit to 'dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide (SQ and oral)', and Figure 9.5 notes that 'oral or injectable GLP-1 RAs are appropriate' when CVD is present. The oral semaglutide evidence rests on SOUL (MACE HR 0.86). PIONEER 6 had shown only noninferiority. GLP-1 RA outcome trials also show fewer strokes, which is relevant here. The trap is the SGLT2 inhibitors. In the MACE column of Table 9.2, only canagliflozin and empagliflozin show benefit. Dapagliflozin (DECLARE-TIMI 58) and ertugliflozin (VERTIS CV) were noninferior but did not reduce MACE, although both reduce HF hospitalization. Empagliflozin would have been a reasonable oral choice, but it is not offered. Take oral semaglutide on an empty stomach with ≤120 mL of water, at least 30 minutes before food or other oral medicines (label).

distractors.A: Dapagliflozin reduces HF hospitalization and CKD progression, but Table 9.2 lists it as neutral for MACE (DECLARE-TIMI 58).
distractors.B: Ertugliflozin was MACE-neutral in VERTIS CV; Table 9.2 lists only HF benefit for it.
distractors.C: Pioglitazone has 'potential benefit' for MACE in Table 9.2, and secondary-prevention data after stroke (IRIS) come from people without diabetes. It is not the agent ADA lists with demonstrated benefit, and it causes weight gain, edema and fractures.
distractors.E: Sitagliptin is MACE-neutral (TECOS).

pearls: SGLT2i MACE benefit: canagliflozin and empagliflozin only; HF benefit: all four listed.
Oral semaglutide carries MACE benefit in Table 9.2 (SOUL).
Patient preference (no injections) is a legitimate driver within the cardioprotective classes.
explanation.objective: Distinguish oral agents with demonstrated MACE reduction from those with only HF or kidney benefit, according to ADA 2026 Table 9.2.

mcq.subtopic: Named-guideline contrast: NICE NG28 (2026) initial therapy
mcq.stem: A 50-year-old man in Manchester, UK, is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His HbA1c is 63 mmol/mol (7.9%). He has no heart failure, ASCVD, CKD or frailty, and he was diagnosed after age 40. BMI 28 kg/m², eGFR 90 mL/min/1.73 m². His general practitioner follows the NICE NG28 guideline as updated in February 2026.
mcq.question: According to NICE NG28 (2026), which initial medicine plan should be offered?

options.text: Modified-release metformin, then an SGLT2 inhibitor added
SGLT2 inhibitor alone, with metformin held in reserve

hints: The 2026 NICE rewrite changed the first-line recommendation for people without comorbidities. It now involves two drug classes.
NICE chose the second class for its effects on HbA1c, weight and cardiovascular events at an acceptable cost; it judged GLP-1-based drugs not cost-effective for people without comorbidity.

explanation.summary: NICE NG28 (2026) offers modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor to adults without relevant comorbidity, starting metformin first and adding the SGLT2 inhibitor once metformin is at the maximum tolerated dose.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Modified-release metformin, then an SGLT2 inhibitor added. The February 2026 update of NICE NG28 recommends modified-release metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor for adults with type 2 diabetes and no relevant comorbidity (1.13.1). The SGLT2 inhibitor is introduced stepwise: start metformin, then add the SGLT2 inhibitor as soon as metformin is at the maximum tolerated dose (1.20.2). NICE judged that this pair outperformed other metformin dual combinations on HbA1c, weight and cardiovascular events, and that GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide were not cost-effective for this group. Contrast this with ADA 2026. ADA does not mandate an SGLT2 inhibitor without comorbidity: Figure 9.4 lists 'metformin or other agent (including combination therapy)' chosen by glycemic and weight goals. ADA ties SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs to ASCVD, HF and CKD irrespective of metformin, and it prefers GLP-1-based therapy before insulin. The Saudi Diabetes CPG 2021 still keeps metformin as the preferred first agent. In an exam, read the lead-in: a question that names NICE must be answered by NICE.

distractors.A: NICE 2026 places a DPP-4 inhibitor as a further medicine (1.25.1), not as first-line, and it prefers modified-release metformin.
distractors.B: Metformin alone was the old NICE first-line; the 2026 update adds an SGLT2 inhibitor for people without comorbidities.
distractors.C: NICE adds SC semaglutide (≤1 mg weekly) at the start only for ASCVD (1.15.1), and considers a GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide for early-onset type 2 diabetes diagnosed before 40 (1.16.1); this man has neither.
distractors.E: SGLT2 inhibitor monotherapy is NICE's option only when metformin is unsuitable (1.13.2).

pearls: NICE NG28 (2026): MR metformin + SGLT2i for nearly everyone, introduced stepwise.
NICE adds SC semaglutide ≤1 mg in ASCVD; DPP-4i is a later add-on.
ADA 2026: no mandatory SGLT2i without comorbidity; cardiorenal agents irrespective of metformin when ASCVD, HF or CKD is present.
explanation.objective: Contrast the NICE NG28 (2026) first-line recommendation for type 2 diabetes without comorbidity with the ADA 2026 approach.

mcq.subtopic: Named-guideline contrast: metformin initiation at eGFR 30–44 (KDIGO 2022)
mcq.stem: A 57-year-old man is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during a nephrology referral for CKD. His eGFR is 36 mL/min/1.73 m² (stable over 6 months) and his UACR is 140 mg/g (16 mg/mmol) on irbesartan 300 mg. His A1C is 7.6% (60 mmol/mol) and his BMI is 30.8 kg/m². The nephrologist starts dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and asks whether metformin can also be started, following the KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in CKD.
mcq.question: According to KDIGO 2022, which recommendation about metformin is correct for this patient?

options.text: Do not start metformin, because it is contraindicated below an eGFR of 45
Start metformin at half the usual dose and titrate to half the maximum dose
Start metformin at the usual dose and titrate to 2,000 mg daily
Start metformin only after UACR has fallen below 30 mg/g
Start metformin only as extended-release, 2,000 mg once daily

hints: KDIGO and ADA draw the line for metformin initiation at different eGFR values. Read the lead-in carefully.
KDIGO's metformin table has a separate row for eGFR 30–44, with dose instructions for both new and established users.

explanation.summary: KDIGO 2022 allows metformin to be started at eGFR 30–44 at half the usual dose, titrated to half the maximum; ADA 2026 says metformin should not be started below eGFR 45.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Start metformin at half the usual dose and titrate to half the maximum dose. KDIGO 2022 recommends metformin for people with type 2 diabetes, CKD and eGFR ≥30 (Rec 4.1.1, 1B), and its practice points list metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor as first-line. Its metformin dosing table says that at eGFR 30–44 metformin may be started at half the dose and titrated to half the maximum dose, and that people already taking it should have the dose halved. The ADA–KDIGO consensus (2022) expresses this as a maximum of about 1,000 mg/day. ADA 2026 Section 9 is stricter: 'metformin should not be started in those whose eGFR is <45 mL/min/1.73 m²'. For people already taking it, ADA says to reduce the dose below 45 and stop it below 30, citing the FDA labeling change, which also advises against starting at eGFR 30–45. So the answer depends on the guideline named. This item names KDIGO, so B is correct; an ADA-keyed item would say do not start. Both guidelines agree that metformin is contraindicated below eGFR 30, that eGFR should be monitored every 3–6 months once it is below 60, and that metformin has no direct kidney-protective effect.

distractors.A: That is close to the ADA/FDA position on starting (do not start at eGFR <45), but metformin is contraindicated only below 30, and KDIGO allows a half-dose start at 30–44.
distractors.C: Full-dose titration to 2,000 mg/day is KDIGO's plan for eGFR ≥45, not 30–44.
distractors.D: Albuminuria has no bearing on metformin eligibility; eGFR determines the dose.
distractors.E: Extended-release formulation does not remove the need for dose reduction at eGFR 30–44, and 2,000 mg/day exceeds KDIGO's half-maximum dose.

pearls: KDIGO 2022: eGFR 30–44 → start at half dose, titrate to half maximum (about 1,000 mg/day); <30 → stop.
ADA 2026 and FDA label: do not start metformin at eGFR <45; reduce below 45 (ADA), stop below 30.
When a stem names a guideline, answer by that guideline.
explanation.objective: Contrast KDIGO 2022 and ADA 2026 recommendations on starting metformin at eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m².

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years has seen the same clinic every 6 months. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, and reports taking them regularly. At each visit he was advised to 'try harder with diet' and the A1C was repeated. He has no ASCVD, heart failure or CKD and no hypoglycemia. He is frustrated and asks whether anything else can be done.

BMI 33.4 kg/m². eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m². His A1C history is shown.

exhibit.title: A1C over 24 months on metformin + dapagliflozin

mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step?

options.text: Order C-peptide and GAD antibodies before any change
Refer to a dietitian and recheck A1C in 6 months
Repeat A1C in 3 months before changing therapy

hints: Read the graph: how long has his A1C been above a goal of <7%, and what happened to his therapy over that time?
ADA says treatment modification for people not meeting goals 'should not be delayed', and names the problem shown here.

explanation.summary: Two years at A1C 8.2–8.6% with no treatment change is therapeutic inertia; intensify now, here with a GLP-1 RA, which also addresses his obesity.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Add subcutaneous semaglutide now. The series shows A1C persistently about 1.2–1.6 percentage points above a goal of <7% for 24 months, with no change in therapy: a textbook picture of therapeutic inertia. ADA Rec 9.15 (grade A) states that treatment modification, including intensification, 'for adults not meeting individualized treatment goals should not be delayed'. Rec 9.14 asks for reevaluation of the medication plan and medication-taking behavior every 3–6 months. Figure 9.4 carries the reminder 'To avoid therapeutic inertia, reassess and modify treatment regularly (3–6 months)'. He reports good adherence and has done lifestyle work, so the next step is a more potent agent. A GLP-1 RA lowers A1C by roughly 1% to ≥2% when added to metformin, and semaglutide is rated 'very high' for weight loss, which suits his BMI of 33 (Figure 9.4, Table 9.2). Tirzepatide would be an equally reasonable choice. Continue DSMES alongside the drug change, not instead of it. Review again in 3 months.

distractors.B: Autoimmune testing is for atypical features (lean, rapid progression, ketosis, early insulin need); an obese man stable for 6 years does not need it before intensification.
distractors.C: Lifestyle advice has already been given repeatedly; another 6-month wait continues the inertia that Rec 9.15 warns against.
distractors.D: Two years of consistent values make another confirmatory A1C pointless; the reassessment interval is for acting, not only measuring.
distractors.E: Swapping dapagliflozin for sitagliptin is a lateral move, not intensification: sitagliptin has intermediate efficacy and no weight benefit.

pearls: Do not delay intensification or deintensification (Rec 9.15).
Reassess the medication plan and medication-taking behavior every 3–6 months (Rec 9.14).
Combine DSMES with timely drug changes; do not use it as a reason to wait.
explanation.objective: Recognize therapeutic inertia from a series of A1C values and intensify therapy without further delay.

mcq.subtopic: Simplifying a complex insulin plan in an older adult
mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old widow with type 2 diabetes for 25 years has moderate dementia (MMSE 17/30) and lives with her daughter, who works full-time. She takes insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime and insulin aspart 8 units before each meal, plus metformin 500 mg twice daily. She injects the lunchtime aspart herself and often cannot remember whether she has taken it; she also skips lunch on many days. Last month she fell in the bathroom at 3 a.m. and was found confused, with a meter reading of 48 mg/dL (2.7 mmol/L). A 14-day CGM report is shown.

BMI 24.5 kg/m², eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best change to her diabetes treatment?

options.text: Add sitagliptin and keep the current insulin plan
Move glargine to the morning, stop aspart and add a noninsulin agent
Switch to premixed 70/30 insulin three times daily
Tighten the A1C goal to <6.5% and titrate aspart

hints: Compare her time below range with the older-adult goal, and look at when the lows occur on the AGP.
Rec 13.14c tells you what to do with complex insulin plans in older adults at high risk of hypoglycemia. Which option actually achieves that?

explanation.summary: Frequent, dangerous hypoglycemia in a cognitively impaired older adult on MDI calls for simplification: morning basal insulin, stop the small prandial doses and add a noninsulin agent.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Move glargine to the morning, stop aspart and add a noninsulin agent. Her time below 70 mg/dL is 9% and below 54 mg/dL is 3%, against goals of <1% below 70 for older adults and <1% below 54 (Rec 6.3c). The AGP shows two low-glucose windows: overnight (bedtime glargine) and mid-afternoon (lunchtime aspart given without a meal, or given twice). Her A1C of 7.2% hides this variability (CV 42%). With moderate dementia and dependence on others for injections, her health is complex/intermediate to very complex. For these groups ADA relaxes the A1C goal (<8.0% [<64 mmol/mol], or less reliance on A1C) and makes avoiding hypoglycemia the priority. ADA recommends deintensifying hypoglycemia-causing drugs and simplifying complex insulin plans in such people (Recs 6.6, 13.14a, 13.14c; Section 9 text on deintensification). Figure 13.3 is the practical tool: change basal insulin from bedtime to morning and titrate it to a fasting glucose of 90–150 mg/dL (5.0–8.3 mmol/L); when prandial doses are ≤10 units, stop them and add a noninsulin agent chosen by comorbidity (Figure 9.4, Table 9.2). A morning injection can be supervised by her daughter.

distractors.A: Adding a drug while leaving the unsafe MDI plan unchanged ignores the cause of the hypoglycemia and adds to polypharmacy.
distractors.B: Raising bedtime basal insulin would deepen the nocturnal lows that already caused a fall.
distractors.D: Three daily premixed injections remain complex, need regular meals and carry a high hypoglycemia risk with skipped lunches.
distractors.E: A goal of <6.5% is inappropriate for an older adult with dementia and frequent hypoglycemia (Rec 6.5); titrating prandial insulin would increase harm.

pearls: Older adults on CGM: time below 70 mg/dL goal is <1% (Rec 6.3c).
Figure 13.3: basal to morning; prandial ≤10 units/dose → stop it and add a noninsulin agent.
Deintensify and simplify when harms or burdens exceed benefits (Recs 6.6–6.7, 13.14a–c).
explanation.objective: Interpret a CGM report to identify hypoglycemia in an older adult and simplify a multiple-daily-injection plan accordingly.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old man drives a truck between Riyadh and Dammam and often eats irregularly on the road. He pays for his medicines himself. He has type 2 diabetes for 5 years and takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. After you discuss local prices, he says he cannot afford a GLP-1 RA, tirzepatide or an SGLT2 inhibitor, and he prefers to stay on tablets. He has no ASCVD, heart failure or CKD.

BP 130/80 mmHg, BMI 27.2 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which addition is most appropriate for him?
hints: ADA names four lower-cost glucose-lowering options. Which of the offered drugs are on that list?
Among the low-cost oral options, which one avoids the adverse effect most dangerous for a long-distance driver who eats irregularly?

explanation.summary: When cost is the barrier, ADA suggests metformin, sulfonylureas, TZDs and human insulin; for a driver with irregular meals, pioglitazone lowers A1C well without hypoglycemia.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Pioglitazone. ADA Rec 9.30 (grade E): in adults with cost-related barriers, consider lower-cost medications (metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones and human insulin) 'within the context of their risks for hypoglycemia, weight gain, cardiovascular and kidney events, and other adverse effects'. Rec 9.29 asks clinicians to screen for financial obstacles, which you have done. By acquisition cost (NADAC) in Table 9.3, generic pioglitazone and sulfonylureas cost a small fraction of DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs (use relative cost only; local prices vary). His occupation decides the choice. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia (Table 9.2), and a professional driver who eats irregularly is at particular risk. Pioglitazone has high glucose-lowering efficacy and no hypoglycemia, and may benefit MASLD, but causes weight gain, fluid retention, HF risk and fractures. Before starting it, confirm that he has no HF or edema, no active bladder cancer and no major fracture risk. Starting at a low dose (15 mg) is reasonable; ADA notes that low-dose pioglitazone may be better tolerated and similarly effective. Revisit cardiorenal agents if his finances change.

distractors.A: ADA Rec 9.31a advises against non-approved compounded products because of uncertain content, safety, quality and effectiveness.
distractors.B: Glimepiride is low-cost and effective, but hypoglycemia with irregular meals is dangerous for a professional driver; it is the weaker choice here.
distractors.C: Human insulin is low-cost but injectable (he prefers tablets), causes hypoglycemia and weight gain, and is not needed at A1C 8.2% without catabolic features.
distractors.D: Linagliptin is well tolerated but has intermediate efficacy and is not among ADA's lower-cost options; by acquisition cost (NADAC, Table 9.3) DPP-4 inhibitors cost far more than generic pioglitazone.

pearls: Lower-cost options (Rec 9.30): metformin, sulfonylureas, TZDs, human insulin, each with trade-offs.
Occupation (driving) and meal pattern shape the choice between a sulfonylurea and pioglitazone.
Low-dose pioglitazone may be better tolerated and similarly effective (Figure 9.4 footnote).
explanation.objective: Select a lower-cost glucose-lowering drug that matches individual hypoglycemia risk when cost-related barriers prevent use of cardiorenal agents.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old self-employed man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years has an A1C that rose from 7.1% (54 mmol/mol) to 8.8% (73 mmol/mol) over 9 months. Nine months ago empagliflozin 25 mg daily and semaglutide 0.5 mg weekly were added to metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. He says he is 'taking everything'. He has no new symptoms, intercurrent illness or steroid use, and his weight has risen by 3 kg. The pharmacy dispensing record is shown.

BMI 31.6 kg/m², eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73 m².

exhibit.title: Pharmacy dispensing record, last 9 months
exhibit.note: All fills paid out of pocket. No other pharmacy used, per the patient.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step?

options.text: Ask whether cost limits his use of medicines
Refer for psychological assessment of adherence

hints: Compare the days covered for each medicine with the 270-day period.
ADA asks clinicians to routinely assess one specific kind of obstacle before escalating therapy.

explanation.summary: Full refills of cheap metformin but few refills of the costly agents point to cost-related nonadherence; ADA asks clinicians to assess financial obstacles before escalating therapy.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Ask whether cost limits his use of medicines. The dispensing record shows complete coverage for inexpensive metformin but only one-third coverage for empagliflozin and about one-fifth for semaglutide. Selective gaps in the expensive drugs, paid out of pocket, are the typical pattern of cost-related nonadherence, and they explain the rising A1C and weight. ADA Rec 9.29 (grade E): 'Routinely assess all people with diabetes for financial obstacles that could impede their diabetes management' and work with the team, including pharmacists and social services, to reduce costs. Rec 9.14 asks for reevaluation of medication-taking behavior at regular intervals. The text notes that cost is a major source of stress and worsens medication-taking. Ask the question without judgment. The answer then shapes the plan: lower-cost options per Rec 9.30, generic versions where available, manufacturer assistance, or prioritizing the agent with the most value for his risk profile. Escalating doses or adding insulin before addressing the barrier would raise cost further and hide the real problem.

distractors.B: Increasing a drug he is not obtaining will not lower A1C and increases the cost barrier.
distractors.C: Nothing suggests autoimmune diabetes; the refill data explain the deterioration.
distractors.D: The pattern (only costly drugs missed) points to an economic, not a psychological, barrier; ask directly first.
distractors.E: Insulin would treat the number, not the cause, adding cost, hypoglycemia and weight while the real barrier persists.

pearls: Routinely screen for financial obstacles (Rec 9.29).
Selective gaps in refills of expensive drugs suggest cost-related nonadherence.
Address the barrier before escalating therapy.
explanation.objective: Recognize cost-related nonadherence from dispensing data and assess financial barriers before intensifying therapy.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, Medication Costs and Affordability

mcq.stem: A 44-year-old woman in Riyadh with type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 34.5 kg/m²) stopped her prescribed semaglutide pen during a supply shortage. A friend recommended an overseas online 'wellness clinic', from which she now buys 'compounded semaglutide with vitamin B12' in a multidose vial. She draws up '20 units' with an insulin syringe weekly as the label instructs. She has had two episodes of severe vomiting after drawing up the wrong volume. Her A1C is 7.6% (60 mmol/mol) and her eGFR is 96 mL/min/1.73 m². Approved semaglutide and tirzepatide pens are again available locally.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best advice?

options.text: Continue the compounded product and check her vitamin B12 level
Continue the compounded product at half the volume
Replace it with an approved GLP-1-based product at a labeled dose
Switch to compounded tirzepatide from the same clinic

hints: What is wrong with this product besides the dosing error: its salt form, the added ingredient, the vial-and-syringe format?
ADA has a specific recommendation about non-approved compounded products, and another about what to use instead.

explanation.summary: ADA advises against non-approved compounded products because of uncertain content, safety, quality and effectiveness; switch to an approved product with a labeled dose and titration.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Replace it with an approved GLP-1-based product at a labeled dose. ADA Rec 9.31a (grade C): 'Use of compounded products that are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is not recommended due to uncertainty about their content and resulting concerns about safety, quality, and effectiveness.' The ADA text lists the problems seen with compounded incretins: salt forms of the active ingredient not proven safe in humans, added ingredients such as vitamin B12 or B6 that were never tested in combination, nonstandard concentrations in multidose vials or syringes without labeling to prevent administration errors, and counterfeit products. Her vomiting after volume errors is exactly the dosing hazard described. When an approved product is unavailable, Rec 9.31b recommends switching to a different approved medication of similar efficacy. Now that approved pens are available locally (in Saudi Arabia, products approved by the SFDA), restart an approved semaglutide or tirzepatide at the starting dose and re-titrate, because she has had a gap and erratic exposure. The GLP-1-based therapy itself remains appropriate for her obesity and glycemia.

distractors.A: Checking B12 does not make an unregulated product safe; ADA recommends against continuing compounded products.
distractors.B: Halving an unknown concentration does not solve the problems of uncertain content and nonstandard dosing.
distractors.D: The class is appropriate and was tolerated as an approved pen; the problem is the product, not the drug class.
distractors.E: A compounded tirzepatide carries the same quality and safety concerns; Rec 9.31a applies to all non-approved compounded incretins.

pearls: Non-approved compounded GLP-1 or GIP/GLP-1 products are not recommended (Rec 9.31a).
