Red flags: salt forms, added vitamins, multidose vials dosed in 'units', online sources.
When restarting after a gap, re-titrate from the starting dose to limit GI adverse effects.
explanation.objective: Advise against non-approved compounded incretin products and transition to an approved product with labeled dosing.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, Therapeutic Strategies With Medication Unavailability

mcq.stem: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a prior myocardial infarction took dulaglutide 4.5 mg weekly for 2 years. During a 4-month national shortage of dulaglutide, she was switched to subcutaneous semaglutide and titrated to 1 mg weekly. On semaglutide she has lost a further 4 kg, her A1C has fallen from 7.4% (57 mmol/mol) to 6.8% (51 mmol/mol), and she has had only mild nausea in the first 2 weeks. Both products now cost her the same. Dulaglutide is back in stock, and the pharmacy asks whether she should 'go back to her original medicine'. She says she is happy with semaglutide.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Restart dulaglutide and continue semaglutide together
Stop semaglutide until the dulaglutide supply is stable

hints: Compare her glycemia, weight, tolerability and cost now with what they were before the shortage.
Which product is now giving her better glycemia and weight, with cardiovascular benefit and acceptable tolerability?

explanation.summary: When a shortage ends, ADA asks you to reassess whether to resume the original drug, not to switch back automatically; she is doing well on semaglutide, which has proven CV benefit, so continuing it is appropriate.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Continue semaglutide. ADA Rec 9.31b recommends switching to a different approved medication of similar efficacy during a shortage, which was done. Rec 9.31c (grade E) says: 'Upon resolution of the unavailability (e.g., shortage), reassess the appropriateness of resuming the original FDA-approved medication.' The text adds that people should be reassessed 'based on their current care needs, preferences, and priorities'. Switching back is therefore not automatic. Here every factor favors continuing. Semaglutide has MACE benefit in Table 9.2, as dulaglutide does, so her ASCVD indication is still met. Her A1C and weight are better than before the shortage, tolerability is good, the cost is equal, and she prefers to continue. Switching back would mean another titration period with GI effects and a possible loss of her recent gains. The same logic could favor resuming the original drug for another person, for example if cost, tolerability or supply reliability differed. That is why the recommendation is to reassess, not to switch back by default.

distractors.B: Two GLP-1 RAs together are duplicate therapy with additive GI and safety risk and no expected benefit.
distractors.C: Rec 9.31c asks for reassessment, not automatic return; switching back would disrupt a regimen that is working better.
distractors.D: Sitagliptin has lower efficacy, no weight or cardiovascular benefit, and would undo her ASCVD-directed therapy.
distractors.E: Stopping effective therapy to wait for a product she does not need creates an avoidable gap in glycemic and cardiovascular protection.

pearls: Shortage → switch to an approved agent of similar efficacy (9.31b); shortage over → reassess, do not reflexively switch back (9.31c).
Decide using current needs, preferences, cost and tolerability.
Dulaglutide, liraglutide and semaglutide all carry MACE benefit in Table 9.2.
explanation.objective: Apply ADA guidance on reassessing, rather than automatically resuming, the original medication after a drug shortage resolves.

mcq.stem: A 51-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 7 years had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. Over the past year, on a structured lifestyle program and semaglutide 1 mg weekly, he lost 16 kg (BMI 35.2 → 30.0 kg/m²). He also takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily and glipizide 10 mg daily. He now has episodes of shakiness during his evening gym sessions; his meter has shown 58–66 mg/dL (3.2–3.7 mmol/L) three times this month. He has no GI adverse effects.
mcq.question: Which medication change is most appropriate?
hints: Weight loss has reduced how much medication he needs. Which of his drugs actually causes the hypoglycemia?
ADA says which therapies to de-escalate first: those with side effects or hypoglycemia and no cardiovascular, kidney or metabolic benefit.

explanation.summary: With weight loss, fewer drugs are needed; ADA advises de-escalating first the drugs that cause hypoglycemia and lack cardiovascular, kidney or metabolic benefit, which here is glipizide.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Stop glipizide. The ADA text notes that 'treatment deintensification may also be needed in the setting of weight loss and/or optimization of lifestyle behaviors' and recommends 'preferential deescalation of therapies that are most likely to cause side effects, hypoglycemia, and/or treatment burden and do not have cardiovascular, kidney, or metabolic benefits for continued use'. Rec 9.15 covers deintensification as well as intensification and says it should not be delayed. Rec 6.6 asks clinicians to deintensify hypoglycemia-causing medications in people at risk. He has recurrent level 1 hypoglycemia during exercise and an A1C of 5.9%, below his likely goal. Of his four drugs, only glipizide causes hypoglycemia; metformin, empagliflozin and semaglutide do not do so on their own (Table 9.2). Glipizide also has no cardiovascular or kidney benefit. Semaglutide and empagliflozin should stay, because they are there for his ASCVD irrespective of A1C (Rec 9.7). Metformin is inexpensive and does not cause hypoglycemia. Recheck glucose patterns in 2–4 weeks; if A1C later rises, he still has room to intensify with safer options.

distractors.A: Reducing semaglutide sacrifices weight and cardiovascular benefit and leaves the cause of the hypoglycemia, glipizide, in place.
distractors.B: Empagliflozin is cardioprotective (MACE and HF benefit) and does not cause hypoglycemia itself; it should continue irrespective of A1C.
distractors.D: Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia and is inexpensive; stopping it does not address the lows.
distractors.E: Semaglutide gives MACE benefit and supports weight maintenance (Rec 8.19); stopping it risks weight regain and loss of cardiovascular protection.

pearls: After weight loss, de-escalate first the drugs that cause hypoglycemia and lack organ benefit (usually sulfonylurea or insulin).
Keep SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA given for cardiorenal indications, irrespective of A1C.
Deintensification, like intensification, should not be delayed (Rec 9.15).
explanation.objective: Choose which glucose-lowering drug to discontinue first when weight loss leads to hypoglycemia.

mcq.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 16 years has taken insulin glargine U-100, 30 units daily, with metformin and a GLP-1 RA. He recently lost his job and his health coverage, and now pays for all his medicines himself. He asks for the least expensive basal insulin that would still control his fasting glucose. His A1C is 7.4% (57 mmol/mol) and he has had no hypoglycemia.
mcq.question: According to ADA 2026 (Rec 9.30 and Table 9.4), which basal insulin is generally the lowest-cost option?
hints: ADA's list of lower-cost glucose-lowering options includes one type of insulin by name.
Table 9.4 compares cost per 1,000 units; one of these products has also been withdrawn from the market.

explanation.summary: Human insulins (NPH, regular, premixed 70/30) are the lower-cost insulins in Rec 9.30 and Table 9.4; the trade-off is more hypoglycemia, especially nocturnal, than with analogs.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) NPH (human) insulin. Rec 9.30 lists human insulin among the lower-cost options for people with cost-related barriers, alongside metformin, sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones. Table 9.4 shows that human NPH vials cost less per 1,000 units than degludec, glargine U-300 and most analog pens, and the footnote notes that some retailers sell human insulin at a much lower price. Use these figures only for relative comparison; prices differ by country and change often. The text adds that human insulins, separate, self-mixed or premixed 70/30, are 'often less costly alternatives to insulin analogs'. The trade-off is in Table 9.2: there is a higher risk of hypoglycemia with human insulin (NPH or premixed) than with analogs, and U-100 glargine reduced level 2 and nocturnal hypoglycemia compared with NPH. So when switching from glargine, he needs a dose conversion (often a lower total dose, sometimes split twice daily), closer fasting and nocturnal monitoring, education, and a glucagon prescription (Rec 9.28). Keep the GLP-1 RA if he can afford it, because it limits the insulin dose; if not, prioritize what he can sustain.

distractors.A: Degludec U-100 is a long-acting analog with lower nocturnal hypoglycemia, but it costs more than human NPH (Table 9.4).
distractors.B: Concentrated degludec U-200 is for large dose volumes and costs more than human NPH; it offers no saving.
distractors.C: Insulin detemir has been removed from the market (ADA Section 9), so it is not an option.
distractors.D: Glargine U-300 has a longer action and lower nocturnal hypoglycemia, but it is among the more expensive basal insulins in Table 9.4.

pearls: Lower-cost insulins: human NPH, regular and NPH/regular 70/30 (Rec 9.30).
The price of lower cost is more hypoglycemia than with analogs; prescribe glucagon.
Use Tables 9.3 and 9.4 for relative, not absolute, cost.
explanation.objective: Identify human NPH insulin as the lower-cost basal option and state its main trade-off.

mcq.subtopic: Switching from a high-risk sulfonylurea in CKD
mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years takes glyburide (glibenclamide) 10 mg twice daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Over 2 months he has had four episodes of confusion and sweating, two at night; his wife measured 52 mg/dL (2.9 mmol/L) during one of them. He lives in Al-Ahsa, keeps a small farm and walks a lot. He has no heart failure. You agree an A1C goal of <7.5% (<58 mmol/mol).

BP 136/80 mmHg, BMI 26.8 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which change to his treatment is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue glyburide and add a bedtime snack
Replace glyburide with NPH insulin at bedtime

hints: Two problems coexist: a drug that is a poor choice at his eGFR, and CKD that needs a protective agent.
ADA advises switching to a class with low hypoglycemia risk in people at high risk, and its CKD recommendation applies at his eGFR.

explanation.summary: Glyburide is generally not recommended in CKD and is causing level 2 hypoglycemia; replacing it with an SGLT2 inhibitor removes the hypoglycemia risk and gives kidney and heart protection.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Replace glyburide with empagliflozin. He has recurrent level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL [<3.0 mmol/L]), including nocturnal episodes, on glyburide with an eGFR of 40. Table 9.2 says glyburide is 'generally not recommended in CKD', because its active metabolites accumulate and prolong hypoglycemia. Rec 6.6 and Rec 13.14a advise deintensifying hypoglycemia-causing drugs, or switching to a class with lower hypoglycemia risk, in people at high risk. He also has CKD (eGFR 40, moderately increased albuminuria), so Rec 9.10 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit irrespective of A1C. Empagliflozin does both jobs. It does not cause hypoglycemia, and it slows CKD progression and reduces cardiovascular events. Its glucose-lowering effect is reduced below eGFR 45 (Table 9.2), but his A1C goal of <7.5% leaves room for that. Metformin may continue at a reduced dose (ADA: reduce below 45, stop below 30). He is already on 1,000 mg/day. Teach sick-day rules and hydration, because he works outdoors in a hot climate.

distractors.A: A snack treats the symptom while leaving a drug that is unsuitable in CKD; nocturnal level 2 hypoglycemia will recur.
distractors.B: A lower glyburide dose still carries prolonged hypoglycemia risk in CKD and still gives no kidney protection.
distractors.C: Glimepiride is safer than glyburide in CKD but is still a sulfonylurea with hypoglycemia risk, and it has no kidney or heart benefit.
distractors.D: NPH insulin also causes hypoglycemia, more so than analogs (Table 9.2), and is unnecessary at an A1C below his goal.

pearls: Glyburide: generally not recommended in CKD (Table 9.2).
High hypoglycemia risk → switch to a class with low hypoglycemia risk (Rec 6.6, 13.14a).
CKD with eGFR 20–60 → SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit, irrespective of A1C (Rec 9.10).
explanation.objective: Replace glyburide with an SGLT2 inhibitor in an older adult with CKD and recurrent hypoglycemia.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years attends the diabetes clinic in Dammam because of 6 months of progressive numbness and tingling in both feet and unsteadiness when walking in the dark. He also reports fatigue. He has taken metformin 1,000 mg twice daily for 11 years and empagliflozin 10 mg daily for 2 years. He eats a mixed diet that includes meat and does not drink alcohol.

BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 84/min, BMI 27.1 kg/m². He has conjunctival pallor. Vibration and joint-position sense are reduced at both great toes, the Romberg test is positive and ankle reflexes are absent. He has no neuropathic pain.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Continue metformin and start vitamin B12 replacement
Increase empagliflozin to 25 mg daily and stop metformin
Refer for nerve conduction studies before any treatment
Start pregabalin for diabetic peripheral neuropathy
Stop metformin and replace it with sitagliptin

hints: Read the red-cell indices and the methylmalonic acid together with the pattern of the neurologic signs.
Table 9.2 names this adverse effect of one of his drugs and the action it calls for.

explanation.summary: Macrocytic anemia, low B12, raised methylmalonic acid and dorsal-column signs after 11 years of metformin mean metformin-associated B12 deficiency: replete B12 and keep metformin.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Continue metformin and start vitamin B12 replacement. Long-term metformin reduces ileal absorption of vitamin B12, and the resulting deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and a neuropathy that can mimic or worsen diabetic neuropathy. This man has a macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, MCV 106 fL), a low serum B12 of 142 pg/mL (105 pmol/L) confirmed by a raised methylmalonic acid, and loss of vibration and joint-position sense with a positive Romberg test. Those dorsal-column signs fit B12 deficiency better than a purely length-dependent diabetic polyneuropathy. ADA Table 9.2 lists 'potential for vitamin B12 deficiency: monitor and replete as appropriate' for metformin, the Section 9 text notes that the deficiency can worsen neuropathy symptoms, and Rec 3.10 advises periodic B12 measurement in people on long-term metformin, especially those with anemia or peripheral neuropathy. The deficiency is correctable, so metformin, which is effective, inexpensive and free of hypoglycemia, can continue. Replacement is commonly given parenterally at first when neurologic signs are present, followed by maintenance; recheck the blood count and B12 after repletion and then periodically. Treating promptly matters because neurologic damage from prolonged deficiency may not fully reverse.

distractors.B: Stopping metformin is unnecessary because the deficiency is correctable, and raising empagliflozin to 25 mg adds little glucose lowering while doing nothing for the anemia or neuropathy.
distractors.C: Nerve conduction studies would not change the immediate plan; the laboratory picture already identifies a treatable cause that should be corrected now.
distractors.D: He has no neuropathic pain, and pregabalin treats symptoms without addressing the B12 deficiency that is driving the deficit.
distractors.E: Table 9.2 calls for monitoring and repletion, not withdrawal; sitagliptin is also less effective than metformin at lowering A1C.

pearls: Long-term metformin plus anemia or neuropathy: check B12 (Rec 3.10).
B12 deficiency is not a reason to stop metformin: replete and continue (Table 9.2).
Loss of vibration and proprioception with a positive Romberg test points to B12 deficiency rather than typical diabetic polyneuropathy.
explanation.objective: Recognize metformin-associated vitamin B12 deficiency and manage it by repletion while continuing metformin.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old schoolteacher in Riyadh was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 weeks ago (A1C 7.6% [60 mmol/mol]). She has no cardiovascular, heart failure or kidney disease. Her primary care physician started immediate-release metformin 1,000 mg twice daily from the first day; she takes it on an empty stomach before leaving for work and again at bedtime.

Since starting, she has had bloating, abdominal cramps and four loose stools a day, and she wants to stop the tablets. She has no fever, blood in the stool or weight loss beyond the 1.5 kg she intended.

BP 124/78 mmHg, BMI 31.4 kg/m². Abdominal examination is normal. eGFR is 98 mL/min/1.73 m², and liver enzymes are normal.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Glimepiride 2 mg with breakfast in place of metformin
Immediate-release metformin 2,000 mg once daily at bedtime
Loperamide as needed with the current metformin dose
Metformin extended-release 500 mg with dinner, titrated slowly
Sitagliptin 100 mg each morning in place of metformin

hints: Look at how the drug was started and how she takes it.
Table 9.2 lists three ways to mitigate this adverse effect of metformin.

explanation.summary: Metformin GI intolerance is mitigated by slow titration, an extended-release formulation and taking it with food; restart low and build up.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Metformin extended-release 500 mg with dinner, titrated slowly. Bloating, abdominal discomfort and diarrhea are the principal adverse effects of metformin, and they are dose related and most common when the drug is started at full dose or taken without food, exactly as happened here. ADA Table 9.2 lists three mitigations: slow dose titration, extended-release formulations and administration with food. The Section 9 text adds that the extended-release form can be given once daily. A practical approach is 500 mg of the extended-release form with the evening meal, increasing by 500 mg every 1–2 weeks as tolerated toward an effective dose (the product label allows up to 2,000 mg/day for the extended-release form). Most people who could not tolerate a rapid start of immediate-release metformin tolerate this approach. Metformin remains a reasonable first agent for her: it is effective, weight neutral, inexpensive, widely available and does not cause hypoglycemia. Her obesity (BMI 31.4 kg/m²) also makes weight a treatment goal, so a GLP-1 RA could be discussed as part of person-centered planning, but abandoning metformin after a correctable start-up problem is not justified.

distractors.A: Glimepiride brings hypoglycemia and weight gain, which matter in a woman with obesity, and it abandons a drug whose adverse effect is easily mitigated.
distractors.B: A single 2,000-mg dose of the immediate-release form would worsen GI symptoms; the problem is the dose and the rate of increase, not the time of day.
distractors.C: Loperamide masks the symptom without addressing the cause and keeps her on a full dose she cannot tolerate.
distractors.E: Sitagliptin is less effective than metformin at lowering A1C, and switching ignores the simple mitigations listed in Table 9.2.

pearls: Metformin GI effects: start low, go slow, take with food, consider extended-release (Table 9.2).
Extended-release metformin can be given once daily (Section 9 text).
Most metformin intolerance reflects too rapid a start rather than true intolerance.
explanation.objective: Manage metformin gastrointestinal intolerance with the mitigation strategies listed by ADA.
references: Metformin extended-release US prescribing information (maximum 2,000 mg/day)

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years and albuminuric chronic kidney disease is reviewed in clinic. His medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily (reduced from 1,000 mg twice daily last year), dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, semaglutide 1 mg weekly, losartan 100 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. He has no symptoms and no recent illness, contrast exposure or new drugs.

BP 132/78 mmHg, BMI 29.8 kg/m². His A1C is 7.0% (53 mmol/mol), potassium is 4.8 mmol/L and UACR is 380 mg/g (43 mg/mmol). His eGFR trend is shown; the last two values were measured 4 weeks apart.
mcq.question: Which change to his glucose-lowering regimen is most appropriate now?

options.text: Reduce metformin to 500 mg once daily

hints: Identify the threshold the last two eGFR values have crossed and which drug it applies to.
One of his drugs is contraindicated below this eGFR; the others are continued for organ protection or need no renal adjustment.

explanation.summary: Confirmed eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² means metformin must stop; the SGLT2 inhibitor and semaglutide continue for kidney and cardiovascular benefit.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Discontinue metformin. His eGFR has fallen steadily and is now below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² on two measurements 4 weeks apart (28 and 27), so this is a stable decline rather than an acute dip. ADA Table 9.2 lists metformin as contraindicated with eGFR <30, and the Section 9 text says the dose should be reduced once eGFR is <45 and the drug stopped once eGFR is <30, because very high circulating levels are associated with lactic acidosis, which occurs mainly when eGFR is <30. The US label gives the same instruction (contraindicated below 30), so ADA and the label agree on this step. His dose was appropriately reduced when eGFR fell below 45; reducing it further would not remove the risk. Dapagliflozin should continue: its glucose-lowering effect is now minimal, but Table 9.2 states that an SGLT2 inhibitor can be continued for cardiovascular and kidney benefit until dialysis or transplantation (Rec 11.7a). Semaglutide needs no dose adjustment for kidney function (Table 9.2), has kidney-outcome evidence and is the preferred glucose-lowering agent at eGFR <30 (Rec 9.11). If A1C rises after metformin stops, the semaglutide dose can be increased.

distractors.A: Continuing metformin below eGFR 30 contravenes both ADA Table 9.2 and the label because of the risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis.
distractors.B: Dapagliflozin is continued for kidney and cardiovascular protection even though its glucose-lowering effect is small at this eGFR; ADA allows continuation until dialysis or transplantation.
distractors.D: Semaglutide needs no renal dose adjustment, has kidney-outcome benefit and is the preferred agent when eGFR is <30 (Rec 9.11).
distractors.E: Dose reduction is the step for eGFR 30–45; below 30 metformin is stopped, not reduced further.

pearls: Metformin (ADA): do not start <45, reduce dose <45, stop <30 mL/min/1.73 m².
SGLT2 inhibitors: keep for organ protection after their glucose effect wanes, until dialysis or transplantation.
At eGFR <30 a GLP-1 RA is the preferred glucose-lowering agent (Rec 9.11).
explanation.objective: Apply ADA eGFR thresholds to stop metformin while continuing cardiorenal agents in advancing CKD.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 RAs)
ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Glucose-Lowering Therapy for People With Chronic Kidney Disease'

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 14 years presents to the emergency department with 3 days of vomiting and poor oral intake after a gastroenteritis illness in her household. Two weeks ago she started a very-low-carbohydrate diet to lose weight. She stopped gliclazide when she became unwell but continued metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and empagliflozin 25 mg daily. She does not drink alcohol.

She looks unwell, with deep, rapid breathing and diffuse abdominal tenderness. BP 104/66 mmHg, pulse 112/min, temperature 37.2 °C.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
hints: Classify the acidosis first (anion gap, ketones, lactate), then look at the glucose.
Section 9 warns that up to a third of people who develop ketoacidosis on one of her drugs present with glucose below 200 mg/dL.

explanation.summary: A high anion gap acidosis with β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L, normal lactate and glucose under 200 mg/dL in a person on an SGLT2 inhibitor is euglycemic DKA.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis. She has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.18, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, anion gap 25 mmol/L) with marked ketonemia (β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L) and a normal lactate, so this is ketoacidosis. Her glucose of 196 mg/dL (10.9 mmol/L) does not exclude DKA: SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose by glycosuria, so ketoacidosis can develop with near-normal glucose. ADA Section 9 notes that up to a third of people treated with SGLT2 inhibitors who develop DKA present with glucose <200 mg/dL (<11.1 mmol/L) and, in one study, 71% with glucose ≤250 mg/dL (≤13.9 mmol/L). She has several listed precipitants: a very-low-carbohydrate eating pattern, prolonged poor intake, dehydration and continuation of the SGLT2 inhibitor during illness (Table 9.2: discontinue during critical illness or prolonged fasting; mitigate with sick-day planning). Management is that of DKA, with intravenous fluids and insulin, plus dextrose because glucose is not high, and empagliflozin is stopped. Rec 9.39 asks clinicians to educate at-risk people on the signs of ketoacidosis, provide blood ketone testing and discourage ketogenic eating, and the Section 9 text states that people who have had DKA should not be treated with SGLT inhibition again.

distractors.A: Alcoholic ketoacidosis requires heavy alcohol use, which she denies; her SGLT2 inhibitor and diet explain the ketoacidosis.
distractors.C: Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state requires marked hyperglycemia (usually ≥600 mg/dL [33.3 mmol/L]) and hyperosmolality, with little ketosis; her osmolality is normal.
distractors.D: Lactate is normal, so this is not lactic acidosis despite metformin use and mild acute kidney injury.
distractors.E: Starvation ketosis produces mild ketonemia, usually with bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L; a pH of 7.18 with β-hydroxybutyrate 5.2 mmol/L is far beyond it.

pearls: Normal glucose does not exclude DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor: measure blood ketones and the anion gap.
Precipitants: very-low-carbohydrate diets, prolonged fasting, dehydration, alcohol, acute illness, surgery.
After SGLT2-inhibitor DKA, do not rechallenge with SGLT inhibition (Section 9).
explanation.objective: Diagnose euglycemic DKA in a person taking an SGLT2 inhibitor and distinguish it from other high anion gap acidoses.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'SGLT Inhibition and Risk of Ketosis'

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity presents to the emergency department with 2 days of severe perineal pain and scrotal swelling. He has taken dapagliflozin 10 mg and metformin 1,000 mg twice daily for 8 months.

Temperature 38.9 °C, pulse 118/min, BP 102/64 mmHg. The perineum and scrotum are swollen, red and exquisitely tender, with pain out of proportion to the visible changes, a dusky patch of skin at the base of the scrotum and palpable crepitus.

White cell count is 21,000/µL (21 × 10⁹/L), C-reactive protein 286 mg/L and plasma glucose 268 mg/dL (14.9 mmol/L).
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Continue dapagliflozin; oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and review in 48 hours
Hold dapagliflozin; outpatient scrotal ultrasound later this week
Stop dapagliflozin; IV antibiotics and emergency surgical exploration
Stop dapagliflozin; topical antifungal cream for candidal intertrigo
Stop dapagliflozin; urine culture and oral nitrofurantoin for 5 days

hints: Fever, hypotension, pain out of proportion and crepitus describe a time-critical infection.
Table 9.2 lists a rare but serious perineal infection for this drug class that needs prompt treatment.

explanation.summary: Perineal pain out of proportion, crepitus, skin discoloration and sepsis on an SGLT2 inhibitor indicate Fournier gangrene: stop the drug, give IV antibiotics and arrange emergency surgery.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Stop dapagliflozin; IV antibiotics and emergency surgical exploration. This is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier gangrene). The clues are pain out of proportion to the visible signs, a dusky skin patch, crepitus from gas-forming organisms, fever, tachycardia, borderline hypotension and a marked inflammatory response. ADA Table 9.2 lists Fournier gangrene among SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effects: rare, with 'prompt treatment if suspected'. The condition progresses quickly along fascial planes and carries high mortality, so treatment is immediate: resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering aerobic and anaerobic organisms, and urgent surgical exploration and debridement, usually by urology or general surgery. Imaging must not delay surgery when the clinical picture is clear. Dapagliflozin is stopped, and glucose is managed with insulin while he is acutely ill. Diabetes and obesity are independent risk factors, so the drug is not necessarily the cause; ADA gives no rechallenge advice, but most clinicians would not restart an SGLT2 inhibitor after this complication. Genital mycotic infection, urinary tract infection and urosepsis are the more common SGLT2-inhibitor genitourinary problems and should not be confused with this emergency.

distractors.A: Oral antibiotics and delayed review are dangerous for necrotizing fasciitis, and continuing the SGLT2 inhibitor is inappropriate during sepsis.
distractors.B: Outpatient imaging would delay life-saving surgery; Fournier gangrene is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment.
distractors.D: Candidal intertrigo causes itching and erythema, not fever, crepitus, skin necrosis or sepsis.
distractors.E: A urinary tract infection does not explain crepitus and skin necrosis, and oral nitrofurantoin has no role in septic necrotizing infection.

pearls: SGLT2 inhibitor + perineal pain out of proportion, fever or crepitus = Fournier gangrene until proven otherwise.
Treatment is surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, without delay for imaging.
Common SGLT2-inhibitor genitourinary effects are mycotic infections and UTIs; Fournier gangrene is rare but lethal.
explanation.objective: Recognize Fournier gangrene as a rare SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effect requiring emergency surgical treatment.

mcq.subtopic: Genital mycotic infection on an SGLT2 inhibitor
mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR 640 mg/g [72 mg/mmol]) started dapagliflozin 10 mg daily 5 months ago for kidney protection. She also takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and lisinopril 40 mg daily. Her A1C is 7.3% (56 mmol/mol).

She presents with 4 days of vulval itching and a thick white vaginal discharge. This is her first such episode; she has no history of recurrent genital or urinary infections, is not immunosuppressed and has no fever or urinary symptoms. Examination shows vulval erythema with satellite lesions. Microscopy of the discharge shows budding yeasts and pseudohyphae.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best management?

options.text: Continue dapagliflozin and add indefinite weekly fluconazole prophylaxis
Continue dapagliflozin without antifungal treatment, as the infection is self-limiting
Continue dapagliflozin; treat this episode and advise on genital hygiene
Stop dapagliflozin until the infection clears, then switch to empagliflozin
Stop dapagliflozin permanently and rely on lisinopril for kidney protection

hints: Ask why she is taking the drug and whether she is in the group Table 9.2 says to avoid.
Table 9.2 mitigates this adverse effect with one measure and reserves avoidance for high-risk people.

explanation.summary: A first, uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis in someone taking an SGLT2 inhibitor for albuminuric CKD is treated with standard antifungal therapy and hygiene advice while the drug continues.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Continue dapagliflozin; treat this episode and advise on genital hygiene. Genital mycotic infections are the most common adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors, because glycosuria favors candidal growth. Most episodes are mild, occur early in treatment and respond to standard topical or single-dose oral antifungal therapy. ADA Table 9.2 advises mitigating the risk with genital hygiene and avoiding use in high-risk individuals, such as people with recurrent infections. She is not high risk: this is a first episode, and she has no history of recurrent infection or immunosuppression. The reason she takes dapagliflozin matters. She has CKD with severely increased albuminuria (UACR 640 mg/g), and ADA recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven kidney benefit for people with type 2 diabetes and CKD, independent of glucose control, to slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular events (Rec 9.10, Rec 11.7a). Stopping it for a treatable infection would forgo that benefit. Her clinician should review the episode and reconsider the drug only if infections become recurrent or complicated.

distractors.A: Indefinite prophylaxis is not justified after a single uncomplicated episode and exposes her to unnecessary drug interactions and resistance.
distractors.B: Symptomatic candidiasis should be treated; leaving it untreated prolongs symptoms and risks complications.
distractors.D: Switching within the class does not change the mechanism (glycosuria), and interrupting therapy is unnecessary for an uncomplicated episode.
distractors.E: Permanent withdrawal throws away proven kidney and cardiovascular benefit in albuminuric CKD for a minor, treatable adverse effect; ACE inhibition alone leaves residual risk.

pearls: Genital mycotic infection is the most common SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effect: treat it, give hygiene advice and continue.
Avoid SGLT2 inhibitors in people at high risk (recurrent infections) per Table 9.2.
When an SGLT2 inhibitor is prescribed for organ protection, weigh the size of that benefit before stopping it for a minor adverse effect.
explanation.objective: Manage an uncomplicated genital mycotic infection without sacrificing SGLT2-inhibitor kidney protection.

mcq.subtopic: Sick-day rules with an SGLT2 inhibitor
mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35%) and CKD G3a (eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m²) telephones the clinic. Since early this morning he has vomited four times and has watery diarrhea; he can sip water but keeps little down. He has no abdominal pain or breathlessness.

His medications are empagliflozin 10 mg daily, metformin extended-release 1,000 mg daily, insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime, sacubitril–valsartan, bisoprolol and furosemide 40 mg daily. His home glucose reading is 212 mg/dL (11.8 mmol/L). He has a blood ketone meter.
mcq.question: Which advice about his glucose-lowering medications is most appropriate today?

options.text: Continue all medications at usual doses, with extra fluids and glucose checks
Hold empagliflozin and metformin; continue glargine; check glucose and ketones
Hold glargine and all oral agents until he is eating normally again
Hold glargine only; continue empagliflozin and metformin with glucose checks
Stop empagliflozin permanently and switch to sitagliptin 50 mg daily

hints: Which of his drugs raise the risk of ketoacidosis or acute kidney injury when he cannot drink?
People on insulin need basal insulin even when they are not eating.

explanation.summary: During vomiting and dehydration, temporarily hold the SGLT2 inhibitor and metformin, keep basal insulin, and check glucose and ketones frequently.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Hold empagliflozin and metformin; continue glargine; check glucose and ketones. Acute illness with vomiting and poor intake brings dehydration, ketosis and a risk of acute kidney injury. ADA Table 9.2 tells clinicians to mitigate SGLT2-inhibitor DKA risk with sick-day planning, to discontinue the drug during critical illness or prolonged fasting, and to pay attention to volume status, particularly when ill, adjusting other volume-contracting agents. Holding empagliflozin for the few days he cannot eat or drink therefore lowers his risk of euglycemic DKA and volume depletion. Metformin is held as well: ADA Section 6 advises considering holding metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors when oral intake cannot be maintained or if there is concern for acute kidney injury, Section 9 links very high metformin levels in acute kidney injury to lactic acidosis, and the product label and KDIGO 2022 sick-day guidance also advise temporary withdrawal. Basal insulin should not be stopped: without it, ketosis develops even when he is not eating. The dose is adjusted to his glucose readings. Rec 9.39 supports blood ketone monitoring in at-risk people on SGLT inhibition. He should seek same-day assessment if vomiting persists, ketones rise or he cannot keep fluids down, and should restart empagliflozin and metformin once eating and drinking normally. Empagliflozin is not stopped permanently: it is an important heart failure drug.

distractors.A: Continuing an SGLT2 inhibitor and metformin through vomiting and dehydration increases the risk of euglycemic DKA, volume depletion and acute kidney injury.
distractors.C: Stopping basal insulin during illness invites ketosis and hyperglycemia; illness often raises insulin needs even without food.
distractors.D: This reverses the correct priorities: it removes the insulin that prevents ketosis and keeps the drugs that are risky during dehydration.
distractors.E: Empagliflozin is a foundational therapy for HFrEF (Rec 9.8); a temporary hold during illness is enough, and sitagliptin has no heart failure benefit.

pearls: Sick days on an SGLT2 inhibitor: hold it, hydrate, check ketones, restart when eating and drinking normally.
Never stop basal insulin during illness; adjust it to glucose readings.
Hold metformin when dehydration threatens acute kidney injury.
explanation.objective: Give sick-day advice that temporarily withholds an SGLT2 inhibitor and metformin while continuing basal insulin.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, metformin and lactic acidosis (text)
ADA 2026 Section 6, illness and sick-day management (text)
KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD guideline (sick-day guidance)

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 18 years takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. Her A1C is 8.4% (68 mmol/mol). She would like a medication that also helps her lose weight. She has no cardiovascular disease, heart failure or kidney disease.

For a year she has had early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating and vomiting of undigested food several times a week. Upper endoscopy was normal. A 4-hour gastric emptying scintigraphy study shows 38% retention at 4 hours (reference <10%). She also has peripheral neuropathy.

BP 134/80 mmHg, BMI 33.2 kg/m², eGFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR 18 mg/g (2.0 mg/mmol).
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
hints: The scintigraphy result establishes a diagnosis that changes which drug class is suitable.
Table 9.2 says one class is not recommended in this condition, whatever the route; one remaining option causes weight gain.

explanation.summary: Documented gastroparesis makes GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide unsuitable; an SGLT2 inhibitor lowers glucose with modest weight loss and no effect on gastric emptying.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Empagliflozin 10 mg daily. She has diabetic gastroparesis: typical symptoms, a normal endoscopy and 38% gastric retention at 4 hours. GLP-1 RAs and the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA tirzepatide slow gastric emptying. ADA Table 9.2 states that GLP-1 RAs are 'not recommended for individuals with gastroparesis', and the same concern applies to tirzepatide, which also delays gastric emptying. These drugs would worsen her nausea, vomiting and erratic glucose absorption. The oral formulation of semaglutide acts on the same receptor, so it is no safer. Among the remaining options, an SGLT2 inhibitor offers intermediate-to-high glucose-lowering efficacy, no hypoglycemia on its own, and intermediate weight loss (Table 9.2 and Figure 9.4). It does not act on the gut, although she should be counseled about volume depletion and DKA risk if vomiting episodes become severe or prolonged (sick-day planning). Pioglitazone has high glucose-lowering efficacy but causes weight gain, which conflicts with her stated goal. Management of the gastroparesis itself (small frequent low-fat, low-fiber meals, glycemic control and, if needed, prokinetics) should proceed in parallel.

distractors.A: Dulaglutide is a GLP-1 RA, and Table 9.2 states that GLP-1 RAs are not recommended in gastroparesis; it would worsen her symptoms.
distractors.C: Oral semaglutide has the same gastric-emptying effect as the injectable form, so the route does not avoid the problem.
distractors.D: Pioglitazone lowers glucose effectively but causes weight gain, contrary to her goal.
distractors.E: Tirzepatide also delays gastric emptying and should be avoided in established gastroparesis.

pearls: GLP-1 RAs (and tirzepatide) are not recommended in gastroparesis (Table 9.2).
Oral semaglutide carries the same GI effects as injectable GLP-1 RAs.
SGLT2 inhibitors give modest weight loss without GI slowing, but need sick-day rules.
explanation.objective: Select a non-incretin agent for a person with type 2 diabetes and documented gastroparesis.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (GLP-1 RAs, dual GIP and GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors, pioglitazone)

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity has taken tirzepatide for 6 months (now 10 mg weekly) with metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, losing 14 kg. He presents with 1 day of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting. He does not drink alcohol and takes no other drugs.

Pulse 104/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, temperature 37.6 °C; he has epigastric tenderness without peritonism. Lipase is 1,420 U/L (reference 13–60 U/L), triglycerides 168 mg/dL (1.9 mmol/L), corrected calcium 9.4 mg/dL (2.35 mmol/L), ALT 32 U/L and bilirubin normal. Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder without stones and a common bile duct of 4 mm. CT confirms interstitial edematous pancreatitis.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for his tirzepatide?

options.text: Continue tirzepatide at the current dose once the pain settles
Discontinue tirzepatide and avoid incretin-based drugs in future
Hold tirzepatide and restart at 2.5 mg weekly once lipase normalizes
Switch to semaglutide 0.25 mg weekly after recovery
Switch to sitagliptin 100 mg daily after recovery

hints: Gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia and hypercalcemia have been excluded.
Table 9.2 tells you what to do if pancreatitis is suspected on this class, and Section 9 says which drugs to avoid after pancreatitis.

explanation.summary: Pancreatitis on tirzepatide with no other cause: discontinue it and avoid GLP-1 RAs, tirzepatide and DPP-4 inhibitors thereafter.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Discontinue tirzepatide and avoid incretin-based drugs in future. He meets the criteria for acute pancreatitis (typical pain, lipase more than three times the upper limit and CT findings), and the usual causes have been excluded: no gallstones or duct dilation, no alcohol, triglycerides 168 mg/dL (1.9 mmol/L) and normal calcium. ADA Table 9.2 notes that acute pancreatitis has been reported with GLP-1 RAs and the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA, although causality has not been established, and advises not to initiate these drugs in people at high risk and to discontinue them if pancreatitis is suspected. Having had pancreatitis while taking an incretin drug, he is now at high risk, and the Section 9 text on pancreatic diabetes says incretin medications (GLP-1 RAs, the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA, and DPP-4 inhibitors) should be avoided in people with a history of pancreatitis. Rechallenge with the same drug at a lower dose, or a switch to another incretin, is therefore inappropriate. After recovery, his glucose and weight goals can be met with other options, for example an SGLT2 inhibitor, continued metformin, structured lifestyle support or metabolic surgery, chosen by shared decision-making.

distractors.A: Continuing the suspected culprit contradicts Table 9.2, which advises discontinuation when pancreatitis is suspected.
distractors.C: Restarting at a lower dose is still rechallenge; a history of pancreatitis is a reason to avoid incretin drugs.
distractors.D: Semaglutide shares the GLP-1 receptor mechanism and the same pancreatitis caution; switching within the incretin family is not advised.
distractors.E: DPP-4 inhibitors are incretin-based drugs, and Table 9.2 also lists pancreatitis for them; Section 9 advises avoiding them after pancreatitis.

pearls: Suspected pancreatitis on a GLP-1 RA or tirzepatide: stop the drug (Table 9.2).
After pancreatitis, avoid all incretin drugs: GLP-1 RAs, tirzepatide and DPP-4 inhibitors (Section 9).
Always exclude gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides and calcium; rapid weight loss on these drugs also raises gallstone risk.
explanation.objective: Discontinue incretin-based therapy after pancreatitis and avoid rechallenge with any incretin class.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (GLP-1 RAs, dual GIP and GLP-1 RA, DPP-4 inhibitors)
ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Pancreatic Diabetes and Cystic Fibrosis–Related Diabetes'

mcq.subtopic: GLP-1 RA boxed warning: MTC and MEN2
mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 4 years takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. Her A1C is 8.2% (66 mmol/mol) and BMI 36.0 kg/m². She has no cardiovascular, heart failure or kidney disease, and her eGFR is 105 mL/min/1.73 m².

She asks for a once-weekly injection that would also help her lose weight. Her brother underwent total thyroidectomy for medullary thyroid carcinoma at age 30, and genetic testing showed a pathogenic RET variant consistent with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A. She has not yet been tested herself. Her thyroid examination is normal.
mcq.question: Taking into account the US prescribing information for these agents, which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
hints: Her family history matters more than her preference for a weekly injection.
Her brother's diagnosis appears as a contraindication on several product labels; which drugs does it rule out?

explanation.summary: A family history of MEN2 (or MTC) is a labeled contraindication to all GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide; choose a non-incretin agent such as an SGLT2 inhibitor.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily. The long-acting GLP-1 RAs (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide and extended-release exenatide) and the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA tirzepatide carry a US boxed warning because they caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents; ADA Table 9.2 records 'thyroid C-cell tumors identified in rodents; human relevance not determined' for the class. These labels contraindicate the drugs in anyone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (the short-acting exenatide twice daily and lixisenatide labels carry no boxed warning, but they are not appropriate choices here either). Her brother has MEN2A with a confirmed RET variant, and she has a 50% chance of carrying it, so dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide are all contraindicated, however attractive their weight effects. An SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin adds intermediate-to-high glucose-lowering efficacy with modest weight loss and no hypoglycemia (Table 9.2). Her weight goal can be supported by intensified lifestyle intervention, structured programs or metabolic surgery (Rec 9.19). Independently of her diabetes, she should be referred for genetic counseling and RET testing, because carriers of MEN2A need surveillance or prophylactic thyroidectomy and screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism.

distractors.B: Dulaglutide is a GLP-1 RA with the boxed warning; a family history of MEN2 is a labeled contraindication.
distractors.C: Liraglutide carries the same boxed warning and contraindication; the daily schedule makes no difference.
distractors.D: Semaglutide is contraindicated for the same reason, despite its high efficacy for weight and glucose.
distractors.E: Tirzepatide carries the same C-cell tumor boxed warning and is contraindicated with a family history of MEN2.

pearls: Personal or family history of MTC or MEN2 = no GLP-1 RA and no tirzepatide (labels; Table 9.2 notes the rodent C-cell signal).
Refer at-risk relatives of a RET carrier for genetic counseling and testing.
Non-incretin options with weight benefit: SGLT2 inhibitors (modest), metformin (neutral to modest loss).
explanation.objective: Recognize the MTC/MEN2 contraindication shared by GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide and select an alternative.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (GLP-1 RAs, dual GIP and GLP-1 RA, SGLT2 inhibitors)
US prescribing information for dulaglutide, liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide (boxed warning)

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 16 years had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and insulin glargine 30 units at bedtime. His A1C is 10.4% (90 mmol/mol) and BMI 34.0 kg/m²; eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73 m². You plan to start semaglutide for cardiovascular risk reduction and glucose lowering.

His last retinal examination, 3 years ago, showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular edema; he missed the follow-up appointments. He has no visual symptoms, and visual acuity is 6/9 (20/30) in each eye.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Defer semaglutide and intensify with prandial insulin instead
Prophylactic panretinal photocoagulation before starting semaglutide
Semaglutide started at 2 mg weekly to reach the glycemic goal quickly
Semaglutide started with no additional eye surveillance
Semaglutide with a dilated eye examination now and close retinal follow-up

hints: He has an established indication for the drug, and two features in Table 9.2 put him at higher risk of an eye problem.
Rapid glucose lowering by any route can transiently worsen retinopathy; what does Table 9.2 advise for people in his risk group?

explanation.summary: Semaglutide remains indicated after MI; because he is older, has diabetes ≥10 years, known retinopathy and a high A1C, he needs a retinal examination now and close monitoring during treatment.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Semaglutide with a dilated eye examination now and close retinal follow-up. He has established ASCVD, so a GLP-1 RA with proven cardiovascular benefit is recommended regardless of A1C (Rec 9.7), and semaglutide also provides very high glucose-lowering and weight efficacy. In SUSTAIN-6, subcutaneous semaglutide was associated with more retinopathy complications (HR 1.76) than placebo. Rapid improvement in glycemia, whether from insulin or incretin therapy, can transiently worsen existing retinopathy. ADA Table 9.2 does not tell clinicians to avoid GLP-1 RAs; it advises close monitoring of retinopathy in those at high risk, defined as older individuals and those with longer duration of type 2 diabetes (≥10 years). He meets both criteria, already has moderate nonproliferative retinopathy, has missed 3 years of eye care and is starting from an A1C of 10.4%. The right step is a dilated examination before or as treatment begins, with follow-up during intensification arranged by the eye specialist, and a standard escalation schedule rather than an accelerated one. Table 9.2 also asks clinicians to look for nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy at eye examinations in people on GLP-1 RAs.

distractors.A: Prandial insulin also lowers glucose rapidly, so it does not avoid early worsening of retinopathy, and it forgoes the cardiovascular benefit that is the main reason for semaglutide after MI.
distractors.B: Panretinal photocoagulation treats proliferative or severe disease identified on examination; it is not given prophylactically before a drug.
distractors.C: Starting at 2 mg skips the labeled escalation from 0.25 mg, increasing GI adverse effects and the speed of A1C fall, which is the risk to be avoided.
distractors.D: Table 9.2 specifically calls for close retinopathy monitoring in high-risk people such as this man.

pearls: GLP-1 RA in older people or those with type 2 diabetes ≥10 years: monitor retinopathy closely; do not withhold the drug (Table 9.2). Known retinopathy and a large, rapid A1C fall are added clinical reasons for an eye examination before starting.
Rapid A1C reduction by any means can transiently worsen retinopathy.
Escalate GLP-1 RA doses on the labeled schedule; do not start at the maintenance dose.
explanation.objective: Plan retinal surveillance when starting a GLP-1 RA in a person at high risk of retinopathy worsening.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (GLP-1 RAs: diabetic retinopathy, NAION)

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has taken linagliptin 5 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily for 2 years. His A1C is 7.4% (57 mmol/mol) and eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m².

He presents with 3 weeks of intense itching followed by tense blisters on the trunk and thighs, some on an urticarial base. The oral mucosa is spared. A skin biopsy shows a subepidermal blister rich in eosinophils, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. The dermatologist diagnoses bullous pemphigoid and starts a potent topical corticosteroid.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his diabetes treatment?

options.text: Continue linagliptin; the eruption is unrelated
Continue linagliptin and add oral prednisolone

hints: One of his drugs has a postmarketing association with this blistering disease.
Table 9.2 says what to do if this condition is suspected, and notes that it is reversible.

explanation.summary: Bullous pemphigoid is a recognized DPP-4 inhibitor adverse effect; discontinue the DPP-4 inhibitor and do not substitute another one.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Discontinue linagliptin. Bullous pemphigoid presents in older adults with pruritus, then tense subepidermal blisters, and is confirmed by linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence. DPP-4 inhibitors have been associated with drug-induced bullous pemphigoid in postmarketing reports. ADA Table 9.2 lists bullous pemphigoid among DPP-4-inhibitor concerns, advises discontinuation if it is suspected, and notes that the effect is reversible on discontinuation. The association is a class effect, so switching to another DPP-4 inhibitor would re-expose him. After withdrawal, dermatologic treatment continues, and his glucose-lowering plan is rebuilt around an individualized goal for a 79-year-old, and topical or systemic corticosteroids for the pemphigoid may temporarily raise glucose and need monitoring. Options include continuing metformin (his eGFR of 48 allows it), adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 RA, or a low-hypoglycemia alternative chosen with him.

distractors.A: The temporal association and the known class link make the drug a probable cause; continuing it can perpetuate the disease.
distractors.B: Adding systemic corticosteroids while keeping the probable trigger treats the effect but not the cause, and steroids will worsen his glycemia.
distractors.D: Dose reduction is not an accepted strategy; Table 9.2 advises discontinuation when bullous pemphigoid is suspected.
distractors.E: Bullous pemphigoid is a DPP-4-inhibitor class association, so sitagliptin would re-expose him.

pearls: DPP-4 inhibitors: bullous pemphigoid (discontinue if suspected) and joint pain (consider stopping if debilitating), both reversible (Table 9.2).
The association is with the class, so do not switch within the class.
Systemic corticosteroids for pemphigoid will raise glucose; plan for it.
explanation.objective: Recognize DPP-4-inhibitor-associated bullous pemphigoid and discontinue the class.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes was admitted last month with new heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) due to ischemic cardiomyopathy. He is now euvolemic on sacubitril–valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and furosemide 20 mg daily.

His glucose-lowering medications, unchanged for 3 years, are metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, saxagliptin 5 mg daily and gliclazide modified-release 60 mg daily. He reports no hypoglycemia.

BP 112/70 mmHg, BMI 28.3 kg/m². A1C 7.6% (60 mmol/mol), eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m², potassium 4.6 mmol/L.
mcq.question: Which change to his glucose-lowering regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace saxagliptin with an SGLT2 inhibitor

hints: One current drug has a heart failure signal in Table 9.2, and his heart failure creates an indication for a different class.
Rec 9.8 applies whatever his A1C is.

explanation.summary: In HFrEF, stop saxagliptin (the DPP-4 inhibitor with a heart failure signal) and add an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF benefit.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Replace saxagliptin with an SGLT2 inhibitor. Two principles converge. First, ADA Table 9.2 lists DPP-4 inhibitors as neutral for heart failure with a 'potential risk' for saxagliptin. In SAVOR-TIMI 53, saxagliptin increased hospitalization for heart failure (HR 1.27) although MACE was neutral, so it is a poor choice in someone who has just been hospitalized with HFrEF. Second, Rec 9.8 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven heart failure benefit for people with type 2 diabetes and HF (HFrEF or HFpEF), irrespective of A1C. Table 9.2 lists HF benefit for canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and ertugliflozin, and dapagliflozin and empagliflozin are also standard HFrEF therapy. Replacing saxagliptin with dapagliflozin or empagliflozin removes a drug with a possible HF harm and adds one with proven HF benefit, with a similar net effect on A1C. Metformin can continue, because he is stable and his eGFR is above 30 (Rec 10.45). Gliclazide is CV-neutral; Rec 9.17 asks for its need and dose to be reassessed when the SGLT2 inhibitor is started, to minimize hypoglycemia.

distractors.A: Pioglitazone increases the risk of HF and fluid retention, and Table 9.2 says not to use it in the setting of HF.
distractors.B: An A1C near goal does not remove the indication for an SGLT2 inhibitor in HF (Rec 9.8), and saxagliptin carries an HF signal.
distractors.C: Insulin does nothing for his heart failure, adds hypoglycemia and weight gain, and leaves saxagliptin in place.
distractors.D: Metformin is safe in stable HF with eGFR >30; replacing it with another DPP-4 inhibitor adds no heart failure benefit and keeps the wrong class.

pearls: Saxagliptin: potential HF risk (Table 9.2; SAVOR-TIMI 53 HHF HR 1.27).
Heart failure (reduced or preserved EF) = SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit, regardless of A1C (Rec 9.8).
Metformin may continue in stable HF if eGFR >30 (Rec 10.45).
explanation.objective: Replace a DPP-4 inhibitor with an HF signal by an SGLT2 inhibitor in a person with HFrEF.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, pioglitazone)

mcq.subtopic: Pioglitazone, fluid retention and heart failure
mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension reports 6 weeks of progressive ankle swelling, a 6-kg weight gain and breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs; for the last week she has needed two pillows at night. Nine months ago pioglitazone 45 mg daily was added to metformin 1,000 mg twice daily because of cost. She also takes amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg daily.

BP 146/84 mmHg, pulse 92/min. Jugular venous pressure is raised 5 cm, there are bibasal crackles and pitting edema to the knees. Echocardiography shows LVEF 56%, an enlarged left atrium and elevated filling pressures (E/e′ 16).
mcq.question: In addition to a loop diuretic for congestion, which change to her glucose-lowering regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace pioglitazone with an SGLT2 inhibitor

hints: Amlodipine causes ankle edema, but not a raised JVP, crackles, orthopnea and an NT-proBNP of 2,850 pg/mL.
Table 9.2 says one of her drugs should not be used in this setting, and Rec 9.8 names the class she now needs.

explanation.summary: New HFpEF with fluid retention on pioglitazone: stop the thiazolidinedione (contraindicated in HF) and start an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF benefit.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Replace pioglitazone with an SGLT2 inhibitor. She has new heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: symptoms and signs of congestion, NT-proBNP 2,850 pg/mL, LVEF 56% with raised filling pressures. Amlodipine causes dependent edema but not pulmonary congestion or a raised JVP, and her albumin, kidney function, UACR and TSH exclude other causes of edema. Thiazolidinediones cause renal sodium and water retention, and ADA Table 9.2 lists pioglitazone as carrying an 'increased risk of HF and fluid retention; do not use in setting of HF'. The drug must stop. Dose reduction does not make it acceptable once HF is present. Rec 9.8 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF benefit for adults with type 2 diabetes and HF, explicitly including HFpEF, and empagliflozin and dapagliflozin reduce HF hospitalization in HFpEF. Replacing pioglitazone with an SGLT2 inhibitor therefore treats her heart failure and keeps glucose near goal; the loop diuretic dose may need review once it starts, because SGLT2 inhibitors are also mildly natriuretic (Table 9.2: adjust other volume-contracting agents). If she also has obesity and symptomatic HFpEF, Rec 9.9a adds tirzepatide and Rec 9.9b a GLP-1 RA with demonstrated HF benefit.

distractors.A: Continuing pioglitazone in established HF contradicts Table 9.2 and will perpetuate the fluid retention.
distractors.B: Fluid retention is dose related, but Table 9.2 says not to use pioglitazone at all in the setting of HF.
distractors.D: Rosiglitazone is also a thiazolidinedione with the same fluid-retention mechanism and HF risk.
distractors.E: Saxagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor with a potential HF risk in Table 9.2, and it provides no HF benefit.

pearls: Pioglitazone: fluid retention and HF risk; do not use in HF (Table 9.2). Also fractures, weight gain, bladder cancer caution.
HFrEF or HFpEF in type 2 diabetes: SGLT2 inhibitor with proven HF benefit (Rec 9.8).
Do not attribute congestion with a raised NT-proBNP to amlodipine edema.
explanation.objective: Identify pioglitazone-associated heart failure and replace it with an SGLT2 inhibitor.
references: ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (pioglitazone, SGLT2 inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors)

mcq.subtopic: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia in an older adult with CKD
mcq.stem:
An 81-year-old widow with type 2 diabetes for 20 years lives with her daughter in Riyadh. She has mild cognitive impairment and CKD G3b (eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73 m²). Her medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily and glyburide (glibenclamide) 5 mg twice daily, unchanged for 6 years.

Her daughter reports two episodes of sweating and confusion in the past month, one before lunch and one in the late afternoon; after the second she fell in the bathroom. Her A1C is 6.4% (46 mmol/mol). The daughter brings a week of fingerstick readings.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best change to her treatment?

options.text: Add a mid-morning snack and continue current doses
Reduce glyburide to 2.5 mg twice daily
Replace glyburide with glimepiride 4 mg daily

hints: Compare her A1C with an appropriate goal for an 81-year-old with cognitive impairment, and count the readings below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
Table 9.2 makes a specific statement about this sulfonylurea in CKD, and Section 13 says what to do with hypoglycemia-causing drugs in high-risk older adults.

explanation.summary: Recurrent daytime hypoglycemia with an A1C of 6.4% in a frail older adult with CKD on glyburide: stop the glyburide (deintensify).
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Stop glyburide and continue metformin. The log shows hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL [3.9 mmol/L]) before lunch or before dinner on every day, down to 58 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L), with symptomatic episodes and a fall. This pattern fits a long-acting sulfonylurea acting through the day. Glyburide has active metabolites that accumulate as kidney function falls, and ADA Table 9.2 states that glyburide is 'generally not recommended in CKD'; her eGFR is 36. Her A1C of 6.4% (46 mmol/mol) is well below a reasonable goal for an 81-year-old with cognitive impairment and CKD: Rec 13.7b calls for less stringent goals that prioritize avoiding hypoglycemia. Rec 13.14a advises deintensifying hypoglycemia-causing medications, or switching to a class with low hypoglycemia risk, for older adults at high risk of hypoglycemia. Stopping glyburide removes the cause. Metformin 500 mg twice daily is appropriate at this eGFR (the dose is already reduced for eGFR <45). If glucose later rises above her individualized goal, a low-hypoglycemia agent such as a DPP-4 inhibitor (with renal dose adjustment), a GLP-1 RA or an SGLT2 inhibitor can be added.

distractors.A: A snack treats the symptom while leaving an inappropriate drug and an overly tight A1C in place; hypoglycemia occurs at two different times of day.
distractors.B: Halving the dose keeps a sulfonylurea that Table 9.2 does not recommend in CKD, in a woman whose A1C does not need it.
distractors.C: Glimepiride 4 mg is a substantial dose that still causes hypoglycemia, and her A1C does not justify any secretagogue now.
distractors.D: Insulin would add hypoglycemia risk and burden; metformin is not the cause of her lows.

pearls: Glyburide: generally not recommended in CKD (Table 9.2); avoid it in older adults.
A1C below goal + hypoglycemia in an older adult = deintensify the hypoglycemia-causing drug (Rec 13.14a).
Glipizide or glimepiride, if a sulfonylurea is needed, should be started conservatively (Table 9.2).
explanation.objective: Deintensify a sulfonylurea causing hypoglycemia in an older adult with CKD and an A1C below goal.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old engineer with type 2 diabetes for 2 years takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. His A1C is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol), weight 118 kg and BMI 38.1 kg/m². He has no cardiovascular disease, heart failure, kidney disease, gastroparesis, pancreatitis or personal or family history of thyroid cancer, and his eGFR is 96 mL/min/1.73 m².

After discussion, he says his priority is the add-on medication that will lower both his A1C and his weight the most. Cost is covered by his employer's insurance.
mcq.question: Which of the following agents best meets his priority?
hints: Rank the options by both glucose-lowering efficacy and weight effect in Table 9.2.
Compare the weight-loss tiers in Figure 9.4 with the glucose-lowering ratings in Table 9.2.

explanation.summary: Tirzepatide is rated very high for both glucose lowering and weight loss, the highest of the listed options.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Tirzepatide. ADA Table 9.2 grades the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA tirzepatide as 'very high' for glucose-lowering efficacy and 'very high' for weight loss, without hypoglycemia on its own. The Section 9 text states that tirzepatide and semaglutide have the highest efficacy for both glucose lowering and weight loss, followed by dulaglutide, liraglutide and extended-release exenatide. Figure 9.4 likewise places semaglutide and tirzepatide in the top tier for weight. Adding a GLP-1 RA or the dual agonist to metformin usually lowers A1C by 1% to ≥2%, compared with about 0.7–1.0% (8–11 mmol/mol) for each oral class added to metformin. With obesity (BMI 38.1 kg/m²) present, ADA prioritizes medications that promote weight loss, and weight management is a distinct treatment goal. Dulaglutide is effective but rated lower for weight than tirzepatide; dapagliflozin gives intermediate weight loss with intermediate-to-high glucose efficacy; sitagliptin is intermediate for glucose and weight neutral; and pioglitazone, although highly effective for glucose, causes weight gain. Tirzepatide is started at 2.5 mg weekly and increased by 2.5 mg every 4 weeks (product label), with counseling on GI adverse effects.

distractors.A: Dapagliflozin has intermediate-to-high glucose efficacy and intermediate weight loss, both lower than tirzepatide.
distractors.B: Dulaglutide is effective, but the Section 9 text ranks it below tirzepatide and semaglutide for weight and glucose lowering.
distractors.C: Pioglitazone has high glucose efficacy but causes weight gain, which conflicts with his priority.
distractors.D: Sitagliptin has intermediate glucose efficacy and is weight neutral; DPP-4 inhibitors produce the smallest A1C reductions.

pearls: Highest glucose and weight efficacy: tirzepatide and semaglutide (Table 9.2, Section 9 text).
GLP-1 RA or dual agonist added to metformin: A1C −1% to ≥2%; each oral class: about −0.7–1.0%.
Weight gain: insulin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone. Weight neutral: DPP-4 inhibitors.
explanation.objective: Rank glucose-lowering classes by glycemic and weight efficacy to match a person's stated priority.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Glucose-Lowering Therapy for People With Metabolic Comorbidities' and 'Combination Therapy'

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. Her A1C is 7.9% (63 mmol/mol) and BMI 35.2 kg/m². She uses a combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol–levonorgestrel) and does not plan a pregnancy for at least 2 years.

After shared decision-making, you are starting tirzepatide 2.5 mg weekly, to be increased by 2.5 mg every 4 weeks toward a maintenance dose of 10 mg weekly. She asks whether this affects her contraception.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate contraception advice?

options.text: Add a barrier method until the maintenance dose has been used for 4 weeks
Double the daily pill dose during tirzepatide dose escalation
No change; tirzepatide does not affect oral contraceptive levels
Stop the pill and use a barrier method only for the first week
Switch to semaglutide, which has no effect on oral contraceptives

hints: Think about what tirzepatide does to the stomach and when that effect is greatest.
Section 9 gives a specific time window for a second contraceptive method with this drug.

explanation.summary: Tirzepatide delays gastric emptying most at initiation and after each dose increase and lowers oral contraceptive exposure; add a second (non-oral or barrier) method until the maintenance dose has been used for at least 4 weeks.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Add a barrier method until the maintenance dose has been used for 4 weeks. GLP-1 RAs and the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA slow gastric emptying, which can reduce absorption of oral drugs. The effect is greatest at initiation and after each dose increase and then wanes. ADA Section 9 states that tirzepatide was shown to lower oral contraceptive levels during its period of greatest effect on gastric emptying. People starting or increasing tirzepatide who take oral contraception should therefore use a second form of contraception until the maintenance dose has been reached and used for at least 4 weeks. The US label words this as switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for 4 weeks after initiation and for 4 weeks after each dose escalation. Because she will escalate every 4 weeks, both formulations cover the same period: from the first dose until 4 weeks after she reaches 10 mg. Rec 9.32a asks clinicians to counsel people of childbearing potential on contraception options and on how glucose-lowering drugs affect contraceptive efficacy. GLP-1 RAs may also lower oral contraceptive levels, but less than tirzepatide does. A long-acting reversible method avoids the issue altogether and is a good option to discuss.

distractors.B: Doubling the pill dose is not a validated strategy and increases estrogen exposure without guaranteeing efficacy.
distractors.C: Tirzepatide has been shown to reduce oral contraceptive exposure during initiation and escalation; 'no change' leaves her unprotected.
distractors.D: One week is far too short: the risk lasts through every escalation and for 4 weeks after the maintenance dose is reached, and stopping the pill is unnecessary.
distractors.E: GLP-1 RAs may also lower oral contraceptive levels, though less than tirzepatide; switching drugs does not remove the need for counseling.

pearls: Tirzepatide + oral contraceptive: back-up or non-oral method from initiation until 4 weeks on the maintenance dose (and after any later increase).
The gastric-emptying effect is greatest at initiation and dose escalation.
Counsel everyone of childbearing potential on contraception and drug interactions (Rec 9.32a).
explanation.objective: Counsel a person starting tirzepatide on the need for back-up contraception during initiation and escalation.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Care Considerations for Individuals of Childbearing Potential'
ADA 2026 Table 9.2 (GLP-1 RAs: impact on drug absorption)

mcq.subtopic: Stopping semaglutide before a planned pregnancy
mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 4 years attends with her husband because they want to start a family. She takes semaglutide 1 mg weekly and follows a structured eating plan; she stopped metformin a year ago because of GI symptoms. She has a copper intrauterine device (IUD), which she plans to have removed next month.

BP 118/74 mmHg, BMI 33.0 kg/m². Her A1C is 6.6% (49 mmol/mol), eGFR 110 mL/min/1.73 m² and UACR 12 mg/g (1.4 mg/mmol). She takes no other medications except folic acid, which she started last week.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best plan?

options.text: Continue semaglutide until pregnancy is confirmed, then stop it
Remove the IUD next month and stop semaglutide on the same day
Stop semaglutide 1 week before removing the IUD
Stop semaglutide now and keep the IUD for at least 2 months
Switch to oral semaglutide, which can continue until conception

hints: Semaglutide has a long half-life; the label gives a minimum interval between the last dose and conception.
Rec 9.32b asks the preconception plan to cover a time frame and glycemic goals, not just a stop date.

explanation.summary: Stop semaglutide at least 2 months before conception, keep contraception in place meanwhile, and use insulin if needed to stay at the preconception glycemic goal.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Stop semaglutide now and keep the IUD for at least 2 months. GLP-1 RAs are not approved for use in pregnancy, and ADA Section 15 states that GLP-1 RAs and dual GIP and GLP-1 RAs should be discontinued before pregnancy, with contraception used while taking them. Because of semaglutide's long half-life, the manufacturer's prescribing information recommends stopping it at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy (Section 15). Section 9 adds that individuals planning pregnancy should be counseled that several months are usually needed, both to eliminate the drug and to adjust to therapy approved in pregnancy so that preconception glycemic goals are reached before conception (Rec 9.32b). Her A1C of 6.6% will probably rise after semaglutide stops, so she should keep the IUD for at least 2 more months, monitor glucose, and start insulin if needed to reach the Section 15 preconception goal (A1C <6.5% [<48 mmol/mol] when achievable without significant hypoglycemia) before attempting conception. Folic acid and other preconception care continue. Weight-loss goals are paused rather than abandoned. ADA gives no US washout interval for tirzepatide; this item does not depend on it.

distractors.A: Stopping only at a positive test exposes the embryo during organogenesis to a drug with limited pregnancy safety data; Section 15 advises discontinuation before pregnancy.
distractors.B: Stopping on the day contraception is removed leaves semaglutide circulating during the first weeks of a possible pregnancy and allows no time to reach glycemic goals on pregnancy-compatible therapy.
distractors.C: One week is far shorter than the labeled minimum of 2 months for semaglutide.
distractors.E: Oral semaglutide is the same molecule with the same long half-life and lack of pregnancy safety data; it must also be stopped before conception.

pearls: Semaglutide: stop at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy (label, cited in ADA Section 15).
Keep contraception until the washout is complete and preconception glycemic goals are met.
Insulin is the bridge if glucose rises after an incretin drug is stopped.
explanation.objective: Plan the discontinuation of semaglutide and the preconception glycemic strategy for a woman with type 2 diabetes planning pregnancy.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Care Considerations for Individuals of Childbearing Potential'
ADA 2026 Section 15, preconception counseling (semaglutide ≥2 months, US prescribing information)

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with metastatic melanoma has received pembrolizumab every 3 weeks for 5 months with a good tumor response. He had no history of diabetes; his A1C was 5.4% (36 mmol/mol) before treatment. He presents with 4 days of polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue and a 4-kg weight loss. He has not received glucocorticoids.

He is alert, pulse 98/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, with mild dehydration. BMI 24.0 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best management?

options.text: Hold pembrolizumab and start prednisone 1 mg/kg daily
Metformin and recheck glucose in 2 weeks
Start basal–bolus insulin and continue pembrolizumab
Stop pembrolizumab permanently and start basal insulin

hints: A C-peptide of 0.2 ng/mL at a glucose near 400 mg/dL tells you about β-cell reserve.
Section 9 says the β-cell destruction in this condition is irreversible, and that has consequences for the cancer drug.

explanation.summary: Abrupt insulin-deficient diabetes on an anti-PD-1 drug is ICI-associated autoimmune diabetes: start insulin (basal plus prandial) and continue the checkpoint inhibitor, because the β-cell loss is irreversible.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Start basal–bolus insulin and continue pembrolizumab. Immune checkpoint inhibitors, most often anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) and anti-PD-L1 agents, can trigger an autoimmune diabetes with rapid β-cell destruction (incidence about ≤1%). It can appear from 1 week to 12 months after the first dose. This man fits: a normal A1C before treatment, an abrupt onset (A1C only 7.4% despite glucose of 412 mg/dL [22.9 mmol/L]), early ketosis and an inappropriately low C-peptide of 0.2 ng/mL (0.07 nmol/L) during marked hyperglycemia. A negative GAD65 result does not exclude the diagnosis. Rec 9.33 asks clinicians to assess the immediate need for insulin because of the risk of DKA. The text recommends considering basal insulin when glucose is >250 mg/dL while evaluation proceeds, adding prandial insulin when insulinopenia is confirmed, as it is here, and providing close monitoring and education.
