Because the β-cell destruction is irreversible, ADA states that the ICI should not be discontinued for severe hyperglycemia; lifelong insulin is generally required, and the decision about cancer therapy remains with the oncologist on oncologic grounds. Other immune-related endocrinopathies (thyroiditis, hypophysitis with adrenal insufficiency) should be screened for.

distractors.A: Glucocorticoids do not reverse ICI-associated diabetes, would worsen hyperglycemia, and are not indicated for this immune-related adverse event.
distractors.B: Metformin cannot replace absent insulin secretion; delay risks DKA in a person with ketosis and a very low C-peptide.
distractors.C: A DPP-4 inhibitor depends on residual β-cell function and is inadequate for insulinopenic, ketosis-prone diabetes.
distractors.E: ADA states that the ICI should not be discontinued for severe hyperglycemia, because the β-cell loss is irreversible and stopping would not restore it; basal insulin alone is also insufficient once insulinopenia is confirmed.

pearls: ICI diabetes: abrupt onset, A1C lower than the glucose suggests, ketosis or DKA, low C-peptide; negative antibodies do not exclude it.
Start insulin (basal if glucose >250 mg/dL; prandial if insulinopenic) and continue the ICI (Rec 9.33).
Insulin is usually lifelong; screen for other immune endocrinopathies.
explanation.objective: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated diabetes with insulin while continuing cancer immunotherapy.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Therapeutic Strategies for Individuals Receiving Cancer Treatment'

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old woman with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer carrying a PIK3CA mutation started alpelisib plus fulvestrant 10 days ago. She had prediabetes (A1C 6.0% [42 mmol/mol]) before treatment and BMI 29.4 kg/m².

Her fasting plasma glucose is now 188 mg/dL (10.4 mmol/L) and a random value 236 mg/dL (13.1 mmol/L). She has mild thirst, no nausea or vomiting and no ketonuria. Her eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m², and she has no history of pancreatitis or heart failure. The oncologist wants to avoid interrupting alpelisib.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of her hyperglycemia?
hints: Think about the pathway the cancer drug blocks and what raising insulin levels would do to it.
Rec 9.35a names the first-line agent for this drug-induced hyperglycemia.

explanation.summary: For PI3Kα-inhibitor hyperglycemia, metformin titrated as tolerated is first line; insulin and sulfonylureas are last resorts, and GLP-1 RAs are not recommended.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Metformin, titrated up as tolerated. Alpelisib and inavolisib inhibit the α isoform of PI3K, which also mediates insulin signaling. Blocking it causes insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose output, and hyperglycemia develops in about 60% of treated people, typically within the first 2 weeks. Pre-existing dysglycemia, BMI >25 kg/m² and age >65 years are risk factors, and she has two of them. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia can force dose reduction or discontinuation of a drug that is controlling her cancer, so prompt treatment matters. Rec 9.35a recommends metformin as first-line treatment, uptitrated as tolerated. It lowers hepatic glucose output and does not raise insulin levels. Rec 9.35b reserves insulin for severe hyperglycemia and hyperglycemic crises, because higher insulin levels may reactivate the PI3K pathway and counteract the antitumor effect. The text gives the same caution for sulfonylureas, which raise insulin secretion. GLP-1 RAs should not be used at present because of their uncertain effect on PI3K-inhibitor efficacy and their nausea and vomiting. Pioglitazone or an SGLT2 inhibitor (with ketone monitoring) are second-line options. Rec 3.8 also supports metformin to prevent this hyperglycemia in high-risk people.

distractors.A: ADA advises against GLP-1 RAs for PI3K-inhibitor hyperglycemia because of uncertain effects on antitumor efficacy (they raise insulin secretion) and added nausea and vomiting.
distractors.B: Sulfonylureas raise insulin levels and are a last resort, like insulin, because insulin may reactivate the PI3K pathway.
distractors.C: Insulin is reserved for severe hyperglycemia or crises (Rec 9.35b); she has moderate hyperglycemia without ketosis.
distractors.E: DPP-4 inhibitors have little evidence in this setting, are less effective than metformin, and work by raising insulin secretion.

pearls: PI3Kα inhibitor (alpelisib, inavolisib) hyperglycemia: metformin first (Rec 9.35a).
Insulin and sulfonylureas are a last resort; avoid GLP-1 RAs (Rec 9.35b, text).
Second line: pioglitazone (slow onset) or an SGLT2 inhibitor with ketone monitoring.
explanation.objective: Select metformin as first-line therapy for PI3Kα-inhibitor-induced hyperglycemia and avoid insulin-raising agents.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Therapeutic Strategies for Individuals Receiving Cancer Treatment'

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with PIK3CA-mutated advanced breast cancer has taken alpelisib with fulvestrant for 3 weeks. Metformin was started for hyperglycemia and titrated to 1,000 mg twice daily; higher doses caused diarrhea. Her fasting glucose readings remain 180–220 mg/dL (10.0–12.2 mmol/L) and pre-dinner readings 200–240 mg/dL (11.1–13.3 mmol/L). She has no vomiting, ketones are negative and she eats a normal mixed diet.

She has no history of genital or urinary infections, heart failure, pancreatitis or gastroparesis. Her eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73 m². The oncologist is concerned that the hyperglycemia will force an alpelisib dose reduction.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?

options.text: Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily with ketone monitoring
Glimepiride 2 mg daily with glucose monitoring
Insulin glargine 10 units daily with fasting glucose titration
Liraglutide 0.6 mg daily, escalated weekly as tolerated
Request an alpelisib dose reduction from the oncologist

hints: She has persistent but not crisis-level hyperglycemia on maximum tolerated metformin.
Which classes does ADA's PI3K-inhibitor text say have shown efficacy, and which does it reserve as a last resort?

explanation.summary: When metformin is not enough for PI3Kα-inhibitor hyperglycemia and there is no crisis, add an SGLT2 inhibitor (with ketone monitoring) or pioglitazone, keeping insulin and sulfonylureas as last resorts.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily with ketone monitoring. Her hyperglycemia persists on the maximum tolerated metformin dose, but she has no ketosis, vomiting or hyperglycemic crisis. ADA's text on PI3K-inhibitor hyperglycemia lists pioglitazone (as monotherapy or with metformin, though its slow onset can limit it) and SGLT2 inhibitors as having shown efficacy. With SGLT2 inhibitors, close monitoring is needed because ketoacidosis has been reported. Both work without raising insulin concentrations, which matters because insulin can reactivate the PI3K pathway and counteract the antitumor effect. Insulin and sulfonylureas should be considered only as a last resort (Rec 9.35b reserves insulin for severe hyperglycemia and crises), and GLP-1 RAs should not be used at this time. Adding dapagliflozin therefore controls glucose and protects the cancer treatment. She should receive the education in Rec 9.39: the signs of ketoacidosis, a blood ketone meter, avoidance of very-low-carbohydrate eating, and holding the drug if she becomes unwell or cannot eat. If glucose becomes severe or a crisis develops, insulin is then appropriate.

distractors.B: Sulfonylureas raise insulin secretion and, like insulin, are reserved as a last resort in PI3K-inhibitor hyperglycemia.
distractors.C: Insulin is reserved for severe hyperglycemia and hyperglycemic crises (Rec 9.35b); hers is persistent but not at that level.
distractors.D: ADA advises against GLP-1 RAs for PI3K-inhibitor hyperglycemia because of uncertain effects on drug efficacy and added GI effects.
distractors.E: Uncontrolled hyperglycemia leading to dose reduction is the outcome ADA wants to prevent; effective glucose-lowering options remain.

pearls: PI3Kα-inhibitor hyperglycemia ladder: metformin → pioglitazone or SGLT2 inhibitor (with ketone monitoring) → insulin only if severe or crisis.
Avoid GLP-1 RAs; sulfonylureas are a last resort.
Good glucose control protects the cancer treatment from dose reduction.
explanation.objective: Choose a second agent for PI3Kα-inhibitor hyperglycemia that does not raise insulin levels.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Therapeutic Strategies for Individuals Receiving Cancer Treatment'

mcq.stem: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin 1,000 mg twice daily (A1C 7.0% [53 mmol/mol]) started prednisone 40 mg each morning with breakfast 5 days ago for an exacerbation of interstitial lung disease. The respiratory team plans 4 weeks at this dose, then a taper. He weighs 82 kg, eats three meals a day and has an eGFR of 78 mL/min/1.73 m². He brings 3 days of fingerstick readings.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.text: Morning NPH insulin with the steroid dose

hints: Describe the daily pattern: when is glucose near normal, and when does it peak?
Match the action profile of the insulin to the action profile of morning prednisone.

explanation.summary: Morning prednisone raises glucose from late morning to evening with near-normal fasting values; morning NPH given with the steroid matches that profile.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Morning NPH insulin with the steroid dose. Glucocorticoids cause hyperglycemia mainly through insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose production. ADA Section 9 describes the typical pattern with morning prednisone: glucose rises after the first meal, peaks in the afternoon and evening, and returns toward baseline by the next morning. His readings match this, with near-normal fasting values and peaks of 268–292 mg/dL (14.9–16.2 mmol/L) before dinner. Monitoring only fasting glucose would miss the problem. Rec 9.36 calls for glucose-lowering adjustments that match the specific glucocorticoid plan, with frequent reassessment as the steroid dose changes. Insulin is the most frequently used treatment. ADA Section 16 notes that NPH, which peaks about 4–6 hours after injection, given together with once-daily intermediate-acting steroids such as prednisone, matches the steroid's hyperglycemic effect, in addition to existing oral therapy. The NPH dose should be titrated to pre-dinner readings and reduced in step with the prednisone taper to avoid hypoglycemia. Noninsulin additions are reserved for stable, chronic steroid doses because of their slow onset and limited evidence.

distractors.A: Bedtime glargine mainly lowers fasting glucose, which is already near goal, and risks overnight hypoglycemia while leaving the afternoon peak untreated.
distractors.B: Correction-only insulin reacts after hyperglycemia has occurred and does not anticipate the predictable steroid-driven rise.
distractors.C: SGLT2 inhibitors act too slowly and weakly for a short, high-dose steroid course; ADA reserves noninsulin additions for stable chronic steroid doses.
distractors.E: A DPP-4 inhibitor gives only modest lowering, too little for afternoon values near 300 mg/dL, and takes time to act.

pearls: Morning prednisone: normal fasting glucose, afternoon and evening peak; check readings later in the day.
NPH with the morning steroid dose matches the profile; taper the NPH with the steroid.
Dexamethasone and other long-acting steroids raise glucose for >24 h and may need basal insulin.
explanation.objective: Match insulin therapy to the time course of morning prednisone-induced hyperglycemia.
references: ADA 2026 Section 16, glucocorticoid therapy and NPH insulin (text)

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man has chronic calcific pancreatitis from previous heavy alcohol use; he has been abstinent for 2 years and takes pancreatic enzyme replacement, which controls his steatorrhea. Diabetes was diagnosed a year ago and treated with metformin 1,000 mg twice daily.

He has lost 5 kg unintentionally over 3 months and reports thirst and nocturia. BMI 20.1 kg/m², BP 118/72 mmHg. A1C is 9.2% (77 mmol/mol), fasting glucose 214 mg/dL (11.9 mmol/L), fasting C-peptide 0.6 ng/mL (0.20 nmol/L) (reference 0.8–3.1 ng/mL [0.26–1.03 nmol/L]), eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine ketones trace.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
hints: Weight loss, a low C-peptide and trace ketones in a lean man point to the dominant defect.
Section 9 names a group of drugs to avoid after pancreatitis and says this type of diabetes may need one treatment early.

explanation.summary: Pancreatic (type 3c) diabetes with weight loss and low C-peptide needs early insulin; incretin drugs are avoided after pancreatitis.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Basal insulin. Chronic pancreatitis destroys islets as well as acinar tissue, causing insulin-deficient diabetes, often with loss of glucagon as well. This man is lean (BMI 20.1 kg/m²), is losing weight, has a low C-peptide and trace ketonuria. These are catabolic features of insulin deficiency. ADA Section 9 states that individuals with pancreatic diabetes may require early insulin initiation, and Rec 9.20 and the text support insulin when catabolic features are present. Basal insulin can be started at 10 units/day or 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day and titrated to the fasting goal (Figure 9.5), with prandial insulin added if needed. Because glucagon reserve may also be reduced, he should be taught hypoglycemia recognition and given glucagon. ADA also says that in people with a history of pancreatitis, incretin medications (GLP-1 RAs, the dual GIP and GLP-1 RA and DPP-4 inhibitors) should be avoided, which excludes semaglutide and sitagliptin. An SGLT2 inhibitor would worsen weight loss and raises DKA risk in insulin-deficient diabetes. A sulfonylurea depends on β-cell reserve, which is limited, and adds hypoglycemia risk without addressing catabolism.

distractors.B: SGLT2 inhibitors cause caloric loss and raise DKA risk in insulin-deficient diabetes, both undesirable in a lean, ketotic man.
distractors.C: A sulfonylurea needs functioning β-cells and adds hypoglycemia risk; it does not reliably correct catabolic insulin deficiency.
distractors.D: Section 9 advises avoiding GLP-1 RAs after pancreatitis, and the weight loss they cause is undesirable here.
distractors.E: DPP-4 inhibitors are incretin-based and should be avoided after pancreatitis; they are also too weak for an A1C of 9.2%.

pearls: Pancreatic diabetes: think insulin early, especially with weight loss or low C-peptide.
History of pancreatitis = avoid GLP-1 RAs, tirzepatide and DPP-4 inhibitors (Section 9).
Loss of glucagon reserve can make hypoglycemia more severe; prescribe glucagon.
explanation.objective: Start insulin early in insulin-deficient pancreatic diabetes and avoid incretin therapy after pancreatitis.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Pancreatic Diabetes and Cystic Fibrosis–Related Diabetes'

mcq.stem:
A 21-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis (homozygous F508del), pancreatic insufficiency and BMI 18.9 kg/m² takes elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor and pancreatic enzymes. She follows the high-calorie diet advised by her CF dietitian.

Her annual 75-g oral glucose tolerance test shows a fasting glucose of 104 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L) and a 2-hour glucose of 236 mg/dL (13.1 mmol/L); a repeat test 2 weeks later gives a similar result. Her A1C is 6.1% (43 mmol/mol). She has lost 1.5 kg over 6 months and her lung function has declined slightly.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the recommended treatment?
hints: CFRD is primarily a disease of insulin deficiency in a person who needs to gain weight.
Section 9 makes one treatment recommendation for CFRD; consider which options her nutritional needs and pancreatic disease rule out.

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes is treated with insulin, with pump therapy including AID considered when appropriate.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Insulin. Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes results mainly from insulin deficiency caused by progressive pancreatic fibrosis, with variable insulin resistance during infection and inflammation. It is associated with weight loss, worse lung function and higher mortality, and treatment with insulin improves weight and pulmonary outcomes. ADA Section 9 states that individuals with CFRD should be treated with insulin therapy and that insulin pump therapy, including AID systems, should be considered when appropriate. Her 2-hour OGTT glucose of 236 mg/dL (13.1 mmol/L), confirmed on repeat testing, establishes CFRD even though her fasting glucose and A1C are only mildly raised; A1C underestimates glycemia in CF, which is why the OGTT is the preferred screening test. Treatment usually begins with basal insulin, prandial insulin, or both, according to the glucose pattern, alongside her high-calorie diet. Oral agents are not recommended as first-line therapy: they do not correct the insulin deficiency, and several would worsen her nutrition or GI symptoms. Close collaboration with the CF team and a dietitian experienced in CF is essential.

distractors.A: Acarbose causes GI symptoms, does not correct insulin deficiency, and interferes with the carbohydrate intake she needs.
distractors.B: People with CF need a high-calorie diet; carbohydrate restriction would worsen her nutrition and weight loss.
distractors.D: Metformin does not address insulin deficiency and its GI effects and weight neutrality are undesirable in an underweight person with CF.
distractors.E: Repaglinide depends on residual β-cell function and is not the recommended treatment; ADA recommends insulin for CFRD.

pearls: CFRD = insulin therapy; consider pumps and AID (Section 9).
Do not restrict calories or carbohydrate in CF.
A1C underestimates glycemia in CF; the OGTT is the preferred screening test.
explanation.objective: Treat cystic fibrosis–related diabetes with insulin.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Pancreatic Diabetes and Cystic Fibrosis–Related Diabetes'

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man without previously known diabetes received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 4 days ago. He takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone 20 mg each morning. He is eating normally. A ureteral stent is in place.

His glucose readings over 2 days are 128–146 mg/dL (7.1–8.1 mmol/L) fasting and 210–290 mg/dL (11.7–16.1 mmol/L) in the afternoon and evening. Serum creatinine is falling (2.1 mg/dL [186 µmol/L] today, from 5.0 mg/dL [442 µmol/L] before transplantation), and he has no ketones.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the preferred glucose-lowering treatment now?
hints: Consider drug interactions, speed of action and graft function in the first postoperative week.
Rec 9.37 names the preferred agent and gives a narrower alternative for mild hyperglycemia only.

explanation.summary: In the early post-transplant period, insulin is preferred for hyperglycemia: it acts immediately, does not interact with immunosuppressants and can be adjusted as steroids taper.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Insulin. Hyperglycemia is common immediately after transplantation because of high-dose glucocorticoids, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus impairs insulin secretion), surgical stress and recovering kidney function. Rec 9.37 makes insulin the preferred agent in the postoperative setting for people with PTDM or pre-existing type 2 diabetes, and the Section 9 text gives the same preference for any hyperglycemia in the early postoperative period, as here, where PTDM cannot yet be diagnosed. The text explains why: it has no interactions with transplant medications, acts immediately and may help prevent progression to PTDM, at the cost of hypoglycemia risk. His pattern, with afternoon and evening peaks under morning prednisolone, suits NPH or basal–prandial insulin timed to the steroid, reduced as the steroid dose falls. A DPP-4 inhibitor can be considered only for mild hyperglycemia (Rec 9.37); values up to 290 mg/dL (16.1 mmol/L) are not mild. A formal diagnosis of PTDM is usually deferred until he is stable on maintenance immunosuppression, and the 2024 international consensus favors an OGTT at about 3 months. Noninsulin drugs such as GLP-1 RAs, SGLT2 inhibitors or metformin may suit long-term management later (Recs 9.38a–9.38c).

distractors.A: SGLT2 inhibitors raise the risk of urinary tract infection, which is especially concerning immediately after kidney transplant with a ureteral stent in place, and their glucose effect depends on recovering graft function.
distractors.C: A DPP-4 inhibitor is an option only for mild hyperglycemia (Rec 9.37); his afternoon values up to 290 mg/dL need insulin.
distractors.D: Metformin should not be started with eGFR <45 or unstable graft function because of lactic acidosis risk; his creatinine is still falling.
distractors.E: GLP-1 RAs act slowly, need dose escalation and add GI effects to those of immunosuppressants; they are a long-term option, not an early postoperative one.

pearls: Early post-transplant hyperglycemia: insulin is preferred (Rec 9.37).
A DPP-4 inhibitor is reserved for mild hyperglycemia early on.
Diagnose PTDM later (OGTT at about 3 months) when immunosuppression is stable.
explanation.objective: Select insulin for hyperglycemia in the early postoperative period after solid organ transplantation.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old woman received a living-donor kidney transplant 10 months ago. Posttransplantation diabetes mellitus was diagnosed by OGTT at 3 months. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone 5 mg daily and insulin glargine 14 units at bedtime. She has gained 9 kg since transplantation and wants help with her weight.

She has had two episodes of graft pyelonephritis in the past 6 months, one with urosepsis. Over the past 3 months her eGFR has fluctuated between 38 and 52 mL/min/1.73 m² during episodes of tacrolimus toxicity. She has no gastroparesis, pancreatitis or thyroid cancer history.

BP 134/82 mmHg, BMI 34.1 kg/m².
mcq.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition for long-term glycemic management?
hints: Rule out each option against her infection history, her fluctuating eGFR and her weight goal.
Rec 9.38b names a class for long-term PTDM management because of its additional cardiometabolic benefits.

explanation.summary: For long-term PTDM with obesity, recurrent graft infections and fluctuating eGFR, a GLP-1 RA offers glucose, weight, cardiovascular and kidney benefits without interacting with immunosuppressants.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Semaglutide. Once the early postoperative period has passed, noninsulin therapy can be used for long-term PTDM management, and the choice should reflect the transplanted organ, the immunosuppressant regimen and metabolic needs (Rec 9.38a). Rec 9.38b states that a GLP-1 RA can be considered for its additional cardiometabolic benefits: cardiovascular, kidney, weight and liver. Large retrospective studies have found no negative interaction with immunosuppressants requiring dose changes. Semaglutide suits her post-transplant weight gain, obesity, albuminuria and raised ALT, and may let her reduce or stop glargine. GI adverse effects need watching because they add to those of mycophenolate, and tacrolimus levels should be checked if vomiting or diarrhea occur. The alternatives fit her poorly. SGLT2 inhibitors raise genitourinary infection risk, which ADA highlights in immunosuppressed kidney recipients with prior UTIs, and she has had two graft pyelonephritis episodes. Metformin should not be started with eGFR <45, and her fluctuating graft function is the scenario in which ADA warns of lactic acidosis. Glipizide adds weight gain and hypoglycemia without metabolic benefit, and pioglitazone adds weight gain and fluid retention.

distractors.A: SGLT2 inhibitors increase genitourinary infection risk; with two recent graft pyelonephritis episodes and immunosuppression, ADA advises weighing prior UTI history carefully after kidney transplant.
distractors.B: Sulfonylureas may be used with stable kidney function but add hypoglycemia and weight gain and confer no metabolic benefit beyond glucose lowering.
distractors.C: ADA advises not initiating metformin at eGFR <45 after transplant and warns about lactic acidosis with fluctuating graft function, which is exactly her situation.
distractors.D: Pioglitazone would worsen weight gain and fluid retention, and it does not match her goals.

pearls: Long-term PTDM: a GLP-1 RA can be considered for cardiometabolic benefits (Rec 9.38b); there is no known interaction with immunosuppressants.
SGLT2 inhibitors after kidney transplant: weigh UTI history, especially early with a stent in place.
Metformin after transplant: do not start if eGFR <45; stop if <30; caution with fluctuating graft function.
explanation.objective: Select a GLP-1 RA for long-term PTDM management when other classes are limited by infection risk, graft function or weight.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 17 and has used basal–bolus insulin since, at about 0.4 units/kg/day. She has never had DKA. Her mother was diagnosed with diabetes at 23 and her maternal grandfather at 26; both were initially labeled as having type 1 diabetes.

GAD65, IA-2 and ZnT8 antibodies are negative. A stimulated C-peptide is 1.8 ng/mL (0.60 nmol/L) with a simultaneous glucose of 160 mg/dL (8.9 mmol/L). Her A1C is 7.8% (62 mmol/mol) and BMI 22.0 kg/m². Genetic testing confirms a pathogenic heterozygous HNF1A variant. She is not planning pregnancy and uses an etonogestrel implant.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best next step in her treatment?

options.text: Add metformin to the current basal–bolus insulin regimen
Continue the current basal–bolus insulin regimen unchanged
Low-dose sulfonylurea, with insulin tapered off
Pramlintide added before meals to reduce insulin doses
Stop all glucose-lowering treatment and monitor annually

hints: In this form of monogenic diabetes, the β-cell's response to one drug class is preserved and exaggerated.
Contrast this gene with the MODY gene that needs no treatment at all.

explanation.summary: HNF1A-MODY is highly sensitive to sulfonylureas; switch to a low-dose sulfonylurea and taper insulin with close glucose monitoring.
explanation.correct: Answer: C) Low-dose sulfonylurea, with insulin tapered off. Negative islet antibodies, preserved C-peptide years after diagnosis, a low insulin requirement and diabetes in three generations diagnosed in the 20s are typical of misclassified MODY, now confirmed as HNF1A-MODY. In HNF1A and HNF4A MODY the β-cell defect lies upstream of the KATP channel, so sulfonylureas, which close the channel directly, are particularly effective, often more so than in type 2 diabetes. ADA Section 2 lists sulfonylureas as first-line therapy for HNF1A- and HNF4A-MODY, and Section 9 states that these individuals can be treated with low-dose sulfonylurea therapy, although some eventually need insulin. Section 9 also notes that adding a DPP-4 inhibitor to the sulfonylurea in HNF1A-MODY may improve glycemic variability and goal attainment. A low starting dose is essential because hypoglycemia is common with standard doses. Insulin is tapered while glucose is monitored closely, and many people can stop it completely. Her genetic diagnosis also enables cascade testing of relatives and genetic counseling about the 50% transmission risk.

distractors.A: Metformin is not the targeted therapy for HNF1A-MODY; the gene-specific choice is a sulfonylurea, which may allow insulin to be stopped.
distractors.B: Continuing insulin unchanged ignores the main benefit of the genetic diagnosis: an oral, sulfonylurea-based regimen that is often more effective.
distractors.D: Pramlintide is an adjunct for insulin-treated type 1 or type 2 diabetes and does not exploit the sulfonylurea sensitivity of HNF1A-MODY.
distractors.E: Stopping treatment is correct for GCK-MODY, not HNF1A-MODY, which is progressive and causes complications if untreated.

pearls: HNF1A- and HNF4A-MODY: low-dose sulfonylurea first (Sections 2 and 9); HNF1A may add a DPP-4 inhibitor.
GCK-MODY: no treatment outside pregnancy.
Neonatal diabetes from KCNJ11 or ABCC8 variants: high-dose sulfonylureas.
explanation.objective: Switch a person with HNF1A-MODY from insulin to low-dose sulfonylurea therapy.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young'

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man was found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 128 mg/dL (7.1 mmol/L) and an A1C of 6.6% (49 mmol/mol) at a pre-employment check in Riyadh. Records from 6 years of annual checks show stable fasting values of 117–132 mg/dL (6.5–7.3 mmol/L). His father has had 'mild diabetes' for 30 years without treatment or complications.

BMI 23.1 kg/m², BP 118/72 mmHg. A 75-g OGTT showed a 2-hour glucose only 36 mg/dL (2.0 mmol/L) above the fasting value. Islet antibodies are negative. His primary care physician started metformin 500 mg twice daily 2 months ago; his A1C has not changed. Genetic testing now shows a heterozygous pathogenic GCK variant.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best management?

options.text: Add a low-dose sulfonylurea to metformin
Continue metformin and recheck A1C in 3 months
Start basal insulin at 10 units daily
Stop metformin and give no drug therapy
Switch metformin to sitagliptin 100 mg daily

hints: The glucose sensor in this condition is reset to a higher level, and the body defends that set point.
ADA Section 2 contrasts the therapy for this gene with sulfonylureas for HNF1A- and HNF4A-MODY.

explanation.summary: GCK-MODY causes mild, stable, nonprogressive fasting hyperglycemia with a low complication risk; glucose-lowering drugs are ineffective and unnecessary outside pregnancy.
explanation.correct: Answer: D) Stop metformin and give no drug therapy. Heterozygous inactivating GCK variants raise the glucose set point of the β-cell, so fasting glucose is mildly but stably elevated and nonprogressive (ADA Table 2.7). The 2-hour OGTT rise is small, less than 54 mg/dL (3 mmol/L) per Table 2.7, as here (36 mg/dL [2.0 mmol/L]). Because glucose is regulated normally around a higher set point, glucose-lowering drugs produce little change, as his unchanged A1C on metformin illustrates, and microvascular complications are rare (Table 2.7). ADA Section 2 states that a diagnosis of GCK-MODY allows 'no therapy', and Section 9 refers to Section 2 for monogenic diabetes. Metformin should therefore be stopped. Pregnancy is the main exception: management in a pregnancy affected by GCK-MODY depends on the fetal genotype. He should be reassured, his father can be offered testing (cascade screening), and routine annual surveillance can replace intensive diabetes follow-up.

distractors.A: Sulfonylureas are the treatment for HNF1A- and HNF4A-MODY, not GCK-MODY, where they have little effect and add hypoglycemia risk.
distractors.B: Metformin has not changed his A1C and is unnecessary because GCK-MODY rarely causes complications.
distractors.C: Insulin would not meaningfully lower his set-point glucose and would expose him to hypoglycemia and burden for no benefit.
distractors.E: A DPP-4 inhibitor is equally unnecessary; no drug is indicated outside pregnancy.

pearls: GCK-MODY: mild stable fasting hyperglycemia, 2-h OGTT rise <54 mg/dL (<3 mmol/L), rare microvascular complications: no treatment (Section 2, Table 2.7).
Drugs barely change glucose in GCK-MODY because the set point is defended.
Pregnancy is the exception; management depends on the fetal genotype.
explanation.objective: Recognize that GCK-MODY needs no glucose-lowering therapy outside pregnancy.
references: ADA 2026 Section 2, monogenic diabetes (GCK-MODY: no therapy; Table 2.7)
ADA 2026 Section 9, 'Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young'

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man in Jeddah with type 2 diabetes for 12 years asks about fasting during the coming Ramadan, which starts in 7 weeks; daily fasts will last about 14 hours. He takes linagliptin 5 mg and gliclazide modified-release 30 mg each morning. He has CKD G4 (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m²) and is followed by nephrology.

He has had no hypoglycemia in the past 3 months, monitors his glucose as advised, has no cardiovascular disease and is cognitively intact and independent. He works in an office. His A1C is 7.2% (55 mmol/mol). He fasted last Ramadan without problems and has attended a Ramadan education session.
mcq.question: According to the IDF-DAR 2021 risk stratification, which of the following is the correct risk category and advice?

options.text: High risk: fasting probably unsafe; advise him not to fast
High risk: he may fast safely if gliclazide is stopped
Moderate risk: fasting safety uncertain; may fast with precautions
Low risk: fasting probably safe once gliclazide is stopped
Low risk: fasting probably safe with his usual care

hints: Look for any single element of his history that IDF-DAR treats as high risk on its own.
The categories are low 0–3, moderate 3.5–6 and high >6; can his favorable features offset a high-risk element?

explanation.summary: An eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² alone scores 6.5 in the IDF-DAR 2021 score (and in ADA Table 5.3), placing him in the high-risk group (>6), where fasting is probably unsafe and he should be advised not to fast.
explanation.correct: Answer: A) High risk: fasting probably unsafe; advise him not to fast. The IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines assess fasting risk with a points-based score. The total places a person in one of three groups: low risk (0–3, fasting probably safe), moderate risk (3.5–6, safety uncertain) or high risk (>6, fasting probably unsafe; the person should be advised not to fast). Several single elements carry 6.5 points and therefore make a person high risk on their own. They include eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², impaired hypoglycemia awareness, unstable macrovascular disease, impaired cognitive function and (in ADA Table 5.3) advanced frailty. ADA Section 5 Table 5.3, adapted from IDF-DAR, uses the same cut-offs and also gives 6.5 points for eGFR <30. This man's otherwise favorable profile (A1C 7.2%, no hypoglycemia, a modern sulfonylurea, good monitoring and a smooth previous Ramadan) cannot offset that weighting. ADA Recs 5.32–5.33 endorse a structured pre-Ramadan risk assessment and planning well in advance; IDF-DAR suggests the pre-Ramadan visit ideally 6–8 weeks before Ramadan. If he still chooses to fast after counseling, his decision should be respected and supported with intensive monitoring, medication adjustment, nephrology input and clear rules on when to break the fast.

distractors.B: Removing gliclazide lowers his score only slightly; the 6.5 points for eGFR <30 still put him above 6, so stopping the drug does not make fasting safe.
distractors.C: Moderate risk (3.5–6) would apply only if his score were ≤6; the kidney element alone exceeds that band.
distractors.D: He cannot be low risk with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², whatever his medications.
distractors.E: A good previous Ramadan and a reasonable A1C do not offset the high weighting for advanced CKD.

pearls: IDF-DAR 2021 score bands: low 0–3, moderate 3.5–6, high >6.
Single 6.5-point elements (eGFR <30, impaired hypoglycemia awareness, unstable macrovascular disease, impaired cognition, advanced frailty) mean high risk on their own.
Assess and plan well before Ramadan (ADA Recs 5.32–5.33; IDF-DAR: ideally 6–8 weeks ahead).
explanation.objective: Apply the IDF-DAR 2021 risk score to classify a person with advanced CKD as high risk for Ramadan fasting.
references: IDF-DAR Diabetes and Ramadan Practical Guidelines 2021 (risk score)

mcq.stem: A 51-year-old woman in Makkah with type 2 diabetes for 6 years plans to fast during Ramadan, which begins in 6 weeks. She takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and glibenclamide (glyburide) 5 mg twice daily. Her A1C is 7.0% (53 mmol/mol), she has had no hypoglycemia, her eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m², and she has no complications. Her IDF-DAR risk score places her in the low-risk group, and she has attended Ramadan-focused education.
mcq.question: According to the IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines, which adjustment to her sulfonylurea is most appropriate for Ramadan?

options.text: Continue glibenclamide 5 mg twice daily, taken at iftar and suhoor
Glibenclamide 10 mg once daily at suhoor
Glibenclamide 5 mg once daily at iftar
Insulin glargine in place of glibenclamide
Switch to gliclazide modified-release, taken at iftar

hints: IDF-DAR treats older and newer sulfonylureas differently during fasting.
IDF-DAR found that lowering the dose of one sulfonylurea did not reduce hypoglycemia.

explanation.summary: IDF-DAR 2021 advises avoiding glibenclamide during Ramadan and using a newer sulfonylurea (gliclazide or glimepiride), with a once-daily dose taken at iftar.
explanation.correct: Answer: E) Switch to gliclazide modified-release, taken at iftar. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia that is most likely in the last hours of the fast. The IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines recommend the newer agents (gliclazide, gliclazide MR or glimepiride), which carry a lower hypoglycemia risk. Once-daily dosing is taken at iftar, and the dose is reduced in people whose glucose is well managed; with twice-daily dosing, the iftar dose stays the same and the suhoor dose is reduced. Glibenclamide is long-acting with active metabolites, and IDF-DAR advises that it should be avoided during Ramadan, noting that lowering its dose did not reduce hypoglycemic events. Her low-risk status and A1C of 7.0% make a switch to gliclazide MR at iftar, at a modest dose titrated by glucose readings, the IDF-DAR-concordant choice. ADA Section 5 Table 5.4 differs slightly: for glyburide it offers 'replace with newer-generation sulfonylurea or reduce dose by 50%'. Both sources accept the switch, but only IDF-DAR rejects dose reduction, which is why this question names IDF-DAR. Metformin continues at the same total dose, split between iftar and suhoor.

distractors.A: Keeping glibenclamide at full dose maintains the agent IDF-DAR advises avoiding, with no dose reduction.
distractors.B: A double dose of a long-acting sulfonylurea at suhoor would peak during the fasting day and maximize hypoglycemia risk.
distractors.C: Halving glibenclamide is an option in ADA Table 5.4, but IDF-DAR 2021 advises avoiding glibenclamide because dose reduction did not lower hypoglycemia.
distractors.D: Starting insulin is unnecessary for a low-risk woman at goal and would add hypoglycemia risk and injection burden.

pearls: Ramadan (IDF-DAR 2021): avoid glibenclamide; use gliclazide, gliclazide MR or glimepiride.
Once-daily sulfonylurea: take at iftar. Twice daily: keep the iftar dose, reduce the suhoor dose.
ADA Table 5.4 also allows 'reduce glyburide by 50%'; IDF-DAR does not.
explanation.objective: Adjust sulfonylurea therapy for Ramadan according to IDF-DAR 2021.
references: IDF-DAR Diabetes and Ramadan Practical Guidelines 2021 (sulfonylureas)

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old man in Riyadh with type 2 diabetes takes insulin glargine U-100 40 units at bedtime and metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. His A1C is 7.3% (56 mmol/mol), his fasting readings are 110–130 mg/dL (6.1–7.2 mmol/L) and he has had no hypoglycemia. He has no cardiovascular or kidney disease.

His IDF-DAR risk assessment places him in the moderate-risk group. After counseling, he chooses to fast and agrees to check his glucose several times a day, including before iftar. He will eat suhoor at about 03:30 and iftar at about 18:00.
mcq.question: According to the IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines, which glargine plan is most appropriate for Ramadan?
hints: Basal insulin is given at the start of the eating period so that its lowest-risk hours fall in the fast.
IDF-DAR reduces once-daily basal insulin by a set percentage range.

explanation.summary: IDF-DAR 2021: reduce once-daily basal insulin by 15–30% and take it at iftar; 30 units (a 25% reduction) at iftar fits.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) 30 units at iftar. During Ramadan, the longest period without food is the daytime fast, and hypoglycemia is most frequent in its last few hours. For people with type 2 diabetes on once-daily basal insulin (NPH, detemir, glargine, glargine-300 or degludec), the IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines advise reducing the dose by 15–30% and taking it at iftar. A 25% reduction from 40 units gives 30 units at iftar. The dose is then titrated every 3 days on SMBG: reduce if fasting-period readings are low and increase if they are consistently above target. He must break the fast if glucose falls below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or rises above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L), or if he feels unwell. ADA Section 5 Table 5.4 agrees on timing for glargine U-100 (at the beginning of the fast-breaking meal); its suggested 25–35% reduction is worded for people who are not well managed, so the dose in this item follows IDF-DAR. The sources differ for glargine-300 and degludec: ADA says no timing change is needed, whereas IDF-DAR still advises iftar dosing. Metformin continues unchanged, split between iftar and suhoor.

distractors.A: A 50% reduction is more than IDF-DAR advises for once-daily basal insulin in type 2 diabetes and risks marked hyperglycemia; it is used for the evening dose of twice-daily basal regimens.
distractors.C: Giving basal insulin at suhoor places its effect over the fasting day; IDF-DAR advises iftar dosing.
distractors.D: The timing is right, but the full dose ignores the recommended 15–30% reduction for the reduced intake.
distractors.E: An unreduced dose given at suhoor combines the two errors and maximizes daytime hypoglycemia risk.

pearls: Ramadan basal insulin (IDF-DAR 2021, type 2): reduce 15–30%, give at iftar.
Break the fast if glucose <70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or >300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L), or if unwell.
ADA Table 5.4: no timing change for glargine-300 or degludec; IDF-DAR: iftar.
explanation.objective: Adjust once-daily basal insulin dose and timing for Ramadan according to IDF-DAR 2021.
references: IDF-DAR Diabetes and Ramadan Practical Guidelines 2021 (basal insulin)

mcq.subtopic: Ramadan: SGLT2 inhibitor (IDF-DAR 2021 vs ADA Table 9.2)
mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man in Dammam with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric CKD (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR 120 mg/g [14 mg/mmol]) has taken empagliflozin 10 mg each morning for 2 years and metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. His A1C is 7.1% (54 mmol/mol). He takes no diuretic, works in an air-conditioned office and has never had DKA or a genital infection.

Ramadan starts in 3 weeks. His IDF-DAR risk score is in the low-risk range, he has attended Ramadan education, and he intends to fast.
mcq.question: According to the IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines, what is the best advice about his empagliflozin during Ramadan?

options.text: Halve the dose and take it at suhoor before the fast
Same dose at iftar, with extra fluids overnight
Same dose at suhoor, before the fast begins each day
Stop it for the whole month and restart after Eid
Switch to sitagliptin for the month, then switch back

hints: He is already established on the drug, and his risk is low.
Contrast IDF-DAR's advice for someone already established on an SGLT2 inhibitor with ADA Table 9.2's wording on 'prolonged fasting'.

explanation.summary: IDF-DAR 2021 continues an established SGLT2 inhibitor during Ramadan at the same dose, taken at iftar, with generous fluids in the non-fasting hours.
explanation.correct: Answer: B) Same dose at iftar, with extra fluids overnight. SGLT2 inhibitors carry a low hypoglycemia risk but cause glycosuria, natriuresis and some volume contraction, so the concerns during a daytime fast are dehydration and, rarely, ketoacidosis. The IDF-DAR 2021 practical guidelines advise no dose change during Ramadan, taking the dose at iftar, and drinking extra fluids during non-fasting hours. They also advise starting these drugs at least 2–4 weeks before Ramadan, not during it, and taking care with loop diuretics, older age and kidney impairment. ADA Section 5 is consistent: guidelines do not advise any change in SGLT2-inhibitor dose during fasting but advise against starting the drug close to fasting, and Table 5.4 lists no dose change. Studies in Ramadan have not shown significant changes in kidney function, dehydration or ketosis. ADA Section 9 Table 9.2 tells clinicians to discontinue SGLT2 inhibitors during prolonged fasting to mitigate DKA risk; for Ramadan, the guideline named in this question (IDF-DAR) continues the drug with these precautions. He should still know the DKA warning signs and hold the drug and break the fast if he becomes unwell or dehydrated.

distractors.A: There is no basis for halving the dose, and suhoor dosing puts the peak diuretic effect in the fasting day.
distractors.C: Taking it at suhoor puts the diuretic effect in the fasting day, when he cannot drink; IDF-DAR advises iftar dosing.
distractors.D: Stopping for a month interrupts kidney-protective therapy; IDF-DAR advises continuing an established SGLT2 inhibitor in a low-risk person, although ADA Table 9.2 mentions holding during prolonged fasting.
distractors.E: Switching drugs forgoes the kidney and cardiovascular benefit; a DPP-4 inhibitor is not a substitute for organ protection.

pearls: Ramadan + established SGLT2 inhibitor (IDF-DAR 2021): same dose, at iftar, extra fluids; do not start during Ramadan.
ADA Table 9.2: hold in 'prolonged fasting'; ADA Section 5 and IDF-DAR: no dose change in Ramadan.
Break the fast and hold the drug if unwell, dehydrated or ketotic.
explanation.objective: Advise on continuing an SGLT2 inhibitor during Ramadan according to IDF-DAR 2021, recognizing the contrast with ADA Table 9.2.
references: IDF-DAR Diabetes and Ramadan Practical Guidelines 2021 (SGLT2 inhibitors)
ADA 2026 Section 5, religious fasting (text) and Table 5.4

mcq.subtopic: SGLT inhibition and ketoacidosis risk mitigation
mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years is lean (BMI 22.8 kg/m²) and has become progressively insulin deficient; a recent fasting C-peptide was 0.4 ng/mL (0.13 nmol/L), and islet antibodies are negative. He takes insulin glargine 18 units daily, metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, which was added 1 year ago for albuminuria (UACR 90 mg/g [10 mg/mmol]). His A1C is 7.4% (57 mmol/mol).

He tells you he is about to start a ketogenic diet (less than 20 g of carbohydrate a day) that a colleague recommended for losing 'belly fat' and cutting his insulin. He has never had DKA.
mcq.question: Which of the following is the best advice?

options.text: Advise against the diet; DKA education and a blood ketone meter
Approve the diet and halve the glargine dose from tomorrow
Approve the diet and stop metformin while he follows it
Approve the diet, with daily urine glucose testing as monitoring
Stop glargine while he follows the diet, with glucose checks

hints: Combine three facts: an SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin deficiency and a very-low-carbohydrate diet.
Rec 9.39 lists three actions for people at risk of DKA on SGLT inhibition.

explanation.summary: An insulin-deficient person on an SGLT2 inhibitor is at risk of DKA; discourage ketogenic eating, educate on ketoacidosis and provide blood β-hydroxybutyrate testing (Rec 9.39).
explanation.correct: Answer: A) Advise against the diet; DKA education and a blood ketone meter. ADA Section 9 notes that people with type 1 diabetes and those with insulin-deficient type 2 diabetes are at increased risk of DKA on SGLT inhibitors. This man's long duration, lean build and low C-peptide put him in that group. Very-low-carbohydrate eating, prolonged fasting, dehydration and excess alcohol are listed precipitants: the diet lowers insulin requirements and promotes ketogenesis, and the SGLT2 inhibitor keeps glucose deceptively low, so ketoacidosis can develop with near-normal glucose. Rec 9.39 asks clinicians to educate at-risk people on the risks and signs of ketoacidosis and how to mitigate them, to provide appropriate tools for ketone measurement (serum β-hydroxybutyrate), and to discourage a ketogenic eating pattern. Because dapagliflozin is giving kidney benefit, the better course is to keep it with these safeguards and redirect his weight goal to a balanced reduced-energy eating plan, reviewing insulin doses as his intake changes. If he insists on the diet, stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor would be the safer trade-off. Cutting or stopping basal insulin in an insulin-deficient person would precipitate DKA.

distractors.B: Halving basal insulin while adding a ketogenic diet to an SGLT2 inhibitor increases DKA risk in an insulin-deficient person.
distractors.C: Metformin is not the concern here; the dangerous combination is SGLT2 inhibition, insulin deficiency and carbohydrate restriction.
distractors.D: Glycosuria is constant on an SGLT2 inhibitor, so urine glucose tells him nothing; blood β-hydroxybutyrate is the recommended measurement.
distractors.E: Stopping basal insulin in insulin-deficient diabetes, particularly with an SGLT2 inhibitor, is a classic route to DKA.

pearls: SGLT inhibition + insulin deficiency + ketogenic diet = high DKA risk.
Rec 9.39: educate on DKA, provide β-hydroxybutyrate testing, discourage ketogenic eating.
Never stop basal insulin in insulin-deficient diabetes; after SGLT2-inhibitor DKA, do not rechallenge.
explanation.objective: Apply Rec 9.39 to mitigate DKA risk in an insulin-deficient person taking an SGLT2 inhibitor.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9, 'SGLT Inhibition and Risk of Ketosis'

mcq.subtopic: Weight-based starting dose and basal:bolus split
mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man with type 1 diabetes since age 12 arrived in Jeddah yesterday to start a new job. His luggage, including his insulin pens and records, was lost in transit. He was using insulin glargine once daily and insulin lispro with meals but cannot recall any doses. His last insulin was a lispro dose 30 hours ago and glargine about 40 hours ago. He feels well apart from thirst.

On examination, he is alert and well hydrated. Weight is 70 kg, BMI 22 kg/m². He has no symptoms or signs of ketoacidosis.
mcq.question: Which multiple-daily-injection plan is the most appropriate starting prescription for him?

options.text: Insulin glargine 6 U once daily and insulin lispro 2 U before each meal
Insulin glargine 18 U once daily and insulin lispro 6 U before each meal
Insulin glargine 28 U once daily and insulin lispro 2 U before each meal
Insulin glargine 35 U once daily and insulin lispro 12 U before each meal
Insulin glargine 50 U once daily with no mealtime insulin

hints: He is a metabolically stable adult with long-standing type 1 diabetes and unknown doses: start from a weight-based total daily dose.
ADA quotes a typical weight-based starting dose for a metabolically stable adult, and a usual basal share of that total.

explanation.summary: For a metabolically stable adult with type 1 diabetes, start about 0.5 U/kg/day (35 U for 70 kg), about half as basal (~18 U glargine) and the rest split over meals (~6 U each).
explanation.correct: Answer: B. He has established type 1 diabetes with absent β-cell function, so he needs basal and prandial insulin at once (Rec 9.1); delay risks ketoacidosis. ADA 2026 Section 9 states that total daily insulin needs in type 1 diabetes usually range from 0.4 to 1 U/kg/day. It cites the ADA/JDRF Type 1 Diabetes Sourcebook figure of 0.5 U/kg/day as a typical starting dose for metabolically stable adults, with about one-half as prandial and one-half as basal insulin. For 70 kg this gives about 35 U/day: glargine about 18 U and lispro about 6 U before each of three meals (36 U in total, 0.51 U/kg). Table 9.1 gives a basal share of 30–50% of the total daily dose for MDI. The doses are then titrated using glucose monitoring, ideally CGM, and once he has seen the diabetes team and relearned carbohydrate counting he can return to ratio-based dosing (Rec 9.3). The lower range of 0.2–0.6 U/kg/day that ADA quotes for newly diagnosed people (partial remission) does not apply after 16 years of disease.

distractors.A: About 12 U/day (0.17 U/kg) is far below the 0.4–1 U/kg/day usually needed in established type 1 diabetes and would leave him hyperglycemic and at risk of ketosis.
distractors.C: The total (34 U) is reasonable, but 82% of it is basal. That exceeds the usual 30–50% basal share and invites overnight and between-meal hypoglycemia, with meals under-covered.
distractors.D: About 71 U/day (1.0 U/kg) is the top of the usual range and is too much as an empiric start in a lean, metabolically stable adult. It risks severe hypoglycemia.
distractors.E: Basal-only treatment does not meet Rec 9.1 for type 1 diabetes, and 50 U of basal insulin alone is excessive and dangerous.

pearls: Type 1 diabetes: total daily dose usually 0.4–1 U/kg/day; typical start for a stable adult 0.5 U/kg/day.
Basal is about 30–50% of the total daily dose; the rest is prandial and correction insulin.
Newly diagnosed people (partial remission) often need only 0.2–0.6 U/kg/day.
explanation.objective: Calculate a safe weight-based starting MDI plan for a metabolically stable adult with type 1 diabetes.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Insulin Therapy (total daily dose 0.4–1 U/kg/day; 0.5 U/kg/day starting dose)

mcq.subtopic: Fasting hyperglycemia on MDI: basal titration from CGM
mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years reviews her 14-day CGM report. She takes insulin glargine U-100 20 U at 10 PM and insulin aspart by carbohydrate ratio (1 U per 10 g) with a correction factor of 1 U per 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) above 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). She eats dinner at 7:30 PM and breakfast at 7:30 AM, does not snack after dinner, and gives no insulin overnight. Her carbohydrate counting was checked by a dietitian last month and is accurate. She has no hypoglycemia symptoms. A1C is 7.6% (60 mmol/mol).

The AGP (exhibit) shows a stable glucose in range from bedtime until about 3 AM, then a steady rise to a pre-breakfast median of about 195 mg/dL (10.8 mmol/L). Post-meal rises return to baseline within 3–4 hours.
mcq.question: Which change is most appropriate now?

options.text: Add an aspart correction dose at 3 AM
Increase the dinner aspart dose by 2 U
Move insulin glargine from 10 PM to 7 AM
Raise the insulin glargine dose by about 10%
Switch insulin glargine to bedtime NPH insulin

hints: Ask when the rise begins relative to the last meal bolus, and which insulin is the only one acting at that hour.
ADA's MDI algorithm says fasting hyperglycemia should prompt review of the overnight pattern and a small-step change to the insulin acting at that time.

explanation.summary: A rise that starts about 7 hours after the dinner bolus, with no snacks and no lows, is a basal problem: raise glargine by about 10% (20 U to 22 U) and reassess.
explanation.correct: Answer: D. Figure 9.2 (type 1 diabetes on MDI) says that fasting hyperglycemia should prompt review of the overnight pattern, using CGM if available, and adjustment of basal insulin when appropriate. Hyperglycemia is corrected with small steps (for example 10% dose changes), reassessed as often as once or twice weekly. Here glucose is flat and in range until 3 AM, about 7 hours after the dinner bolus and well after the dinner aspart has stopped acting, and then rises steadily to about 195 mg/dL (10.8 mmol/L) before breakfast. There is no snack, no nocturnal hypoglycemia (TBR 1%, 0% <54 mg/dL), and post-meal rises come back to baseline, so the prandial doses are well matched. The only insulin acting between 3 and 7 AM is the basal dose, so the cause is too little basal insulin for the early-morning rise in insulin need. Raising glargine by about 10% (to 22 U) and repeating the CGM review in a few days is the causal fix. ADA notes (Table 9.1) that long-acting analogs may not cover a strong dawn phenomenon as well as pump therapy; if titration fails without causing nocturnal lows, an insulin pump or AID system (preferred by ADA) is the next consideration.

distractors.A: A scheduled 3 AM correction is a reactive fix. It disrupts sleep and treats the number rather than the basal deficit.
distractors.B: Dinner aspart acts for about 3–5 hours. Increasing it would lower glucose in the late evening, when it is already in range, and would not reach the 3–7 AM rise.
distractors.C: Glargine U-100 lasts about 24 hours at this dose. Moving it to the morning does not increase the amount of basal insulin acting overnight, and on the day of the change the two doses overlap.
distractors.E: NPH given at bedtime peaks overnight and causes more nocturnal hypoglycemia than long-acting analogs (Table 9.1). Analogs are preferred in type 1 diabetes (Rec 9.2).

pearls: Pre-breakfast rise that starts hours after the dinner bolus, with no snack or lows, means basal titration.
Adjust insulin in small steps (about 10%) and reassess once or twice weekly (Figure 9.2).
Long-acting analogs may not cover a strong dawn phenomenon as well as a pump (Table 9.1).
explanation.objective: Attribute fasting hyperglycemia on MDI to basal insulin by reading the overnight CGM pattern, and titrate the basal dose.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Insulin Therapy (basal dose titrated to overnight and fasting glucose)

mcq.subtopic: Prandial dose arithmetic: carbohydrate ratio and correction factor
mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old man with type 1 diabetes uses insulin degludec once daily and insulin aspart with meals. His settings are:
• Insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio: 1 U per 10 g
• Correction (sensitivity) factor: 1 U lowers glucose by 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L)
• Premeal glucose target: 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L)

Before lunch his CGM and a fingerstick both read 220 mg/dL (12.2 mmol/L), with a flat trend arrow. He plans to eat a lunch containing 60 g of carbohydrate. His last aspart dose was at breakfast 5 hours ago. He does not plan to exercise this afternoon.
mcq.question: Which aspart dose should he give before lunch?
hints: Calculate the meal dose and the correction dose separately, then add them.
The correction dose covers only the glucose above target, divided by the sensitivity factor.

explanation.summary: Meal dose 60 g ÷ 10 = 6 U; correction (220 − 120) ÷ 40 = 2.5 U; total 8.5 U.
explanation.correct: Answer: C. ADA Rec 9.3 asks that most adults with type 1 diabetes be taught to match mealtime insulin to carbohydrate intake and to add a correction dose based on current glucose and trend. Table 9.1 describes MDI mealtime and correction insulin as rapid-acting analog dosed from the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR), the insulin sensitivity factor (ISF) and the glucose target. The calculation has two parts. The meal (carbohydrate) dose is 60 g ÷ 10 g/U = 6 U. The correction dose is (current glucose − target) ÷ ISF = (220 − 120) ÷ 40 = 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5 U; in SI units, (12.2 − 6.7) ÷ 2.2 ≈ 2.5 U. The total is 8.5 U. Insulin on board does not need to be subtracted, because his last aspart dose was 5 hours ago, beyond the usual action time of a rapid-acting analog, and the trend arrow is flat. If the trend were rising or falling, Rec 9.3 supports a small adjustment for glycemic trend. Table 9.1 adds the rule for adjusting settings: change the ICR only if post-meal glucose is consistently out of target despite accurate counting, and change the ISF or target if corrections do not consistently bring glucose into range.

distractors.A: 6.0 U covers the carbohydrate only and ignores the 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) above target.
distractors.B: 7.0 U results from correcting only to 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) instead of the 120 mg/dL target: 6 + 1 U.
distractors.D: 11.0 U doubles the correction (100 ÷ 20 = 5 U instead of 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5 U), plus the 6 U meal dose. It risks hypoglycemia 2–4 hours after lunch.
distractors.E: 11.5 U divides the whole glucose value (220 ÷ 40 = 5.5 U) rather than the excess over target, a common arithmetic error.

pearls: Prandial dose = carbohydrate grams ÷ ICR + (glucose − target) ÷ ISF, minus active insulin if any.
Change the ICR for consistent post-meal errors; change the ISF or target for failed corrections (Table 9.1).
Education in carbohydrate counting and correction dosing is a grade B recommendation (Rec 9.3).
explanation.objective: Calculate a mealtime insulin dose from the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio, sensitivity factor and target.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 22 years reports 4 months of erratic glucose values with frequent unexplained hypoglycemia, sometimes 2–3 hours after a meal dose and sometimes overnight. She takes insulin glargine 26 U at bedtime and insulin lispro by carbohydrate ratio, all with pens and 4-mm needles. She has not changed her diet, activity or doses. She admits she injects "in the same comfortable spots" around the umbilicus because it hurts less there. CGM shows a coefficient of variation of 44% with time below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) of 8%.

On examination, there are two soft, smooth, raised areas about 4–5 cm across on either side of the umbilicus, with reduced sensation. Thyroid function, morning cortisol, celiac serology and kidney function are normal. A1C is 7.4% (57 mmol/mol).
mcq.question: Which is the best next step in management?

options.text: Change insulin glargine to insulin degludec
Lengthen the pen needle from 4 mm to 8 mm
Rotate injections away from the affected areas

hints: Her examination finding explains both the variability and the lows; what does she do every day that created it?
ADA explains what causes this examination finding and what it does to insulin absorption; ask which option removes the cause rather than changing the drug or the device.

explanation.summary: Repeated injection into the same sites has caused lipohypertrophy, which makes absorption erratic; rotate into healthy tissue and watch for hypoglycemia as absorption improves.
explanation.correct: Answer: D. The soft, smooth, raised periumbilical areas are lipohypertrophy: an accumulation of subcutaneous fat caused by the local adipogenic action of insulin at a site of repeated injections. ADA 2026 (Insulin Administration Technique) states that lipohypertrophy contributes to erratic insulin absorption, increased glycemic variability and unexplained hypoglycemic episodes, exactly her pattern (CV 44%, TBR 8%). People using insulin should be taught proper site rotation and how to recognize and avoid lipohypertrophic areas, and Table 4.1 makes examination of injection sites and assessment of technique part of every comprehensive evaluation. Injecting into healthy tissue usually improves absorption, so the same doses may act more strongly: she should increase glucose monitoring (her CGM helps) and reduce doses if lows appear in the first days. Her other causes of hypoglycemia (adrenal, thyroid, celiac, kidney) have been excluded. Changing insulin products, devices or needle length does not fix a problem caused by where she injects.

distractors.A: A flatter basal analog does not correct absorption from lipohypertrophic tissue, which also affects her prandial lispro.
distractors.B: ADA recommends 4-mm needles for all ages and body types; longer needles raise the risk of intramuscular injection and do not solve lipohypertrophy.
distractors.C: Pump infusion sites can also develop lipohypertrophy. Education and rotation come first; a device change skips the cause.
distractors.E: Insulin antibodies are a rare cause of erratic glucose. The examination already shows a common, reversible explanation.

pearls: Lipohypertrophy: soft, smooth, raised areas several centimetres across, causing erratic absorption and unexplained lows.
Examine injection sites at every comprehensive visit (Table 4.1).
After moving to healthy tissue, the same dose may act more strongly: monitor and lower doses if needed.
explanation.objective: Recognize lipohypertrophy as a cause of glycemic variability and hypoglycemia and manage it with site rotation and education.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Insulin Administration Technique

mcq.subtopic: Needle length and inadvertent intramuscular injection
mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes plays football at a club most afternoons. He takes insulin glargine 18 U every morning after breakfast and insulin aspart with meals. Over 2 months he has had several episodes of hypoglycemia (CGM 48–60 mg/dL [2.7–3.3 mmol/L]) within 1–3 hours of his morning glargine on training days, and also on some rest days. He injects glargine into the front of the thigh with 8-mm pen needles at 90 degrees without a skin pinch, and he notes occasional stinging and small bruises at the site. He eats the same breakfast daily and carbohydrate counting is accurate.

On examination, BMI is 19.5 kg/m² and he is very muscular, with little subcutaneous fat on the thighs. Injection sites show no lipohypertrophy. A1C is 7.1% (54 mmol/mol); TSH and morning cortisol are normal.
mcq.question: Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Add a 15-g carbohydrate snack before every injection
Change from insulin pens to vial and syringe
Inject with the 8-mm needle at 90 degrees into the deltoid
Switch to a 4-mm pen needle and use the abdomen or buttocks

hints: Stinging, bruising and early lows after a long-acting insulin suggest the insulin is not going where it should.
ADA names three factors that raise the risk of inadvertent intramuscular injection. How many apply to him, and which option changes them?

explanation.summary: A lean athlete injecting with 8-mm needles into the thigh is injecting intramuscularly; switch to 4-mm needles and truncal sites to restore predictable subcutaneous absorption.
explanation.correct: Answer: E. ADA 2026 (Insulin Administration Technique) states that insulin should be injected into subcutaneous tissue, not muscle. Absorption from intramuscular sites differs from subcutaneous absorption and is influenced by muscle activity, so inadvertent IM injection causes unpredictable absorption and is associated with frequent, unexplained hypoglycemia. The risk is higher in younger, leaner people, with injections into limbs rather than truncal sites (abdomen, buttocks), and with longer needles. He has every risk factor: lean, muscular thighs, 8-mm needles at 90 degrees without a pinch, and stinging and bruising, which suggest IM placement. Lows within 1–3 hours of a long-acting analog fit fast IM absorption, made worse by exercising the injected muscle. ADA recommends 4-mm pen needles across ages and body types to reduce IM delivery; short needles work as well as longer ones and are better tolerated, including in people with obesity. Moving to the abdomen or buttocks adds a further margin. If lows persist once technique is corrected, the dose can then be reviewed.

distractors.A: Routine snacks treat the symptom, add calories and leave absorption unpredictable.
distractors.B: The delivery device is not the problem; syringe needles are also longer than 4-mm pen needles.
distractors.C: In a lean, muscular young man the deltoid is another limb site with a high IM risk, especially with an 8-mm needle.
distractors.D: A fixed dose cut ignores the cause; with IM injection, absorption remains erratic and he could become hyperglycemic on other days.

pearls: Use 4-mm pen needles for all ages and body types, including obesity.
IM risk: young, lean people; limbs; longer needles.
Unexplained lows plus stinging or bruising at the site suggest IM injection.
explanation.objective: Identify inadvertent intramuscular insulin injection as a cause of unexplained hypoglycemia and correct needle length and site.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Insulin Administration Technique (4-mm needles; IM injection risk)

mcq.subtopic: Choosing an insulin delivery system: AID
mcq.stem:
A 37-year-old software engineer with type 1 diabetes for 20 years takes insulin glargine 22 U at night and insulin lispro by carbohydrate ratio, and has used CGM for 3 years. Over 6 months he has had nocturnal hypoglycemia 2–3 times a week, despite two reductions of his glargine dose, with daytime highs after each reduction. He had one episode of severe hypoglycemia last month and now has reduced awareness of lows. He counts carbohydrates well and is keen to use technology. His insurer covers diabetes devices.

CGM (14 days): TIR 70–180 mg/dL 54%, TAR 181–250 mg/dL 30%, TAR >250 mg/dL 8%, TBR 54–69 mg/dL 6%, TBR <54 mg/dL 2%, GMI 7.5% (58 mmol/mol), coefficient of variation 41%. A1C is 7.3% (56 mmol/mol).
mcq.question: Which is the best next step for him?

options.text: Conventional insulin pump without sensor integration
Insulin pump with predictive low-glucose suspend only
Switch insulin glargine to insulin degludec

hints: Compare his CGM metrics with the Section 6 goals: is the problem only lows, only highs, or both?
Table 9.1 ranks delivery systems by time in range and time below range.

explanation.summary: AID systems should be offered to adults with type 1 diabetes and are the preferred delivery method; they give the highest time in range and lowest time below range.
explanation.correct: Answer: B. Rec 9.27 says automated insulin delivery should be offered to all adults with type 1 diabetes on insulin, according to needs and preferences, and Section 7 (Rec 7.25a) makes AID the preferred insulin delivery method over MDI, conventional CSII and sensor-augmented pumps. ADA's Section 9 text states that AID systems are superior to sensor-augmented pumps with low-glucose suspend or predictive low-glucose suspend for increasing time in range and reducing hypoglycemia, and Table 9.1 ranks systems: TIR highest and TBR lowest with hybrid closed loop, then low-glucose suspend, then sensor-augmented open loop, then conventional CSII. He misses both CGM goals (Rec 6.3b and 6.3c: TIR >70%, TBR <4% and <1% below 54 mg/dL), has had severe hypoglycemia, and each manual basal cut has caused highs, exactly the problem an algorithm that raises and lowers insulin delivery every few minutes solves. He is numerate, motivated and covered, so he can use AID safely. Glucagon (Rec 9.28) and hypoglycemia-awareness education should also be reinforced.

distractors.A: Pramlintide is an approved adjunct but lowers A1C only modestly (0.3–0.4%) and adds hypoglycemia risk unless prandial insulin is reduced; it does not address nocturnal lows.
distractors.C: A pump without sensor integration gives flexible basal rates but the smallest gains in TIR and TBR of the pump options in Table 9.1.
distractors.D: Predictive low-glucose suspend reduces nocturnal lows but cannot raise insulin delivery for highs; AID is superior for time in range.
distractors.E: Degludec or glargine U-300 may cause slightly less hypoglycemia than glargine U-100, but this will not fix both his highs and lows as AID can.

pearls: Offer AID to all adults with type 1 diabetes on insulin (Rec 9.27); it is the preferred delivery method (Rec 7.25a).
Table 9.1: hybrid closed loop > low-glucose suspend > sensor-augmented open loop > conventional CSII for TIR and TBR.
CGM goals: TIR >70%, TBR <70 mg/dL <4%, TBR <54 mg/dL <1%.
explanation.objective: Select automated insulin delivery for an adult with type 1 diabetes who has both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia on MDI with CGM.

mcq.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes on insulin degludec and insulin aspart (MDI) and CGM has needle fatigue. She asks to replace her mealtime aspart injections with inhaled insulin, which she has read about online. She has had mild intermittent asthma since childhood and uses an albuterol (salbutamol) inhaler a few times a year, most recently 2 months ago. She has never smoked. Spirometry done for a work medical 6 months ago showed a normal FEV1.

A1C is 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) with TIR 72%.
mcq.question: Which is the best response to her request?

options.text: Inhaled insulin after a repeat baseline spirometry confirms a normal FEV1
Inhaled insulin, as she has never smoked and her asthma is mild
Inhaled insulin with spirometry repeated after 6 months of use
Switch mealtime aspart to regular human insulin given by pen

hints: Which lung conditions does ADA list as contraindications to inhaled insulin, regardless of severity?
Spirometry is required before and after starting, but it does not override a contraindication.

explanation.summary: Inhaled insulin is contraindicated in chronic lung disease such as asthma or COPD, however mild; she should continue injectable prandial insulin.
explanation.correct: Answer: A. Rec 9.1 allows prandial insulin to be injected or inhaled, and Rec 9.2 lists inhaled insulin with analogs as preferred over injectable human insulin. Inhaled insulin is regular human insulin in monomer form with a faster onset and shorter duration than rapid-acting analogs. However, ADA 2026 (Alternative Insulin Routes) states that it can reduce lung function (FEV1), is contraindicated in people with chronic lung disease such as asthma and COPD, and is not recommended for people who smoke or who recently stopped smoking. Everyone needs spirometry (FEV1) before starting and after starting it. Asthma, even mild intermittent asthma with a normal FEV1, is a chronic lung disease, so inhaled insulin is not an option for her. Her needle fatigue can be addressed in other ways: 4-mm pen needles and technique review, a connected pen (Rec 7.23), or an insulin pump or AID system, which reduces injections to one infusion-set change every few days. ADA describes clinically meaningful A1C reductions with inhaled insulin, but in the Affinity 1 trial it was noninferior, not superior, to injectable aspart for A1C; its advantages are timing, weight and less hypoglycemia.

distractors.B: Spirometry is required before starting, but a normal FEV1 does not remove the contraindication of asthma.
distractors.C: Never smoking removes one exclusion, but chronic lung disease of any severity remains a contraindication.
distractors.D: Follow-up spirometry is part of monitoring once treatment is allowed; it does not make treatment safe in asthma.
distractors.E: Regular human insulin by injection does not solve needle fatigue and, per Rec 9.2, analogs are preferred to injectable human insulin.

pearls: Inhaled insulin: contraindicated in asthma and COPD; not recommended in current or recent smokers.
Spirometry (FEV1) before and after starting inhaled insulin.
Inhaled insulin acts faster and shorter than rapid-acting analogs; in Affinity 1 its A1C effect was noninferior, not greater, vs aspart.
explanation.objective: Recall the pulmonary contraindications and monitoring requirements for inhaled insulin.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Alternative Insulin Routes

mcq.subtopic: SGLT2 inhibitors in type 1 diabetes: euglycemic DKA
mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 10 years presents to the emergency department with 1 day of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and malaise. Six weeks ago a private weight-loss clinic started empagliflozin 10 mg daily. Since then she has followed a very-low-carbohydrate diet and reduced her insulin glargine from 24 U to 16 U and her lispro doses by about a third "to avoid lows". She drinks no alcohol and has no diarrhea. Her home meter readings have been 150–200 mg/dL (8.3–11.1 mmol/L).

On examination, she is tachypneic, pulse 112 beats/min, BP 108/66 mmHg, with dry mucous membranes.
mcq.question: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bicarbonate loss from the gastrointestinal tract
Diabetic ketoacidosis associated with SGLT2 inhibition

hints: Compute the acid–base picture first: is this a high anion gap acidosis, and what are the measured unmeasured anions?
Check the lactate and the ethanol level, then ask how her new medication and her very-low-carbohydrate diet change the usual glucose picture of ketoacidosis.

explanation.summary: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with β-hydroxybutyrate 5.1 mmol/L and glucose <200 mg/dL in a person with type 1 diabetes on an SGLT2 inhibitor is euglycemic DKA.
explanation.correct: Answer: C. She has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.21, bicarbonate 12, anion gap 22) with marked ketonemia (β-hydroxybutyrate 5.1 mmol/L) and normal lactate, so this is ketoacidosis. ADA 2026 (SGLT Inhibition and Risk of Ketosis) states that people with type 1 diabetes are at increased risk of DKA with SGLT inhibitors: it occurs in about 4% of users, 5–17 times the risk of those not treated. SGLT2 inhibitors are not approved for type 1 diabetes. Risk factors include very-low-carbohydrate eating, prolonged fasting, dehydration and excess alcohol, and up to a third of people with SGLT2 inhibitor-associated DKA present with glucose <200 mg/dL (<11.1 mmol/L), which delays diagnosis. Cutting her insulin by a third removed the remaining brake on ketogenesis. Management follows the DKA protocol (fluids, IV insulin with dextrose because glucose is near normal, potassium), and the drug should be stopped. ADA states that people who have had DKA should not be treated with SGLT inhibition again, and Rec 9.39 asks for education, ketone-measuring tools and discouragement of ketogenic diets for anyone at risk who is treated with these drugs.

distractors.A: She drinks no alcohol and ethanol is undetectable; the drug, diet and insulin cuts explain the picture.
distractors.B: Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss gives a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis; her gap is 22 and she has no diarrhea.
distractors.D: Lactate is normal (1.4 mmol/L); the anion gap is explained by ketones.
distractors.E: Starvation ketosis causes mild ketonemia and at most a slight fall in bicarbonate; a pH of 7.21 with β-hydroxybutyrate 5.1 mmol/L in type 1 diabetes is DKA.

pearls: SGLT inhibitor DKA in type 1 diabetes: about 4% of users, 5–17-fold higher risk; SGLT2 inhibitors are not approved for type 1 diabetes.
Up to a third present with glucose <200 mg/dL: measure ketones when unwell.
After SGLT inhibitor-associated DKA, do not restart SGLT inhibition.
explanation.objective: Diagnose euglycemic DKA in a person with type 1 diabetes treated off-label with an SGLT2 inhibitor and identify its precipitants.
references: ADA 2026 Section 9 text, SGLT Inhibition and Risk of Ketosis
ADA 2026 Section 9 text, Noninsulin Treatments for Type 1 Diabetes

mcq.stem: A 35-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 18 years uses an automated insulin delivery system. Her A1C is 7.4% (57 mmol/mol) with TIR 66%, and most time above range comes from glucose peaks 1–2 hours after meals. Her BMI has risen to 29 kg/m² over 5 years. She asks whether a noninsulin medication could be added to her insulin to help with post-meal peaks and weight. She has no history of DKA, gastroparesis or pancreatitis.
mcq.question: According to ADA 2026, which noninsulin agent is approved for use with insulin in adults with type 1 diabetes?
hints: Separate the agents ADA describes as approved for type 1 diabetes from those approved only for type 2 diabetes or for other indications.
One of the options is specifically contraindicated in type 1 diabetes because of DKA.

explanation.summary: Pramlintide, an amylin analog, is the noninsulin adjunct approved for adults with type 1 diabetes; it lowers A1C about 0.3–0.4% with 1–2 kg weight loss.
explanation.correct: Answer: D. ADA 2026 (Noninsulin Treatments for Type 1 Diabetes) states that pramlintide, based on the β-cell peptide amylin, is approved for adults with type 1 diabetes.
